At a temperature around $200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the racemisation of pinene can be followed in the gaseous phase by measuring the optical rotation.

If, for example, you take the (+)-enantiomer of $\alpha$-pinene

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1985-4-fig1.png

an equilibrium is gradually established between the two enantiomers (optical isomers). The two opposing reactions are both of the first order.

In 1927 D. F. Smith obtained the following data in his study of racemisation of $\alpha$-pinene:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} T/\mathrm{K} & \alpha_1 & \alpha_2 & t/\mathrm{min} \\ \hline 490.9 & 32.75 & 18.01 & 579 \\ 490.9 & 29.51 & 15.59 & 587 \\ 503.9 & 30.64 & 8.74 & 371 \\ 505.4 & 12.95 & 8.05 & 120 \\ 510.1 & 23.22 & 6.15 & 216 \end{array}$$

$\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ are the values for optical rotation in terms of the dimensions of the polarimeter scale; $t$ is the time which has elapsed between the two measurements.

Problems:

4.1 What is the value for the equilibrium constant for the racemisation? What is the corresponding value of $\Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ$ (racemisation)? What is the relationship between the forward and backward rate constants, $k_1$ and $k_{-1}$, in a state of dynamic equilibrium?

4.2 State the rate equation for the racemisation of pinene. Derive a relationship which could be used to calculate the rate constant for the conversion of the (+)-enantiomer into the (−)-enantiomer using the data given in the table.

4.3 Calculate the rate constant for this reaction at the four temperatures given in the table.

4.4 Calculate the average value of the activation energy for this reaction. You should take the average of the values at a minimum of three temperatures or use a graphical method.

HINT: If the loss of concentration of a substance obeys the rate equation:

$$-\frac{\mathrm{d}c}{\mathrm{d}t} = k\,(2c - \mathit{constant})$$

Then the dependence of concentration on time is given by:

$$\ln\frac{2c_0 - \mathit{constant}}{2c - \mathit{constant}} = 2kt$$

where $c_0$ is the initial concentration at time $t = 0$.

$$\mathbf{A} + \ce{OH-} \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftarrows}} \mathbf{M} + \ce{H2O} \qquad \text{the first reaction step}$$

$$\mathbf{M} + \mathbf{A} \xrightarrow{k_1} \mathbf{B} \qquad \text{the second reaction step}$$

The rate of the formation of substance $\mathbf{B}$ is given by the equation:

$$v = k_2\,[\mathbf{M}]\,[\mathbf{A}] \qquad (1)$$

8.2 In the beginning of the reaction the reaction mixture contained 1 mmol of glucose-6-phosphate. Calculate the amounts of glucose-6-phosphate, glucose-1-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate in the mixture at equilibrium. (As the reaction take place in a constant volume, the ratio of the amounts of substances equals that of their concentrations.)

problems.title: [Platinum(II) complexes with antitumour activity]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [Platinum(II) complexes with antitumour activity]

Compounds containing divalent platinum with the general formula $\ce{PtX2(amine)2}$ (X = $\ce{Cl2}$, $\ce{SO4^{2-}}$, malonate, etc.) have met a lot of scientific interest because of their biological activity, particularly in view of their properties in the treatment of tumours. The best known compound used clinically is $\ce{PtCl2(NH3)2}$. This compound, in which platinum is coordinated in a planar square, has two geometrical isomers of which only one shows the antitumour activity.

1.1 Sketch the spatial structures of the two possible isomers.

1.2 How many isomers has $\ce{PtBrCl(NH3)2}$? Sketch all of them.

It is possible to replace the amine ligands by one ligand containing two donor atoms (N). Then one obtains a chelating ligand, such as 1,2-diaminoethane (en).

1.3 Show graphically that $\ce{PtBrCl(en)}$ has only one stable structure.

The ligand en can be substituted via methylation to form dmen or pn (racemic).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1986-1-fig1.png

1.4 Give spatial structures of all isomers of the following compounds: $\ce{PtCl2(dmen)}$, $\ce{PtCl2(pn)}$, $\ce{PtBrCl(dmen)}$ and $\ce{PtBrCl(pn)}$.

These compounds can isomerise in aqueous solution through dissociation of a ligand and transient replacement of the stronger ligands by the weak ligand water. $\ce{Cl-}$ and $\ce{Br-}$ are replaced relatively easily, but it is more difficult to replace the amine ligands, which usually requires heating.

1.5 Considering each of the isomers in the previous questions a-d, indicate which Isomers can be converted to another at room temperature. Give both the original molecule and the products.

1.6 $\ce{PtCl2(en)}$ reacts with $\ce{Br-}$ in a molar proportion of 1:2 at room temperature. Which compound would you expect to form in what proportion? You can assume that the Pt-Br and Pt-Cl bonds are equally strong and that there is no perturbing influence from hydrolysis.

1.7 Using the equation to express chemical equilibrium, show that hydrolysis hardly ever occurs in blood but that it does occur in the cells. Note: $\ce{PtCl2(NH3)2}$ hydrolyses to and 2 $\ce{Cl-}$. In cells the $\ce{Cl-}$ concentration is low; in blood it is fairly high.

After hydrolysis in the tumour cell a reactive platinum ion is formed to which two $\ce{NH3}$ groups are still bound, as it was found in the urine of patients treated with this compound. The reactive platinum ion appears to be bound to cellular DNA, where the bonding occurs via guanine to one of the N-atoms.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1986-1-fig2.png

As a result of the two reactive sites of platinum and the two unreactive $\ce{NH3}$ ligands, it can form additionally a second bond to DNA. Research has shown that this happens in particular with a second guanine base from the same strand of DNA.

1.8 Show by calculations which of the two isomers in question a) can form this bond. (Note: Pt-N distance = $210\,\mathrm{pm}$, DNA base distance = $320\,\mathrm{pm}$).

problems.title: [Triphosphates in detergents]
problems.problem:
Problem 2. [Triphosphates in detergents]

The compound $\ce{Na5P3O10}$ is used as an additive for detergents to bind the $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ ions present in water in order to prevent the precipitation of their fatty acid salts on the laundry.

2.1 Draw the structure of the ions $\ce{(P3O10)^{5-}}$ and $\ce{(P3O9)^{3-}}$ assuming that P-P bonds do not occur.

2.2 Assuming an octahedral coordination of the $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ ion give a drawing of the $\mathrm{Mg(P_3O_{10})(H_2O)_n)^{3-}}$ ion also indicating the value for n.

The complex ions of $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ and triphosphate are well soluble in water. They are, among other things, responsible for the wild growth of algae in surface waters. They could be removed by precipitation as an insoluble compound.

2.3 Give some possibilities (ions) to precipitate the triphosphates bound to $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ or $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$.

2.4 Calculate the mass of $\ce{Na5P3O10}$ (in grams) necessary in a washing machine to reduce the amount of $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ in 20 litres of city water ($0.225\,\mathrm{g/l}$) to an acceptable maximum of $0.02\,\mathrm{g/l}$. Effects of pH, the precipitation of $\ce{Ca(OH)2}$, and possible effects by other positive ions, can be neglected. The following data is given:

$$K_1 = \frac{[\ce{Ca^{2+}}][\ce{P3O10^{5-}}]}{[\ce{CaP3O10^{3-}}]} = 1.0\times10^{-6}$$

Molar mass of $\ce{Na5P3O10}$ is $366\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, the molar mass of Ca is $40\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

problems.title: [Colour of dyes and the particle-in-a-box model]
problems.problem:
Problem 3. [Colour of dyes and the particle-in-a-box model]

In order to explain why dyes are coloured, they can be considered as rod-like, one-dimensional molecules over which the electrons are distributed. The wave lengths of the electrons should fit to the available space which is the length $l$. When absorbing light, an electron makes a transition from a lower to a higher energy state. The energy difference is given by:

$$\Delta E = h\times \mathit{coverlambda} \quad \text{where} \quad \lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$

[The term printed as "coverlambda" presumably stands for $c/\lambda$.]

3.1 Give a general expression for possible wavelengths of the electron as a function of the length $l$.

In the 'particle in the box' model, only the variations in the kinetic energy of the electrons are considered.

3.2 Give an expression for the possible energies that electrons in the molecule can have (as a function of $l$).

3.3 Show that for a chain of length $l$ with $k$ electrons, the longest wavelength absorption occurs at:

$$\lambda = \frac{8mcl^2}{h(k+1)} \quad \text{for even values of } k$$

3.4 Derive an expression for the wavelength of the first electronic transition as a function of the number of C-atoms for even values of n.

3.5 Calculate the minimum number of C-atoms (conjugated systems) to obtain a visible colour. C-C bond length is $142\,\mathrm{pm}$.

The retina in the human eye contains rhodopsin, a light absorbent.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1986-3-fig1.png

The molecule in the part of C-atoms 7 through 12 is planar. The angle between the bonds C5-C6, C7-C8, C11-C12 and C13-C14 is about 39°. According to the 'particle in the box' theory fragment C7 through C12 should absorb at about $213\,\mathrm{nm}$. In reality the absorption of retinal occurs at $308\,\mathrm{nm}$.

3.6 Give a reason for the longer wavelength that is observed in practice using the above mentioned theories.

3.7 When retinal is bound to opsin to form rhodopsin, the absorption occurs around $600\,\mathrm{nm}$. Which atoms must be forced into one plane by the protein? Show by calculation that it's true.

problems.title: [Intramolecular catalysis of amide hydrolysis]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [Intramolecular catalysis of amide hydrolysis]

The high efficiency of catalysis by enzymes is mainly due to an enzyme-reactant complex in which the reacting group is placed in a favourable position for the reaction with respect to the catalyzing groups of the enzyme. Studies are carried out with model compounds in which a catalyzing group has been introduced in the proximity of the reaction centre of the molecule. As an example we consider the hydrolysis of the amide bond in compound $\mathbf{A}$. This reaction proceeds in water at $39\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and pH = 2 more than a million times faster than the hydrolysis of compound $\mathbf{B}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1986-4-fig1.png

The relation between the rate constant $k_\mathrm{hyd}$ and pH for the hydrolysis of $\mathbf{A}$ at $39\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is shown in figure below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1986-4-fig2.png

Further observation:

Addition of water to the iso-imide $\mathbf{C}$ gives a rapid reaction, which initially yields $\mathbf{A}$. Subsequently, hydrolysis of $\mathbf{A}$ occurs. The amid carbonyl group in $\mathbf{A}$ is labelled with $\ce{^{13}C}$ and the hydrolysis is allowed to take place in $\ce{H2^{18}O}$ at pH = 2 and $39\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The diacid formed upon hydrolysis is isolated, converted into a disilver salt and completely decarboxylated with bromine in a anhydrous reaction medium. The carbon dioxide formed is a mixture of particles of masses 44, 45, 46 and 47 which are formed in equal amounts.

4.1 Why is the hydrolysis of $\mathbf{A}$ so much faster than that of $\mathbf{B}$?

4.2 Explain why the rate of hydrolysis of $\mathbf{A}$ is independent on pH in the range between pH = 0 to pH = 2.

4.3 Why does $k_\mathrm{hyd}$ decrease so rapidly at pH values higher than 3.

4.4 Give a detailed reaction mechanism for the hydrolysis of $\mathbf{A}$. Indicate which step in the reaction is rate determining.

4.5 Show that the observations further made are consistent with the reaction mechanism given under d.

problems.title: [Lactic acid, dilactide, polylactide and the herbicide Barnon]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Lactic acid, dilactide, polylactide and the herbicide Barnon]

Bacterial conversion of saccharose leads to (S)-(+)-2-hydroxypropanoic acid (L-(+)-lactic acid), which forms a cyclic ester out of two molecules. This dilactide can be polymerized to a polylactide, which is used in surgery.

5.1 Give the spatial structures and Fischer projection of L-(+)-lactic acid and its dilactide.

5.2 Sketch the structure of the polylactide discussed above (at least three units). What is its tacticity (iso-, syndio- or atactic)?

5.3 Draw the isomeric dilactides formed out of racemic lactic acid. Show the configuration of the chiral centres.

L-(+)-lactic acid is used for the preparation of the herbicide Barnon that is used against wild oats. In this case (+)-lactic acid is esterified with 2-propanol and then the hydroxyl group is treated with methanesulfonyl chloride. The product is then submitted to a $\mathrm{S_N2}$-reaction with 3-fluoro-4-chloro-phenylamine, where the methanesulfonate group leaves as $\ce{CH3SO3-}$. Finally a benzoyl group is introduced with the help of benzoyl chloride.

5.4 Draw the Fischer projection of the various consecutive reaction products.

problems.title: [Restriction endonucleases Cla I and Taq I]
problems.problem:
Problem 6. [Restriction endonucleases Cla I and Taq I]

In recombinant DNA technology specific endonucleases can recognize and hydrolyse the phosphoric ester bound in each of both strands. Cla I for example hydrolyses the bond between two nucleotides in the sequence:

$$\text{5'-pApT}\,|\,\text{pCpGpApT-3'}$$

6.1 Give the base sequence of the complementary strand in the 5' - 3' direction and indicate with arrows the location where the hydrolysis by Cla I would occur.

6.2 How often on average will this sequence occur in one strand of DNA molecule of $10^5$ base pairs? You can assume that the four bases occur equally often and that they randomly distribute in the two chains.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1986-6-fig1.png

Taq I hydrolyses a long double strand DNA molecule into fragments which are on average 256 base pairs long. The 3' end of these fragments treated by cleavage turns out to be a thymine(T)- and the 5' end a cytosine(C) -end.

6.3 How long is the sequence recognized by Taq I?

6.4 Give the two possible base sequences (in the direction 5' - 3') which form the recognition pattern for Taq I (must obviously have some symmetry).

The DNA of a phage which occurs as a close circle contains only 5'-pApTpCpGpApT-3' sequence in each of the two strands. After treatment with ClaI equilibrium is established: circular DNA $\rightleftharpoons$ linear DNA.

6.5 Give a schematic drawing of the circular and linear molecules. Indicate the bases adjacent to the cleaning site in both strands. Indicate also the 3' and 5' ends.

In Fig. 1 the percentage of linear DNA is given as a function of temperature, measured in a solution of $0.15\,\mathrm{M}$ NaCl buffered with citrate at pH = 6.5. With Taq I as cleavage enzyme, the same curve is obtained.

6.6 Is the reaction as written endothermic or exothermic? Explain your answer.

6.7 Show, considering the information given, which of the two base sequences of the answer to 6.4 is the correct one.

6.8 What would look the curve for Taq I like if the recognition pattern would have been the other possibility of d)?

A large DNA molecule is cut into fragments with the aid of Cla I. One fragment is isolated, purified and mixed in the ratio of 1:1 with phage DNA which was also cleaved with Cla I. Thereby recombinant molecules can be formed through the reaction:

$$\text{phage-DNA} + \text{fragment DNA} \rightleftharpoons \text{recombinant-DNA}$$

6.9 Would the enthalpy of this reaction be positive, negative or about zero? Explain your answer.

6.10 Which combination of temperature, DNA concentration and ionic strength (high or low in each case) will give the maximum percentage of recombinant molecules?

problems.title: [Continuous production of C with a reactor and two distillations]
problems.problem:
Problem 7. [Continuous production of C with a reactor and two distillations]

The equilibrium constant of the reaction $\mathrm{A_{(g)}} + 2\,\mathrm{B_{(g)}}\ \_\ 2\,\mathrm{C_{(g)}}$ [the reaction arrow is printed as an underscore] is $K_\mathrm{p} = 10.0\,\mathrm{MPa^{-1}}$. The starting materials are supplied at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and heated to $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ where complete equilibration takes place. Below $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the reaction rate is negligibly small. The whole process is executed continuously in a stationary state. The boiling points at $0.1\,\mathrm{MPa}$ of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ are $40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, respectively. The three compounds have the same heat of evaporation: $q\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The heat capacities of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ may be neglected. A schematic diagram of a distillation is shown below (Fig. 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1986-7-fig1.png

The total heat used at each of the two distillations is $3q\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ (of the top product). Apart from distillation columns (each with its own evaporator and condenser) the pieces of apparatus shown of Fig. 2 are available.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1986-7-fig2.png

7.1 Draw a flow diagram of the process in which all flows are given (flow sheet) and in which the starting materials are used as efficiently as possible using as few pieces of apparatus as possible.

7.2 Express the equilibrium constant in terms of the degree of conversion and of total pressure for the case that the feed to the reactor is stoichiometric. What is the value of the degree of conversion when total pressure is $0.100\,\mathrm{MPa}$?

7.3 Number all flows. Calculate the composition of each flow in $\mathrm{mol\,s^{-1}}$ for a rate of production of 1 mole of $\mathbf{C}$ per second under the conditions of part b.

7.4 In what respect can the reaction conditions influence the composition of the mixture that leaves the reactor? (Refer to question b.)

7.5 The process requires energy. For the conditions of b explain where energy should be supplied in the flow diagram drawn in part a. Derive an expression for the total energy needed.

problems.title: [Carbohydrate in waste water of a sewage plant]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [Carbohydrate in waste water of a sewage plant]

Treating waste water in a sewage plant, $45\,\%$ of its carbohydrate $\ce{(CH2O)_n}$ is completely oxidized, $10\,\%$ undergoes anaerobic decomposition by fermentation (two components) and the rest remains in the sludge. The total gas formation is $16\,\mathrm{m^3}$ per day ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$).

1.1 What is the amount of carbohydrate remaining in the sludge measured in kg per day?

1.2 Using the heat of combustion of methane ($-882\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$), calculate the amount of energy that can be produced by combustion of the methane formed per day.

1.3 Knowing that the concentration of the carbohydrate in the waste water is $250\,\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$, calculate the daily amount of waste water processed in the plant in $\mathrm{m^3}$ of water per day.

problems.title: [Hydrated sodium phosphate salt]
problems.problem:

$500\,\mathrm{mg}$ of a hydrated sodium salt of phosphoric acid are dissolved in $50.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 0.1 molar sulphuric acid. This solution is diluted with distilled water to $100.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and $20.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of it are titrated with 0.100 molar $\ce{NaOH}$ solution using thymolphthalein as indicator. The average of the burette reading is $26.53\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. The pH at the end-point is 10.00.

Problems:

2.2 What is the stoichiometric formula of the salt?

The cumulative protonation constants are given by

$$\beta_n = \frac{[\ce{H_nPO4^{n-3}}]}{[\ce{PO4^{3-}}][\ce{H+}]^n}$$

where $\log\beta_1 = 11.70$; $\log\beta_2 = 18.6$; $\log\beta_3 = 20.6$.

problems.title: [Potentiometric titration of chloride and cyanide]
problems.problem:
Problem 3. [Potentiometric titration of chloride and cyanide]

$25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of a neutral solution containing potassium chloride and potassium cyanide are potentiometrically titrated with a standard 0.1000 molar silver nitrate solution at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ using a silver electrode and a normal calomel half-cell with $\ce{KNO3}$ - salt bridge. The protonation of cyanide ions is negligible. The potentiometric curve obtained (emf (V)) vs. burette readings (in $\mathrm{cm^3}$) is shown in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1

3.1 The end points of the reactions taking place during the titration, are marked with A, B and C. Write the balanced ionic equation for each reaction.

3.4 Calculate the emf readings at the points A and C in volts.

3.5 What is the molar ratio $\ce{Cl-}/\ce{CN-}$ in the solution and in the precipitate at point C?

Data:

$K_{sp}(\ce{AgCN}) = 10^{-15.8}$

$$\beta_2 = \frac{[\ce{Ag(CN)2^-}]}{[\ce{Ag+}][\ce{CN-}]^2} = 10^{21.1}$$

problems.title: [The periodic system of Flatlandia]
problems.problem:
Problem 1. [The periodic system of Flatlandia]

The periodic system of the elements in our three-dimensional world is based on the four electron quantum numbers $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$; $l = 0, 1, \ldots, n-1$, $m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots, \pm 1$; and $s = \pm 1/2$. In Flatlandia, a two-dimensional world, the periodic system is thus based on three electron quantum numbers: $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$; $m_l = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots, \pm (n-1)$; and $s = \pm 1/2$ where $m_l$ plays the combined role of $l$ and $m_l$ of the three dimensional world. The following tasks relate to this two-dimensional world, where the chemical and physical experience obtained from our world is supposed to be still applicable.

1.1 Draw the first four periods of the Flatlandian periodic table of the elements. Number them according to their nuclear charge. Use the atomic numbers ($Z$) as symbols of the specific element. Write the electron configuration for each element.

1.2 Draw the hybrid orbitals of the elements with $n = 2$. Which element is the basis for the organic chemistry in Flatlandia? Find the Flatlandian analogous for ethane, ethene and cyclohexane. What kind of aromatic ring compounds are possible?

1.3 Which rules in Flatlandia correspond to the octet and the 18-electron rules in the three dimensional world?

1.4 Predict graphically the trends in the first ionization energies of the Flatlandian elements with $n = 2$. Show graphically how the electronegativities of the elements increase in the Flatlandian periodic table.

1.5 Draw the molecular orbital energy diagrams of the neutral homonuclear diatomic molecules of the elements with $n = 2$. Which of these molecules are stable in Flatlandia?

1.6 Consider simple binary compounds of the elements ($n = 2$) with $Z = 1$. Draw their Lewis structure, predict their geometries and propose analogues for them in the three dimensional world.

1.7 Consider elements with $n \le 3$. Propose an analogue and write the chemical symbol from our world for each of these Flatlandian elements. On the basis of this chemical and physical analogue predict which two-dimensional elements are solid, liquid or gaseous at normal pressure and temperature.

problems.title: [Fluorides of an element A and their hydrolysis]
problems.problem:
Problem 2. [Fluorides of an element A and their hydrolysis]

Upon heating of a mixture of $\mathbf{A}$ and fluorine (molar ratio 1 : 9, pressure approximately $1\,\mathrm{MPa}$) to $900\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ three compounds ($\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$) are formed. All three products are crystalline solids at ambient temperature with melting points below $150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The fluorine content of $\mathbf{C}$ is found to be $36.7\,\%$ and that of $\mathbf{D}$ $46.5\,\%$ (by weight). When $\mathbf{B}$ is treated with anhydrous $\ce{HOSO2F}$ at $-75\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ a compound $\mathbf{E}$ is formed:

$$\mathbf{B} + \ce{HOSO2F} \rightarrow \mathbf{E} + \ce{HF}$$

$\mathbf{E}$ is a solid which is stable for weeks at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, but decomposes in days at room temperature. The electron density distribution of $\mathbf{E}$ obtained through X-ray diffraction studies is shown on two intersecting, mutually perpendicular planes (see Fig. 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-1988-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1

The numbers indicated on the maps relate to the electron density in the neighbourhood of the atoms of $\mathbf{E}$ as a function of the spatial coordinates. The maxima found in these maps coincide with the locations of the atoms and the values are approximately proportional to the number of electrons in the atom in question.

2.1 Show where the maxima lie by drawing the contour curves around the maxima, connecting points of equal electron densities. Label each maximum to show the identities of the atoms in $\mathbf{E}$.

2.2 When $450.0\,\mathrm{mg}$ of $\mathbf{C}$ was treated with an excess of mercury, $53.25\,\mathrm{ml}$ of $\mathbf{A}$ was liberated at a pressure of $101.0\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and a temperature of $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Calculate the relative atomic mass of $\mathbf{A}$.

2.3 Identify $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$.

2.4 Use the valence-shell electron-pair repulsion theory (VSEPR) to propose electron-pair geometries for $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$. Using the two electron density maps, sketch the molecular geometry of $\mathbf{E}$.

The original mixture was hydrolysed in water. $\mathbf{B}$ reacts to $\mathbf{A}$ while liberating oxygen and producing aqueous hydrogen fluoride. Hydrolysis of $\mathbf{C}$ leads to $\mathbf{A}$ and oxygen (in molar ratio of 4 : 3) and yields an aqueous solution of $\mathbf{A}\ce{O3}$ and hydrogen fluoride. $\mathbf{D}$ hydrolyses to an aqueous solution of $\mathbf{A}\ce{O3}$ and hydrogen fluoride.

2.5 Write the equations for the three hydrolysis reactions.

2.6 Quantitative hydrolysis of a mixture of $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ gives $60.2\,\mathrm{ml}$ of gas (measured at $290\,\mathrm{K}$ and $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$). The oxygen content of this gas is $40.0\,\%$ (by volume). The amount of $\mathbf{A}\ce{O3}$ dissolved in water is titrated with an aqueous 0.1 molar $\ce{FeSO4}$ solution and $36.0\,\mathrm{ml}$ used thereby. During the titration $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ is oxidized to $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ and $\mathbf{A}\ce{O3}$ is reduced to $\mathbf{A}$. Calculate the composition (% by moles) of the original mixture of $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$.

problems.title: [Combustion of fuel in a car engine and catalytic conversion of CO]
problems.problem:
Problem 3. [Combustion of fuel in a car engine and catalytic conversion of CO]

A typical family car has four cylinders with a total cylinder volume of $1600\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and a fuel consumption of $7.0\,\mathrm{l}$ per $100\,\mathrm{km}$ when driving at a speed of $90\,\mathrm{km/h}$. During one second each cylinder goes through 25 burn cycles and consumes $0.4\,\mathrm{g}$ of fuel. Assume that fuel consists of 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, $\ce{C8H18}$. The compression ratio of the cylinder is 1:8.

3.1 Calculate the air intake of the engine ($\mathrm{m^3/s}$). The gasified fuel and air are introduced into the cylinder when its volume is largest until the pressure is $101.0\,\mathrm{kPa}$. Temperature of both incoming air and fuel are $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Air contains $21.0\,\%$ (by volume) of $\ce{O2}$ and $79.0\,\%$ of $\ce{N2}$. It is assumed that $10.0\,\%$ of the carbon forms $\ce{CO}$ upon combustion and that nitrogen remains inert.

3.2 The gasified fuel and the air are compressed until the volume in the cylinder is at its smallest and then ignited. Calculate the composition (% by volume) and the temperature of the exhaust gases immediately after the combustion (exhaust gases have not yet started to expand). The following data is given:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} \text{Compound} & \Delta H_\mathrm{f}\ (\mathrm{kJ/mol}) & C_p\ (\mathrm{J/mol\,K}) \\ \hline \ce{O2(g)} & 0.0 & 29.36 \\ \ce{N2(g)} & 0.0 & 29.13 \\ \ce{CO(g)} & -110.53 & 29.14 \\ \ce{CO2(g)} & -395.51 & 37.11 \\ \ce{H2O(g)} & -241.82 & 33.58 \\ \text{2,2,4-trimethylpentane} & -187.82 & \end{array}$$

3.3 Calculate the final temperature of the leaving gases assuming that the piston has moved to expand the gases to the maximum volume of the cylinder and that the final gas pressure in the cylinder is $200\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

3.4 To convert $\ce{CO(g)}$ into $\ce{CO2(g)}$ the exhaust gases are led through a bed of catalysts with the following work function:

$$\frac{n(\ce{CO})}{n(\ce{CO2})} = \frac{1}{4}\,k \left[\frac{n(\ce{CO})}{n(\ce{CO2})}\right]_1 v\, e^{-\frac{T}{T_0}}$$

where $[n(\ce{CO}) / n(\ce{CO2})]_1$ is the molar ratio before the catalyst, $v$ is the flow rate in $\mathrm{mol/s}$ and $T$ the temperature of the gases entering the catalyst (the same as the temperature of the leaving exhaust gases). $T_0$ is a reference temperature ($373\,\mathrm{K}$) and $k$ is equal to $3.141\,\mathrm{s/mol}$. Calculate the composition (% by volume) of the exhaust gases leaving the catalyst.

problems.title: [Photodecomposition of silver chloride; weak acids; conditional formation constant]
problems.problem:
Problem 4. [Photodecomposition of silver chloride; weak acids; conditional formation constant]

Chloride ions are analytically determined by precipitating them with silver nitrate. The precipitate is undergoing decomposition in presence of light and forms elemental silver and chlorine. In aqueous solution the latter disproportionates to chlorate(V) and chloride. With excess of silver ions, the chloride ions formed are precipitated whereas chlorate(V) ions are not.

4.1 Write the balanced equations of the reactions mentioned above.

4.2 The gravimetric determination yielded a precipitate of which $12\,\%$ by mass was decomposed by light. Determine the size and direction of the error caused by this decomposition.

4.3 Consider a solution containing two weak acids HA and HL, 0.020 molar and 0.010 molar solutions, respectively. The acid constants are $1\times10^{-4}$ for HA and $1\times10^{-7}$ for HL. Calculate the pH of the solution.

4.4 M forms a complex ML with the acid $\ce{H2L}$ with the formation constant $K_1$. The solution contains another metal ion N that forms a complex NHL with the acid $\ce{H2L}$. Determine the conditional equilibrium constant, $K'_1$ for the complex ML in terms of $[\ce{H+}]$ and $K$ values.

$$K_1 = \frac{[\mathrm{ML}]}{[\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{L}]}$$

$$K'_1 = \frac{[\mathrm{ML}]}{[\mathrm{M'}][\mathrm{L'}]}$$

$[\mathrm{M'}]$ = total concentration of M not bound in ML

$[\mathrm{L'}]$ = the sum of the concentrations of all species containing L except ML

In addition to $K_1$, the acid constants $K_{a1}$ and $K_{a2}$ of $\ce{H2L}$ as well as the formation constant $K_\mathrm{NHL}$ of NHL are known.

$$K_\mathrm{NHL} = \frac{[\mathrm{NHL}]}{[\mathrm{N}]\,[\mathrm{L}]\,[\ce{H+}]}$$

You may assume that the equilibrium concentration $[\ce{H+}]$ and $[\mathrm{N}]$ are known, too.

problems.title: [Synthesis of a secondary alcohol from phenol; mass spectrum of a bromo compound]
problems.problem:
Problem 5. [Synthesis of a secondary alcohol from phenol; mass spectrum of a bromo compound]

A common compound $\mathbf{A}$ is prepared from phenol and oxidized to compound $\mathbf{B}$. Dehydration of $\mathbf{A}$ with $\ce{H2SO4}$ leads to compound $\mathbf{C}$ and treatment of $\mathbf{A}$ with $\ce{PBr3}$ gives $\mathbf{D}$. In the mass spectrum of $\mathbf{D}$ there is a very strong peak at $m/e = 83$ (base peak) and two molecular ion peaks at $m/e$ 162 and 164. The ratio of intensities of the peaks 162 and 164 is 1.02. Compound $\mathbf{D}$ can be converted to an organomagnesium compound $\mathbf{E}$ that reacts with a carbonyl compound $\mathbf{F}$ in dry ether to give $\mathbf{G}$ after hydrolysis. $\mathbf{G}$ is a secondary alcohol with the molecular formula $\ce{C8H16O}$.

5.1 Outline all steps in the synthesis of $\mathbf{G}$ and draw the structural formulae of the compounds $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{G}$.

5.2 Which of the products $\mathbf{A}$ – $\mathbf{G}$ consist of configurational stereoisomeric pairs?

5.3 Identify the three ions in the mass spectrum considering isotopic abundances given in the text.

problems.problem:
