Problem 4 (9 points). Beach Sand Mineral in Kerala

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2001-4-fig1.png

Beach sand mineral, monazite, is a rich source of thorium, available in large quantities in the state of Kerala in India. A typical monazite sample contains about 9% $\ce{ThO2}$ and 0.35% $\ce{U3O8}$. $\ce{^{208}Pb}$ and $\ce{^{206}Pb}$ are the stable end-products in the radioactive decay series of $\ce{^{232}Th}$ and $\ce{^{238}U}$, respectively. The isotopic atom ratio $\ce{^{208}Pb}/\ce{^{232}Th}$, measured mass spectrometrically, in a monazite sample was found to be 0.104. Proteins (polypeptides) are known to assume a variety of backbone conformations. In one conformation, the backbone is in almost fully extended arrangement (as in a parallel or anti–parallel $\beta$–sheet), and in another conformation it is in a fully folded arrangement (as in an $\alpha$–helix).

$\beta$ – lactamase and drug resistance

Penicillins are effective drugs in combating bacterial infections. An alarming development over the years has, however, been the emergence of drug resistant bacteria. problems.title: Oxygen in Your Life
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (6 points). Oxygen in Your Life

[Problem I-1 of the paper.] Theme I – Chemistry of Life. Life runs on chemistry. Understanding and monitoring life processes receive much attention in chemistry.

Oxygen is of vital importance for all of us. Oxygen enters the body via the lungs and is transported to the tissues in our body by blood. There it can deliver energy by the oxidation of sugars:

$$\ce{C6H12O6 + 6 O2 -> 6 CO2 + 6 H2O}$$

This reaction releases $400\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of energy per mol of oxygen. $\ce{O2}$ uptake by blood is at four heme (Hm) groups in the protein hemoglobin (Hb).

Free Hm consists of an $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ ion attached to four N atoms of a porphyrin$^{2-}$ ligand. Oxygen can bind at the coordination site of $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ giving a $\mathrm{Hm{\cdot}O_2}$ complex. Carbon monoxide can be complexed similarly, giving a $\mathrm{Hm{\cdot}CO}$ complex. $\ce{CO}$ is a poison as it binds more strongly to Hm than $\ce{O2}$ does. The equilibrium constant $K_1$ for the reaction:

$$\mathrm{Hm} + \ce{CO} \ce{<=>} \mathrm{Hm{\cdot}CO} \qquad (1)$$

is 10000 times larger than the equilibrium constant $K_2$ for the reaction:

$$\mathrm{Hm} + \ce{O2} \ce{<=>} \mathrm{Hm{\cdot}O_2} \qquad (2)$$

Each Hb molecule can take up four molecules of $\ce{O2}$. Blood in contact with $\ce{O2}$ absorbs a fraction of this amount, depending on the oxygen pressure, as shown in Figure 1 (curve 1). Also shown are the curves (2) and (3) for blood with two kinds of deficient Hb. These occur in patients with certain hereditary diseases.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-1-fig1.png

Relevant data: $\ce{O2}$ pressure in lungs is $15\,\mathrm{kPa}$; in the muscles it is $2\,\mathrm{kPa}$. The maximum flow of blood through heart and lungs is $4\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$. The red cells in blood occupy 40% of the blood volume; inside the cells the concentration of Hb is $340\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$; Hb has a molar mass of $64\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}$. $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. $T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$.

I-1-1 Using the relation between $K$ and the standard Gibbs energy $\Delta G^0$ for a reaction, calculate the difference between the $\Delta G^0$ values for the heme reactions (1) and (2).

I-1-2 Estimate from Figure 1 (to 2 significant figures) how many moles of $\ce{O2}$ are deposited in muscle tissue when one mole of Hb travels from the lungs to the muscles and back again for the three different types of Hb.

I-1-3 The special S-shaped uptake curve 1 is the result of subtle structural features of Hb. The deficient Hb shown in curve 2 is not optimal because:

• The binding with $\ce{O2}$ is too weak.
• The binding with $\ce{O2}$ is too strong.
• The maximum oxygen capacity is too low.
• The deficiency is caused by carbon monoxide poisoning.

I-1-4 Calculate how much oxygen (in $\mathrm{mol\,s^{-1}}$) can be deposited in tissue by blood with normal Hb (1).

I-1-5 Calculate the maximum power that the body can produce (assuming it is limited by oxygen transfer).

problems.title: Nitrogen Cycle in Nature
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (7 points). Nitrogen Cycle in Nature

[Problem I-2 of the paper.]

Ammonia is a toxic substance to marine animals at levels exceeding 1 ppm. Nitrifying bacteria play an important role in the conversion of $\ce{NH3}$ first to nitrite and then to nitrate, the storage form of nitrogen in the soil.

$$\ce{NH3 + 2 O2 + NADH} \xrightarrow[\text{bacteria}]{\textit{Nitrosomonas}} \ce{NO2^- + 2 H2O + NAD^+}$$

NADH is the biochemical reducing agent of the coenzyme nicotinamide dinucleotide (NAD), $\ce{NAD^+}$ is the oxidized form of the coenzyme NAD.

$$\ce{2 NO2^- + O2} \xrightarrow[\text{bacteria}]{\textit{Nitrobacter}} \ce{2 NO3^-}$$

I-2-1 Give the oxidation states of N in the following series:

$$\ce{NH3 -> NO2^- -> NO3^-}$$

The spectrophotometric analysis of nitrite is based on a reaction with an indicator. The coloured product then obtained has an absorbance maximum at $\lambda = 543\,\mathrm{nm}$.

For quantitative analyses a calibration curve has to be made, in which absorbance at the maximum absorbance wavelength $\lambda = 543\,\mathrm{nm}$ is plotted against nitrite concentration in a series of standards.

I-2-2 The measurements are performed at the wavelength with the maximal absorbance because:

• There is no interference of impurities
• There is no contribution of stray light
• There is optimal accuracy of the measurement
• None of these statements

Mark the correct answer.

The absorption is measured with a single beam spectrophotometer. However 5% of the light, the so-called stray light $I_\mathrm{s}$, strikes the detector directly (see Figure 2).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-2-fig1.png

Figure 2

I-2-3 Calculate the value of the absorbance $A$ shown by the spectrophotometer if $\varepsilon = 6000\,\mathrm{M^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$, $l = 1\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $c = 1\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M}$.

For a nitrite determination in water the following data have been measured.

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{concentration of nitrite nitrogen (ppm)} & \text{absorbance at } 543\,\mathrm{nm}\ (1.000\,\mathrm{cm}\ \text{cuvet}) \\ \hline \text{blank} & 0.003\ \text{(due to impurities in the solvent)} \\ 0.915 & 0.167 \\ 1.830 & 0.328 \end{array}$$

I-2-4 Determine from the data given above, using the values corrected for the solvent impurities, the slope $m$ and the intercept $b$ of the calibration curve $A = m\,c + b$.

The duplicate analyses of a water sample are given below. The measurements have been performed at a wavelength of $543\,\mathrm{nm}$ and in a $2.000\,\mathrm{cm}$ cuvet.

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{water sample} & \text{absorbance} \\ \hline \text{analysis 1} & 0.562 \\ \text{analysis 2} & 0.554 \end{array}$$

For the calculation of the concentration of the nitrite nitrogen ($c$ in ppm) the equation obtained by the method of least squares

$$\text{corrected absorbance} = 0.1769\,c + 0.0015$$

may be applied, using the measurements in a $1.000\,\mathrm{cm}$ cuvet.

I-2-5 Calculate the average nitrite nitrogen concentration in ppm and $\mathrm{\mu g\,mL^{-1}}$. Hint: Take the blank from problem I-2-4.

problems.title: Inulin, a New Renewable Raw Material
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (6 points). Inulin, a New Renewable Raw Material

[Problem II-1 of the paper.] Theme II – Chemistry of Industrial Relevance. In our daily life we use many products that are produced on an industrial scale. Mastering the underlying chemistry is at the heart of this business.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-3-fig1.png

Inulin, which is produced from chicory roots in Belgium and The Netherlands, is used as a food additive as it has a beneficial effect on the intestinal flora. It is also used as source of fructose which is 1.9 times sweeter than sucrose, and for the production of mannitol which is used in chewing gum. Inulin is a linear polymer of fructose units with a glucose unit at one end; its Haworth projection formula is shown at the left. In this problem inulin has 10 fructose units ($n = 9$).

II-1-1 Inulin may be hydrolyzed under $\ce{H+}$-catalysis conditions. Of the four options below ($\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$) indicate which C–O bond cleavage is most likely to occur.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-3-fig2.png

Mark the correct cleavage mechanism for the most efficient hydrolysis.

Hydrolysis with isotopically labelled water can provide information about the mechanism of hydrolysis using modern NMR techniques, which can "see" deuterium ($\ce{^2H}$) and the oxygen isotope $\ce{^{17}O}$.

II-1-2 Indicate which labelled water can best be used for this purpose. Mark the correct answer.

• $\ce{^2H2O}$
• $\ce{H2^{17}O}$
• $\ce{^2H2^{17}O}$
• None of them.

Upon catalytic hydrogenation glucose gives sorbitol ($\mathbf{S}$), whilst fructose ($\mathbf{F}$) gives mannitol ($\mathbf{M}$) and sorbitol ($\mathbf{S}$).

II-1-3 Draw the Fischer projections of fructose ($\mathbf{F}$), sorbitol ($\mathbf{S}$) and mannitol ($\mathbf{M}$). [The answer template reads $\mathbf{F} \rightarrow \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{M}$.]

1.00 Mole of inulin in 2.00 kg of water with added catalysts, is subjected to hydrolysis and hydrogenation at $95\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in a one step process. The selectivity of the hydrogenation of fructose to mannitol / sorbitol is 7 / 3.

II-1-4 How many moles of mannitol and sorbitol are obtained?

After completion of the reactions the catalysts are removed and the reaction mixture is cooled to $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The solubility of $\mathbf{M}$ is $0.40\,\mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}$ in water at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the solubility of $\mathbf{S}$ is so high that it will not precipitate.

II-1-5 Calculate how many moles of $\mathbf{M}$ will precipitate.

Problem 4 (6 points). Production of Methanol

[Problem II-2 of the paper.]

Methanol ($\ce{CH3OH}$) is a chemical that is used for the production of additives in gasoline and many common plastics. A factory, producing methanol, is based on the reaction:

$$\ce{CO + 2 H2 <=> CH3OH}$$

Hydrogen and $\ce{CO}$ are obtained by the reaction:

$$\ce{CH4 + H2O <=> CO + 3 H2}$$

The three units of the factory, namely, the "reformer" for the hydrogen / carbon monoxide production, the "methanol reactor" and a "separator" to separate methanol from $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{H2}$, are schematically shown in Figure 1. Four positions are indicated by $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-4-fig1.png

Figure 1

The flow of methanol at position $\gamma$ is $n[\ce{CH3OH}, \gamma] = 1000\,\mathrm{mol\,s^{-1}}$. The factory is so designed that 2/3 of the $\ce{CO}$ is converted to methanol. Excess $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{H2}$ at position $\delta$ are used to heat the first reactor. Assume that the reformer reaction goes to completion.

II-2-1 Calculate the flow of $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{H2}$ at position $\beta$.

II-2-2 Calculate the flow of $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{H2}$ at position $\gamma$.

II-2-3 Calculate the flows of $\ce{CH4}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ needed at position $\alpha$.

II-2-4 At point $\gamma$ all species are gases. Calculate the partial pressures in MPa for $\ce{CO}$, $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{CH3OH}$ at position $\gamma$ using the equation:

$$p_\mathrm{i} = p\,\frac{n_\mathrm{i}}{n_\mathrm{tot}}$$

wherein $n_\mathrm{i}$ is the flow and $p_\mathrm{i}$ the partial pressure of the compound i, $n_\mathrm{tot}$ is the total flow at the position considered, and $p$ the total pressure in the system. ($p = 10\,\mathrm{MPa}$)

When the methanol reactor is large enough the reaction goes to equilibrium. The partial pressures at point $\gamma$ obey the equation:

$$K_\mathrm{p} = \frac{p_{\ce{CH3OH}}\,p_0^{2}}{p_{\ce{CO}}\,p_{\ce{H2}}^{2}}$$

wherein $p_0$ is a constant ($0.1\,\mathrm{MPa}$) and $K_\mathrm{p}$ is a function of temperature as is shown in Figure 2 (the vertical scale is logarithmic).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-4-fig2.png

Figure 2

II-2-5 Calculate $K_\mathrm{p}$ and indicate at which temperature $T$ the reaction must be operated to achieve this equilibrium.

problems.title: Phospholipids in Membranes
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (6 points). Phospholipids in Membranes

[Problem III-1 of the paper.] Theme III – Chemistry of Functional Molecules in Nature. A challenge in chemistry is to discover what nature does and how the structures of biologically active molecules are related to what they do.

Biological cell membranes are complex, functional, non-covalent molecular assemblies, largely consisting of lipids and proteins. Their function is of vital importance for life processes. They separate the cell from its environment and also determine the specific flow of information between the cell contents and the environment. Phospholipids are among the most important components of cell membranes. An example is compound $\mathbf{A}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-6-fig1.png

Upon dispersion in water (above a low critical concentration) compound $\mathbf{A}$ forms closed bilayer structures, called liposomes, which are employed as model compounds for aspects of the chemistry of the structurally much more complex cell membranes. Liposomes are globular aggregates with the polar or ionic head groups in contact with water and with the alkyl tails sequestered in a hydrophobic core. The bilayer structure encloses an aqueous inner compartment.

Double-tailed synthetic surfactants also form closed bilayer assemblies similar to liposomes but now called vesicles. An example is di-$n$-dodecyldimethylammonium chloride ($\mathbf{DDAC}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-6-fig2.png

III-1-1 (a) How many stereoisomers are possible for compound $\mathbf{A}$?

(b) How many stereoisomers are possible for the trialkylphosphate $\mathbf{B}$?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-6-fig3.png

A precursor for the synthesis of compound $\mathbf{A}$ is the acetonide $\mathbf{C}$ derived from glycerol. Part of the $\ce{^1H}$-NMR spectrum of compound $\mathbf{C}$ is shown below.

III-1-2 Which signal number in the $\ce{^1H}$-NMR spectrum corresponds to proton $\mathbf{H_c}$?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-6-fig4.png

The bilayer of a liposome can be characterized by $V$ (the volume of the hydrocarbon chains), $a_0$ (optimal cross-sectional surface area of the head groups of the phospholipid in the aggregate) and $l_\mathrm{c}$ (the maximum chain length that the alkyl group can assume). A good approximation for unbranched alkyl tails containing $n$ carbon atoms yields:

$$V = (27.4 + 26.99\,n)\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{nm^3}$$

$$l_\mathrm{c} = (0.154 + 0.1265\,n)\,\mathrm{nm}$$

For very large $n$ values, the intertail interactions dominate over the head group repulsions.

III-1-3 Calculate the minimum cross-sectional surface area of the head groups for such very large $n$ values.

Vesicles formed from $\mathbf{DDAC}$ (above its critical vesicle concentration, cvc) catalyse the unimolecular decarboxylation of 6-nitro-benzisoxazole-3-carboxylate ($\mathbf{6\text{-}NBIC}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-6-fig5.png

In water at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ $k_1 = 3.1\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. At the concentration $c_1$ of $\mathbf{DDAC}$ at which $\mathbf{6\text{-}NBIC}$ becomes fully bound to the vesicles, $k_1 = 2.1\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

III-1-4 Sketch a plot of $k_1$ vs. $[\mathbf{DDAC}]$ for $[\mathbf{DDAC}] = 0 \rightarrow 3\,c_1$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-6-fig6.png

III-1-5 The main reason for the efficient catalysis of the decarboxylation of $\mathbf{6\text{-}NBIC}$ by $\mathbf{DDAC}$ vesicles is:

• The decarboxylation is catalysed by the $\ce{Cl^-}$ ions bound to the surface of the vesicles.
• Efficient loss of hydration of the carboxylate group of vesicle-bound 6-NBIC.
• Strong binding of $\ce{CO2}$ in the interior of the vesicle.
• Strong binding of the organic reaction product to the vesicles relative to that of 6-NBIC.

Mark the correct answer.

Problem 7 (6 points). Glutathione, an Essential Mini-Peptide

[Problem III-2 of the paper.]

Glutathione, abbreviated as GSH, is a small peptide that is present in almost all tissues of animals. GSH fulfils important biological functions, such as detoxification of electrophilic chemicals and reduction of (organic) peroxides in blood. An electrophilic compound reacts irreversibly with GSH, especially in the liver, to give a primary product that is converted by a series of biotransformations into a so-called mercapturic acid, which is excreted via the urine. Oxidants react with GSH to give the disulfide GSSG, which can be enzymatically reverted to GSH with reductases. The ratio GSH/GSSG in most cells is $\geq 500$.

The $\ce{^1H}$-NMR spectrum of $\mathbf{A}$ in $\ce{(CD3)2SO}$ is shown in Figure 1. When the product is pretreated with $\ce{D2O}$, the signals at $\delta$ 12.8 and $\delta$ 6.8 are no longer present and the signal 3 is simplified.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-7-fig2.png

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Signals} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4/5 & 6 & 7 \\ \hline \text{Protons} & & & & & & \end{array}$$

(b) How many carbon atoms are present in compound $\mathbf{A}$ that do not carry any protons?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-7-fig3.png

III-2-3 Eating fresh fruit and vegetables is healthy

problems.title: Lighting Lamps
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (7 points). Lighting Lamps

[Problem IV-1 of the paper.] Theme IV – Chemistry Related to Light and Energy. Chemistry plays a major role in meeting our needs of light and energy. Our life is unthinkable without artificial light and energy for mobility.

Since 1891 lighting lamps have been manufactured in The Netherlands. The improvement today in comparison to the first lamp is enormous, especially with the introduction of the gas discharge lamps. The life-time has increased by orders of magnitude. The colour is also an important aspect. Rare earth metal compounds like $\ce{CeBr3}$ are now included to reach a colour temperature of $6000\,\mathrm{K}$ in the lamp. These compounds are ionic solids at room temperature, and upon heating they sublime partially to give a vapour of neutral metal halide molecules. To achieve a high vapour pressure, the sublimation enthalpy should be as low as possible.

IV-1-1 Give a thermochemical cycle (Law of Hess) for sublimation of $\ce{CeBr3}$, via a vapour of mononuclear ions. ($H_\mathrm{l} = H_\mathrm{lattice}$; $H_\mathrm{e} = H_\mathrm{electrostatic}$; $H_\mathrm{s} = H_\mathrm{sublimation}$; $H$ is not absolute, $H$ means $\Delta H$)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-8-fig1.png

The lattice energy of the solid can be calculated using the Born–Landé formula:

$$H_\mathrm{l} = f\,\frac{Z_+ Z_- A e^2}{r_+ + r_-}\left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)$$

The factor $fe^2$ (necessary in order to calculate the lattice energy in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) amounts to 139 when the ionic radii are substituted in nm. The Madelung constant $A$ for the lattice is 2.985. The Born exponent $n$ is 11. The charges of the ions $Z_+$ and $Z_-$ are integer numbers ($Z_-$ is negative). For the calculation of the energy of gaseous $\ce{CeBr3}$ (when formed from ions) the same Born-Landé formula can be used without $A$. The structure of $\ce{CeBr3}$ in the gas phase is planar triangular. The radius of $\ce{Ce^{3+}}$ is $0.115\,\mathrm{nm}$ and of $\ce{Br^-}$ is $0.182\,\mathrm{nm}$.

IV-1-2 Calculate the enthalpy of sublimation of $\ce{CeBr3}$ (in integers; be aware of the signs!)

Attempts to make a better lamp have been undertaken by adding a stoichiometric amount of $\ce{CsBr}$ to the $\ce{CeBr3}$ in the lamp leading at room temperature to solid $\ce{CsCeBr4}$. When the sublimation temperature decreases the life time of the lamp will increase likewise. The $\ce{CsCeBr4}$ lattice has a $\ce{NaCl}$ structure with $\ce{Cs+}$ as cations and tetrahedral $\ce{CeBr4^-}$ as complex anions. Sublimation of $\ce{CsCeBr4}$ leads to a vapour of $\ce{CsBr}$ and $\ce{CeBr3}$ molecules.

IV-1-3 Give the reaction equations of the thermochemical cycle (Law of Hess) for this process in which some steps involve $\ce{CeBr4^-}$ ions, mononuclear ions and/or neutral molecules in the gas phase.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2002-8-fig2.png

IV-1-4 Calculate the enthalpy of sublimation of $\ce{CsCeBr4}$ (in integers). Use the Born–Landé formula for all steps in the process and report the separate energies also (be aware of the signs!). The Madelung constant for $\ce{NaCl}$ is 1.75. The Cs–Ce distance in the lattice is $0.617\,\mathrm{nm}$. The $\ce{CeBr4^-}$ anion is a tetrahedron in which the ratio between the edge and the distance between a corner of the tetrahedron and the centre of gravity (body-radius) amounts to $(2\sqrt{6})/3 = 1.633$. The Born exponent of $\ce{CsBr}$ is 11. The radius of $\ce{Cs+}$ is $0.181\,\mathrm{nm}$.

problems.title: Vehicle Traction Batteries
problems.problem:
Problem 10 (5 points). Vehicle Traction Batteries

[Problem IV-3 of the paper.]

Battery-powered electric vehicles (EV's) are likely to become increasingly common in the next 50 years because of growing concern over pollution caused by vehicles using combustion engines. The reason for the current meagre commercial success of EV's is that the battery specifications must have a performance and cost profile comparable to conventionally powered vehicles.

Lead-acid batteries are extensively used as portable power sources for vehicles and traction. A lead-acid battery capable of efficient recharging has an energy density of $45\,\mathrm{Wh/kg}$.

In the current evolution of EV batteries, the most promising long-term solution is the rechargeable light weight lithium-ion battery. Such batteries are under intensive investigation worldwide and hold also promise for the storage of electricity from solar cells. Their weight is 1/3 of a lead-acid battery. Lithium is used as a negative electrode. It has a high specific capacity and electrode potential. A common positive electrode material is the environmentally benign spinel-type $\ce{LiMn2O4}$. The spinel structure comprises a matrix of cubic close-packed oxide ions, stabilised by lithium ions in tetrahedral sites and manganese ions in octahedral sites. In $\ce{LiMn2O4}$ half of the manganese ions has an oxidation state +3 and half the oxidation state +4.

A lead-acid battery is represented by:

$$\ce{Pb(s)} \mid \ce{PbSO4(s)} \mid \ce{H2SO4(aq)} \mid \ce{PbSO4(s)} \mid \ce{PbO2(s)} \mid (\ce{Pb(s)})$$

A lithium battery is represented by:

$$\ce{Li(s)} \mid \ce{Li+}\text{-conducting (solid) electrolyte(s)} \mid \ce{LiMn2O4(s)}$$

Upon discharge the insertion product $\ce{Li2Mn2O4}$ is formed. Charging the battery leads to the products $\ce{Li(s)}$ and $\ce{LiMn2O4}$.

IV-3-1 Give the electrochemical reactions at the electrodes of the lead-acid battery during discharge.

IV-3-2 Give the electrochemical reactions at the electrodes of the lithium-ion battery upon discharge.

IV-3-3 Give the coordination numbers of the lithium ions and of the manganese ions in the spinel structure of $\ce{LiMn2O4}$.

A typical family car of $1000\,\mathrm{kg}$ requires at least $5\,\mathrm{kWh}$ of energy to move $50\,\mathrm{km}$, which corresponds with the consumption of about $5.0\,\mathrm{L}$ or $3.78\,\mathrm{kg}$ of petrol. This conventional car has a petrol tank volume of $50\,\mathrm{L}$. The weight of the tank is $10\,\mathrm{kg}$. The fuel consumption is $10\,\mathrm{km\,L^{-1}}$.

IV-3-4 Calculate the extra weight of the car if the petrol tank is replaced by an equivalent battery in an EV based on (a) lead-acid battery and (b) lithium battery. Assume that in all cases the engine efficiency is the same.

(a) Extra weight of a lead-acid battery car.

(b) Extra weight of a lithium battery car.

Problem 26 (5 points). CO spectrum

Rotational energy levels of diatomic molecules are well described by the formula $E_J = B\,J(J+1)$, where $J$ is the rotational quantum number of the molecule and $B$ its rotational constant. $B$ is related to the reduced mass $\mu$ and the bond length $R$ of the molecule through the equation $B = \dfrac{h^{2}}{8\pi^{2}\mu R^{2}}$.

In general, spectroscopic transitions appear at photon energies which are equal to the energy difference between appropriate states of a molecule ($h\nu = \Delta E$). The observed rotational transitions occur between adjacent rotational levels, hence $\Delta E = E_{J+1} - E_J = 2B(J+1)$. Consequently, successive rotational transitions that appear on the spectrum (such as the one shown here) follow the equation $h(\Delta\nu) = 2B$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2003-26-fig1.png

problems.title: Gas velocity
problems.problem:
Problem 30 (5 points). Gas velocity

The experiment described here gives a simple way to determine the mean velocity $u$ of the molecules in the gas phase of a volatile liquid. A wide shallow container (a Petri dish) half filled with ethanol is placed on an electronic balance with its lid next to it and the balance is zeroed at time $t = 0$. Balance readings are recorded as shown on the diagram.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2003-30-fig1.png

At $t = 5\,\mathrm{min}$ the lid is placed over the dish. The liquid no longer evaporates, but the trapped molecules push against the lid, hence lowering the measurement of the balance by $\delta m$. Therefore, the force exerted on the lid is $f = \delta m\,g$. The force is also equal to the rate of change of the momentum of the evaporating molecules, i.e., $f = \tfrac{1}{2}\,u\,\mathrm{d}m/\mathrm{d}t$. Using the data provided determine the mean velocity of ethanol molecules at $290\,\mathrm{K}$. Assume $g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

problems.title: Aluminium
problems.problem:
Problem 34 (22 points). Aluminium

(Total number of points for this Question: 22. Points marked for each subquestion)

One of the largest factories in Greece, located near the ancient city of Delphi, produces alumina ($\ce{Al2O3}$) and aluminium metal using the mineral bauxite mined from the Parnassus mountain. Bauxite is a mixed aluminium oxide hydroxide – $\ce{AlO_{x}(OH)_{3-2x}}$ where $0<x<1$.

Production of Al metal follows a two-stage process:

(i) Bayer process: Extraction, purification and dehydration of bauxite (typical compositions for industrially used bauxites are $\ce{Al2O3}$ 40-60%, $\ce{H2O}$ 12-30%, $\ce{SiO2}$ free and combined 1-15%, $\ce{Fe2O3}$ 7-30%, $\ce{TiO2}$ 3-4%, F, $\ce{P2O5}$, $\ce{V2O5}$, etc., 0.05-0.2%). This involves dissolution in aqueous NaOH, separation from insoluble impurities, partial precipitation of the aluminium hydroxide and heating at $1200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Complete and balance the following chemical reactions of stage (i)

$$\begin{array}{c} \ce{Al2O3 + OH^-} + \underline{\qquad} \longrightarrow \ce{[Al(OH)4(H2O)2]^-} \\ \ce{SiO2 + OH^-} \longrightarrow \ce{SiO2(OH)2^{2-}} \\ \ce{SiO2(OH)2^{2-}} + \underline{\qquad} \longrightarrow \ce{CaSiO3 v} + \underline{\qquad} \\ \ce{[Al(OH)4(H2O)2]^-} \longrightarrow \underline{\qquad}\downarrow + \ce{OH^- + H2O} \\ \ce{Al(OH)3} \longrightarrow \ce{Al2O3} + \underline{\qquad} \end{array}$$

ii) Héroult-Hall process: Electrolysis of pure alumina dissolved in molten cryolite, $\ce{Na3AlF6}$. Typical electrolyte composition ranges are $\ce{Na3AlF6}$ (80-85%), $\ce{CaF2}$ (5-7%), $\ce{AlF3}$ (5-7%), $\ce{Al2O3}$ (2-8% intermittently recharged). Electrolysis is carried out at $940\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, under constant pressure of 1 atm, in a carbon-lined steel cell (cathode) with carbon anodes. Balance the main reaction of the electrolysis:

$$\ce{Al2O3(l)} + \mathrm{C(anode)} \longrightarrow \ce{Al(l) + CO2(g)}$$

Since cryolite is a rather rare mineral, it is prepared according to the following reaction. Complete and balance this reaction:

$$\ce{HF + Al(OH)3 + NaOH -> Na3AlF6} + \underline{\qquad}$$

During the electrolysis process several parallel reactions take place that degrade the graphite (C) anodes or reduce the yield.

iii) By using the thermodynamic data given below, which are taken to be independent of temperature, determine the thermodynamic quantities $\Delta H$, $\Delta S$ and $\Delta G$ at $940\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for the reaction:

$$\ce{C(graphite) + CO2(g) -> 2CO(g)}.$$

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c} & \ce{Al(s)} & \ce{Al2O3(s)} & \mathrm{C\ (graphite)} & \ce{CO(g)} & \ce{CO2(g)} & \ce{O2(g)} \\ \hline \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & 0 & -1676 & 0 & -111 & -394 & \\ S^\circ\ (\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}) & 28 & 51 & 6 & 198 & 214 & 205 \\ \Delta_\mathrm{fus}H\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & 11 & 109 & & & & \end{array}$$

iv) At the same temperature and using the data from the table in part (iii) determine the quantities $\Delta H$ and $\Delta G$ for the reaction

$$\ce{2Al(l) + 3CO2(g) -> Al2O3(l) + 3CO(g)}$$

given that $\Delta S = -126\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. (Show your calculations)

v) Pure aluminium is a silvery-white metal with a face-centered cubic (fcc) crystal structure. Aluminium is readily soluble in hot concentrated hydrochloric acid producing the cation $\ce{[Al(H2O)6]^{3+}}$, as well as in strong bases at room temperature producing hydrated tetrahydroxyaluminate anion, $\ce{[Al(OH)4]^-(aq)}$. In both cases liberation of $\ce{H2}$ occurs. $\ce{AlF3}$ is made by treating $\ce{Al2O3}$ with HF gas at $700\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, while the other trihalides, $\ce{AlX3}$, are made by the direct exothermic reaction of Al with the corresponding dihalogen. Write all 4 chemical reactions described above.

vi) The $\ce{AlCl3}$ is a crystalline solid having a layer lattice with 6-coordinate Al(III), but at the melting point ($192.4\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) the structure changes to a 4-coordinate molecular dimer, $\ce{Al2Cl6}$. The covalently bonded molecular dimer, in the gas phase and at high temperature, dissociates into trigonal planar $\ce{AlCl3}$ molecules.

For the molecular dimer $\ce{Al2Cl6}$, in the gas phase, two different Al — Cl distances ($206$ and $221\,\mathrm{pm}$) were measured. Draw the stereostructure of the dimer, and write down the corresponding Al — Cl distances.

vii) What is the hybridization of the Al atom(s) in $\ce{Al2Cl6}$ and $\ce{AlCl3}$?

(If you do not have the amount from 1.2a) assume that $1.00\,\mathrm{m^{3}}$ natural gas corresponds to $40.00\,\mathrm{mol}$ natural gas.)

According to the PUC the combustion energy will be $9.981\,\mathrm{kWh}$ per $\mathrm{m^{3}}$ of natural gas if all products are gaseous. How large is the deviation (in percent) from the value you obtained in b)?

The swimming pool inside the house is $3.00\,\mathrm{m}$ wide, $5.00\,\mathrm{m}$ long and $1.50\,\mathrm{m}$ deep (below the floor). The tap water temperature is $8.00\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the air temperature in the house (dimensions given in the figure below) is $10.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assume a water density of $\rho = 1.00\,\mathrm{kg\,L^{-1}}$ and air behaving like an ideal gas.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2004-1-fig1.png

1.3 Calculate the energy (in MJ) which is required to heat the water in the pool to $22.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and the energy which is required to heat the initial amount of air ($21.0\%$ of $\ce{O2}$, $79.0\%$ of $\ce{N2}$) to $30.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at a pressure of $1.013\cdot10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$.

In February, the outside temperature is about $5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in Northern Germany. Since the concrete walls and the roof of the house are relatively thin ($20.0\,\mathrm{cm}$) there will be a loss of energy. This energy is released to the surroundings (heat loss released to water and/or ground should be neglected). The heat conductivity of the wall and roof is $1.00\,\mathrm{W\,K^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$.

1.4 Calculate the energy (in MJ) which is needed to maintain the temperature inside the house at $30.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ during the party (12 hours).

$1.00\,\mathrm{m^{3}}$ of natural gas as delivered by PUC costs $0.40$ € and $1.00\,\mathrm{kWh}$ of electricity costs $0.137$ €. The rent for the equipment for gas heating will cost him about $150.00$ € while the corresponding electrical heaters will only cost $100.00$ €.

1.5 What is the total energy (in MJ) needed for Peter's "winter swimming pool" calculated in 1.3 and 1.4? How much natural gas will he need, if the gas heater has an efficiency of $90.0\%$? What are the different costs for the use of either natural gas or electricity? Use the values given by PUC for your calculations and assume $100\%$ efficiency for the electric heater.

Table 1: Composition of natural gas

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{Chemical substance} & \text{mol fraction } x & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^{0}\cdot(\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}})^{-1} & S^{0}\cdot(\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}})^{-1} & C_p^{0}\cdot(\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}})^{-1} \\ \hline \ce{CO2(g)} & 0.0024 & -393.5 & 213.8 & 37.1 \\ \ce{N2(g)} & 0.0134 & 0.0 & 191.6 & 29.1 \\ \ce{CH4(g)} & 0.9732 & -74.6 & 186.3 & 35.7 \\ \ce{C2H6(g)} & 0.0110 & -84.0 & 229.2 & 52.5 \\ \ce{H2O(l)} & - & -285.8 & 70.0 & 75.3 \\ \ce{H2O(g)} & - & -241.8 & 188.8 & 33.6 \\ \ce{O2(g)} & - & 0.0 & 205.2 & 29.4 \end{array}$$

Equation:

$$J = E\cdot(A\cdot\Delta t)^{-1} = \lambda_\mathrm{wall}\cdot\Delta T\cdot d^{-1}$$

• $J$: energy flow $E$ along a temperature gradient (wall direction z) per area $A$ and time $\Delta t$
• $d$: wall thickness

problems.title: Kinetics at catalyst surfaces

problems.title: Monovalent alkaline earth compounds?
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (21 points). Monovalent alkaline earth compounds?

In the past there have been several reports on compounds of monovalent calcium. Until recently the nature of these "compounds" was not known but they are still of great interest to solid state chemists.

Attempts to reduce $\ce{CaCl2}$ to $\ce{CaCl}$ have been made with

(a) Calcium (b) Hydrogen (c) Carbon

3.1 Give the corresponding reaction equations that could potentially lead to the formation of $\ce{CaCl}$.

After an attempt to reduce $\ce{CaCl2}$ with the stoichiometric 1:1 molar amount of Ca one obtains an inhomogeneous grey substance. A closer look under the microscope reveals silvery metallic particles and colorless crystals.

3.2 What substance are the metallic particles and the colorless crystals?

When $\ce{CaCl2}$ is attempted to be reduced with elemental hydrogen a white product forms. Elemental analysis shows that the sample contains $52.36$ m/m% of calcium and $46.32$ m/m% of chlorine.

3.3 Determine the empirical formula of the compound formed!

When $\ce{CaCl2}$ is attempted to be reduced with elemental carbon a red crystalline product forms. The molar ratio of Ca and Cl determined by elemental analysis is $n(\mathrm{Ca}):n(\mathrm{Cl}) = 1.5:1$. During the hydrolysis of the red crystalline substance the same gas is evolved as during the hydrolysis of $\ce{Mg2C3}$.

3.4 a) Show the two acyclic constitutional isomers of the gas that is formed by hydrolysis.

b) What compound is formed by the reaction of $\ce{CaCl2}$ with carbon? (Provided that monovalent calcium does not exist.)

As none of these attempts lead to the formation of $\ce{CaCl}$ more consideration has to be given as to the hypothetical structure of $\ce{CaCl}$. One can assume that $\ce{CaCl}$ is likely to crystallize in a simple crystal structure.

It is the radius ratio of cation $r(\mathrm{M}^{m+})$ and anion $r(\mathrm{X}^{x-})$ of salts that often determines the crystal structure of a particular compound as shown for MX compounds in the table below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} \text{Coordination number of M} & \text{Surrounding of X} & \text{Radius ratio } r_\mathrm{M}/r_\mathrm{X} & \text{Structure type} & \text{estimated } \Delta_\mathrm{L}H^{0} \text{ for CaCl} \\ \hline 3 & \text{Triangular} & 0.155\text{–}0.225 & \text{BN} & -663.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ 4 & \text{Tetrahedral} & 0.225\text{–}0.414 & \text{ZnS} & -704.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ 6 & \text{Octahedral} & 0.414\text{–}0.732 & \text{NaCl} & -751.9\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ 8 & \text{Cubic} & 0.732\text{–}1.000 & \text{CsCl} & -758.4\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \end{array}$$

$\Delta_\mathrm{L}H^{0}(\mathrm{CaCl})$ is defined for the reaction $\ce{Ca+(g) + Cl-(g) -> CaCl(s)}$

3.5 a) What type of structure is $\ce{CaCl}$ likely to have? [$r(\ce{Ca+}) \approx 120\,\mathrm{pm}$ (estimated), $r(\ce{Cl-}) \approx 167\,\mathrm{pm}$]

Not only the lattice energy $\Delta_\mathrm{L}H^{0}$ for $\ce{CaCl}$ is important for the decision whether $\ce{CaCl}$ is thermodynamically stable or not. In order to decide whether it is stable to decompositon into its elements, the standard enthalpy of formation $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^{0}$ of $\ce{CaCl}$ has to be known.

3.5 b) Calculate the value of $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^{0}(\mathrm{CaCl})$ with the aid of a Born-Haber-cycle.

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l|r} \text{heat of fusion} & \Delta_\mathrm{fusion}H^{0}(\mathrm{Ca}) & & 9.3\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \text{ionization enthalpy} & \Delta_\mathrm{1.\,IE}H(\mathrm{Ca}) & \ce{Ca -> Ca+} & 589.7\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \text{ionization enthalpy} & \Delta_\mathrm{2.\,IE}H(\mathrm{Ca}) & \ce{Ca+ -> Ca^{2+}} & 1145.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \text{heat of vaporization} & \Delta_\mathrm{vap}H^{0}(\mathrm{Ca}) & & 150.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \text{dissociation energy} & \Delta_\mathrm{diss}H(\ce{Cl2}) & \ce{Cl2 -> 2 Cl} & 240.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \text{enthalpy of formation} & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^{0}(\ce{CaCl2}) & & -796.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \\ \text{electron affinity} & \Delta_\mathrm{EA}H(\mathrm{Cl}) & \ce{Cl + e- -> Cl-} & -349.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} \end{array}$$

To decide whether $\ce{CaCl}$ is thermodynamically stable to disproportionation into Ca and $\ce{CaCl2}$ the standard enthalpy of this process has to be calculated. (The change of the entropy $\Delta S$ is very small in this case, so its influence is negligible.)

3.6 Does the disproportionation of $\ce{CaCl}$ take place from a thermodynamic point of view? Base your decision on a calculation!

problems.title: Determining atomic masses
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (20 points). Determining atomic masses

The reaction of the element X with hydrogen leads to a class of compounds that is analogous to hydrocarbons. $5.000\,\mathrm{g}$ of X form $5.628\,\mathrm{g}$ of a molar 2:1 mixture of the stoichiometric X-analogues of methane and ethane, respectively.

4.1 Determine the molar mass of X from this information. Give the chemical symbol of X, and the 3D-structure of the two products.

The following more complex case is of great historical interest.

The mineral Argyrodite is a stoichiometric compound that contains silver (oxidation state $+1$), sulphur (oxidation state $-2$) and an unknown element Y (oxidation state $+4$). The ratio between the masses of silver and Y in Argyrodite is $m(\mathrm{Ag}):m(\mathrm{Y}) = 11.88:1$. Y forms a reddish brown lower sulfide (oxidation state of Y is $+2$) and a higher white sulfide (oxidation state of Y is $+4$). The coloured lower sulfide is the sublimate obtained by heating Argyrodite in a flow of hydrogen. The residues are $\ce{Ag2S}$ and $\ce{H2S}$. To convert $10.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of Argyrodite completely, $0.295\,\mathrm{L}$ of hydrogen are needed at $400\,\mathrm{K}$ and $100\,\mathrm{kPa}$.

4.2 Determine the molar mass of Y from this information. Give the chemical symbol of Y, and the empirical formula of Argyrodite.

The atomic masses are correlated with spectroscopic properties.

To determine the vibrational frequency $\tilde{\nu}$ expressed in wave numbers of chemical bonds in IR spectra chemists use Hooke's law which focuses on the frequency of the vibration (attention to units!):

$$\tilde{\nu} = \frac{1}{2\pi c}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}$$

• $\tilde{\nu}$: vibrational frequency of the bond, in wavenumbers ($\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$)
• $c$: speed of light
• $k$: force constant, indicating the strength of the bond ($\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}} = \mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}$)
• $\mu$: reduced mass in $\mathrm{AB_4}$, which is given by $\mu = \dfrac{3m(\mathrm{A})\,m(\mathrm{B})}{3m(\mathrm{A}) + 4m(\mathrm{B})}$
• $m(\mathrm{A})$, $m(\mathrm{B})$: the masses of the two bond atoms

The vibrational frequency of the C–H bond of methane is known to be $3030.00\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. The vibrational frequency of the Z-analogue of methane is known to be $2938.45\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$. The bond enthalpy of a C–H bond in methane is $438.4\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The bond enthalpy of a Z–H bond in the Z-analogue of methane is known to be $450.2\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

4.3 Determine the force constant $k$ of a C–H bond using Hooke's law. Estimate the force constant $k$ of a Z–H bond, assuming that there is a linear proportionality between force constant and bond enthalpy. Determine the atomic mass of Z from this information. Give the chemical symbol of Z

problems.title: Biochemistry with Thermodynamics
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (18 points). Biochemistry with Thermodynamics

Structure of $\ce{ATP^{4-}}$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2004-5-fig1.png

Shifting chemical equilibria with ATP:

Animals use free energy from the oxidation of their food to maintain concentrations of ATP, ADP, and phosphate far from equilibrium. In red blood cells the following concentrations have been measured:

$$c(\ce{ATP^{4-}}) = 2.25\,\mathrm{mmol\,L^{-1}}\qquad c(\ce{ADP^{3-}}) = 0.25\,\mathrm{mmol\,L^{-1}}\qquad c(\ce{HPO4^{2-}}) = 1.65\,\mathrm{mmol\,L^{-1}}$$

Free energy stored in ATP can be released according to the following reaction:

$$\ce{ATP^{4-} + H2O <=> ADP^{3-} + HPO4^{2-} + H+}\qquad \Delta G^{\circ\prime} = -30.5\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\qquad (1)$$

As the pH is close to 7 in most living cells, biochemists use $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ instead of $\Delta G^{\circ}$. The standard state of $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ is defined as having a constant pH of 7. In equations with $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ and $K'$ for reactions at pH = 7 the concentration of $\ce{H+}$ is therefore omitted. Standard concentration is $1\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$.

5.1 Calculate the actual $\Delta G'$ of reaction (1) in the red blood cell at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and pH = 7.

In living cells many so-called "anabolic" reactions take place, which are at first sight thermodynamically unfavourable because of a positive $\Delta G$. The phosphorylation of glucose is an example:

$$\text{glucose} + \ce{HPO4^{2-}} \rightleftarrows \text{glucose 6-phosphate}^{2-} + \ce{H2O}\qquad \Delta G^{\circ\prime} = +13.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\qquad (2)$$

5.2 Calculate first the equilibrium constant $K'$ of reaction (2) and then the ratio $c(\text{glucose 6-phosphate})/c(\text{glucose})$ in the red blood cell in chemical equilibrium at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and pH = 7.

To shift the equilibrium to a higher concentration of glucose 6-phosphate, reaction (2) is coupled with hydrolysis of ATP:

$$\text{glucose} + \ce{ATP^{4-}} \overset{\text{hexokinase}}{\rightleftarrows} \text{glucose 6-phosphate}^{2-} + \ce{ADP^{3-} + H+}\qquad (3)$$

5.3 Calculate $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ and $K'$ of reaction (3). What is now the ratio $c(\text{glucose 6-phosphate})/c(\text{glucose})$ in the red blood cell in chemical equilibrium at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and pH = 7?

ATP synthesis:

An adult person ingests about $8000\,\mathrm{kJ}$ of energy ($\Delta G'$) per day with the food.

5.4 a) What will be the mass of ATP that is produced per day if half of this energy is used for ATP synthesis? Assume a $\Delta G'$ of $-52\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for reaction (1), and a molecular weight of $503\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ for ATP.

b) What mass of ATP does the human body contain on average if the mean lifetime of an ATP molecule until its hydrolysis is 1 min?

c) What happens to the rest of the free energy, which is not used for ATP synthesis? Mark on the answer sheet. [Answer sheet: mark one correct answer.]

• It is used to reduce the entropy of the body.
• It is released from the body in the O–H bonds of the water molecule and the C=O bonds of the carbon dioxide molecule.
• It is used to regenerate the state of the enzymes which act as catalysts in the production of ATP.
• It heats the body of the person.

In animals the energy obtained by the oxidation of food is used to pump protons out of specialized membrane vesicles, the mitochondria. ATP-synthase, an enzyme, will allow protons to re-enter the mitochondria if ATP is simultaneously synthesized from ADP and phosphate.

5.5 a) How many protons ($\ce{H+}$) are in a spherical mitochondrium with a diameter of $1\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ at pH = 7?

b) How many protons have to enter into each of the 1000 mitochondria of a liver cell via the ATP-synthase to allow the production of a mass of $0.2\,\mathrm{fg}$ of ATP per cell? Assume that 3 protons have to enter for the synthesis of 1 molecule of ATP.

problems.title: Diels-Alder Reactions
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (20 points). Diels-Alder Reactions

The Diels-Alder reaction, a concerted [4+2]-cycloaddition between a diene and an olefin to yield a cyclohexene, was discovered in 1928 here in Kiel. Prof. Otto Diels and his coworker Kurt Alder mixed p-benzoquinone with an excess of cyclopentadiene and obtained the following result:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2004-6-fig1.png

6.1 Draw the structure of $\mathbf{A}$ (without stereochemical information).

The Diels-Alder reaction is a concerted, one-step reaction that proceeds with high stereospecificity. For example, only a single stereoisomer $\mathbf{C}$ is formed in the following reaction

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2004-6-fig2.png

If you use the E-isomer of the alkene instead, you will obtain two other stereoisomers $\mathbf{D1}$ and $\mathbf{D2}$.

6.2 Give the structures of $\mathbf{D1}$ and $\mathbf{D2}$.

Accordingly, in the original reaction (formation of $\mathbf{B}$ from cyclopentadiene and benzoquinone) Diels and Alder found only one of the following six conceivable stereoisomers of $\mathbf{B}$ (see next page).

Hints:

• keep the stereospecific formation of $\mathbf{C}$ in mind and
• the sterically less hindered isomer forms.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2004-6-fig3.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2004-6-fig4.png

6.3 Which single isomer of the six stereoisomers 1–6 of $\mathbf{B}$ shown above did they isolate?

After prolonged heating (15 h, $120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) of the originally isolated stereoisomer $\mathbf{B}$ (melting point mp: $157\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), Diels and Alder obtained two new stereoisomers $\mathbf{E}$ (mp: $153\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and $\mathbf{F}$ (mp: $163\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Equilibration of $\mathbf{B}$ with a catalytic amount of a strong base at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ gave a further stereoisomer $\mathbf{G}$ (mp: $184\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2004-6-fig5.png

6.4 Decide the questions on the answer sheet concerning the Diels-Alder reaction. [Answer sheet: for each statement, tick true, false or no decision possible.]

• The Diels-Alder reaction is reversible
• The formation of $\mathbf{B}$ in the original reaction is thermodynamically controlled
• $\mathbf{B}$ is thermodynamically more stable than $\mathbf{E}$
• $\mathbf{E}$ is thermodynamically less stable than $\mathbf{F}$
• $\mathbf{G}$ is an enantiomer of $\mathbf{B}$
• $\mathbf{G}$ is thermodynamically more stable than $\mathbf{F}$

Hint: You do not need to know, which of the six stereoisomers 1–6 (shown above) corresponds to either $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$ or $\mathbf{G}$ in order to anwer this question.

The Diels-Alder reaction plays also an important role in the following reaction sequence.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2004-6-fig6.png

6.5 Draw the structures for $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$.

Hints:

• $\mathbf{K}$ has only one methyl group.
• $\mathbf{L}$ is the Diels-Alder adduct of $\mathbf{K}$ and the alkene shown.

problems.title: Gold Capital of Asia
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (42 points). Gold Capital of Asia

A

Chiufen, the old mining town located within the hills in the northeast Taiwan, is a place where you can really experience Taiwan's historical legacy. It was the site of one of the largest gold mines in Asia. Accordingly, Chiufen is often referred to as the Gold Capital of Asia. The compound $\ce{KCN}$ is traditionally used to extract gold from ore. Gold dissolves in cyanide ($\ce{CN-}$) solutions in the presence of air to form $\ce{Au(CN)2-}$, which is stable in aqueous solution.

$$\ce{4 Au(s) + 8 CN^-(aq) + O2(g) + 2 H2O(l) <=> 4 Au(CN)2^-(aq) + 4 OH^-(aq)}$$

4A-1 (2 pt) Draw a structure for $\ce{Au(CN)2-}$ showing the spatial arrangements of the atoms.

4A-2 (4 pt) How many grams of $\ce{KCN}$ are needed to extract $20\,\mathrm{g}$ of gold from ore? Show your work.

Aqua regia, a 3:1 mixture (by volume) of concentrated hydrochloric acid and nitric acid, was developed by the alchemists as a means to "dissolve" gold. The process is actually a redox reaction with the following simplified chemical equation:

$$\ce{Au(s) + NO3^-(aq) + Cl^-(aq) <=> AuCl4^-(aq) + NO2(g)}$$

4A-3 (4 pt) Write down the half reactions, and use them to obtain a balanced redox reaction for this process.

4A-4 (2 pt) What are the oxidizing and reducing agents for 4A-3 process?

Gold is too noble to react with nitric acid. However, gold does react with aqua regia because the complex ion $\ce{AuCl4-}$ forms. Consider the following half-reactions:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{Au^{3+}(aq) + 3 e^- -> Au(s)} & E^\circ = +1.50\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{AuCl4^-(aq) + 3 e^- -> Au(s) + 4 Cl^-(aq)} & E^\circ = +1.00\,\mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

An electrochemical cell can be formed from these two redox couples.

4A-5 (6 pt) Calculate the formation constant for $\ce{AuCl4-}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$:

$$K = [\ce{AuCl4-}]\,/\,[\ce{Au^{3+}}]\,[\ce{Cl-}]^4$$

4A-6 (2 pt) The function of $\ce{HCl}$ is to provide $\ce{Cl-}$. What is the purpose of the $\ce{Cl-}$ for the above reaction. Select your answer from the following choices.

(a) $\ce{Cl-}$ is an oxidizing agent

(b) $\ce{Cl-}$ is a reducing agent

(c) $\ce{Cl-}$ is a complexing agent

(d) $\ce{Cl-}$ is a catalyst

B

Gold Nanoparticles

The synthesis and characterization of gold nanoparticles is currently an active research area. The Brust-Schiffrin method for the synthesis of gold nanoparticle (AuNP) allows the facile preparation of thermally stable and air-stable AuNPs of reduced polydispersity with a controlled size distribution ranging in diameter between $1.5$ and $5.2\,\mathrm{nm}$. The preparative procedure is briefly described as follows. An aqueous solution of $\ce{HAuCl4}$ is mixed with a toluene solution of tetra-$n$-octylammonium bromide. The solution is mixed with dodecanethiol and is treated with an excess of $\ce{NaBH4}$. Formation of the AuNPs is evidenced by the immediate, pronounced darkening of the toluene phase. After ca. 24 h, the toluene solvent is removed with a rotary evaporator and the resulting solid washed on a frit with ethanol and hexane to remove excess thiol. These AuNPs can be repeatedly isolated and re-dissolved in common organic solvents without irreversible aggregation or decomposition.

4B-1 (2 pt) Is the methodology for this fabrication referred to a top-down or a bottom-up approach? Select your answer from the following choices.

(a) top-down approach, which entails reducing the size of the smallest structures to the nanoscale

(b) bottom-up approach, which involves manipulating individual atoms and molecules into nanostructures

4B-2 (2 pt) The trimethyl-$n$-octylammonium bromide can also be used as a phase-transfer reagent. It can carry $\ce{AuCl4-}$ from an aqueous phase to an organic phase. Which property does trimethyl-$n$-octylammonium bromide possess to function as an efficient phase-transfer reagent? Select your answer from the following choices.

(a) one side of the molecule is electropositive, the other side is electronegative.

(b) one side of the molecule is hydrophilic, the other side is hydrophobic.

(c) one side of the molecule is acidic, the other side is basic.

4B-3 (2 pt) What is the function of $\ce{NaBH4}$ in this preparation? Select your answer from the following choices.

(a) reducing agent

(b) oxidizing agent

(c) neutralization agent

(d) complexing agent

(a) $10^{2}$

(b) $10^{3}$

(c) $10^{4}$

(d) $10^{5}$

(a) 20–30%

(b) 40–50%

(c) 60–70%

(d) 80–90%

problems.title: Alkalinity of Water and Solubility of CO2
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (40 points). Alkalinity of Water and Solubility of $\ce{CO2}$

The capacity of water to accept $\ce{H+}$ ions is called alkalinity. Alkalinity is important in water treatment and in the chemistry and biology of natural waters. Generally, the basic species responsible for alkalinity in water are $\ce{HCO3-}$, $\ce{CO3^{2-}}$, and $\ce{OH-}$. At pH values below 7, $\ce{H+}$ in water detracts significantly from alkalinity. Therefore, the complete equation for alkalinity in a medium where $\ce{HCO3-}$, $\ce{CO3^{2-}}$, and $\ce{OH-}$ are the only contributors to alkalinity can be expressed as

$$\text{alkalinity} = [\ce{HCO3-}] + 2[\ce{CO3^{2-}}] + [\ce{OH-}] - [\ce{H+}]$$

The contributions made by different species to alkalinity depend upon pH. Relevant chemical equations and equilibrium constants (at 298 K) are shown below:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{CO2_{(g)} <=> CO2_{(aq)}} & K_{\ce{CO2}} = 3.44\times10^{-2} \\ \ce{CO2_{(aq)} + H2O <=> H2CO3} & K_{\ce{H2CO3}} = 2.00\times10^{-3} \\ \ce{H2CO3 <=> HCO3- + H+} & K_\mathrm{a1} = 2.23\times10^{-4} \\ \ce{HCO3- <=> CO3^{2-} + H+} & K_\mathrm{a2} = 4.69\times10^{-11} \\ \ce{CaCO3_{(s)} <=> Ca^{2+} + CO3^{2-}} & K_\mathrm{sp} = 4.50\times10^{-9} \\ \ce{H2O <=> H+ + OH-} & K_\mathrm{w} = 1.00\times10^{-14} \end{array}$$

Note: Calculations must be shown.

6-1 (4 pt) Natural waters (river or lake water) generally contain dissolved $\ce{CO2}$. The ratio of $[\ce{H2CO3}] : [\ce{HCO3-}] : [\ce{CO3^{2-}}]$ in a water at $[\ce{H+}] = 1.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{M}$ will be: (a) : 1.00 : (b). Calculate (a) and (b).

6-2 (4 pt) Gaseous $\ce{CO2}$ in the atmosphere can be regarded as a contributor to the alkalinity of water in equilibrium with air. Calculate the concentration of $\ce{CO2_{(aq)}}$ (mol/L) in pure water that is in equilibrium with the unpolluted air at $1.01\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$ and $298\,\mathrm{K}$ containing $0.0360\%$ (molar ratio) $\ce{CO2}$. (assuming standard pressure $= 1.01\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$)

If you are unable to solve this problem, assume that concentration of $\ce{CO2_{(aq)}} = 1.11\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{M}$ for further calculations.

The solubility ($S$) of $\ce{CO2}$ in water can be defined as $S = [\ce{CO2_{(aq)}}] + [\ce{H2CO3}] + [\ce{HCO3-}] + [\ce{CO3^{2-}}]$. The solubility of atmospheric $\ce{CO2}$ in water that is in equilibrium with the unpolluted air at $298\,\mathrm{K}$ and $1.01\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$ will vary with alkalinity.

6-3 (6 pt) Find the solubility of atmospheric $\ce{CO2}$ in pure water (mol/L). Neglect dissociation of water.

6-4 (6 pt) Find the solubility of atmospheric $\ce{CO2}$ in water (mol/L) initially containing $1.00\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ $\ce{NaOH}$.

At $298\,\mathrm{K}$, $1.01\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{Pa}$ unpolluted air is in equilibrium with natural water saturated with $\ce{CaCO3}$. The following main equilibrium may exist:

$$\ce{CaCO3_{(s)} + CO2_{(aq)} + H2O <=> Ca^{2+} + 2 HCO3-}$$

6-5 (4 pt) Calculate the equilibrium constant for the above equation.

If you are unable to solve this problem, assume that equilibrium constant $K_\mathrm{eq} = 5.00\times10^{-5}$ for further calculations.

6-6 (6 pt) Calculate the concentration of $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ (mg/L) in $\ce{CaCO3}$-saturated natural water that is in equilibrium with atmospheric $\ce{CO2}$.

If you are unable to solve this problem, assume that concentration of $\ce{Ca^{2+}_{(aq)}} = 40.1\,\mathrm{mg/L}$ for further calculations.

6-7 (6 pt) Find the alkalinity (mol/L) of the above solution.

6-8 (4 pt) In an underground lake saturated with $\ce{CaCO3}$, the water has a high content of $\ce{CO2}$. The concentration of $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ in this lake was found to be as high as $100\,\mathrm{mg/L}$. Assume the lake and the air above is a closed system, calculate the effective pressure of $\ce{CO2}$ (Pa) in air which is in equilibrium with this $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ content.

problems.title: Kinetic Behavior of Ozone
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (28 points). Kinetic Behavior of Ozone

Ozone ($\ce{O3}$) is a form of oxygen. It is a natural component of the stratosphere, where it shields the earth from life-destroying ultraviolet radiation. On absorbing light in this region, ozone is converted to dioxygen molecules.

For the overall reaction of ozone decomposition,

$$\ce{2 O3 -> 3 O2}.$$

One of the proposed mechanisms is expressed as

$$\begin{array}{lr} \ce{O3} \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} \ce{O + O2} & \qquad (1) \\ \ce{O3 + O} \xrightarrow{k_2} \ce{2 O2} & \qquad (2) \end{array}$$

where $k_1$, $k_{-1}$, and $k_2$ are the rate constants.

7-1 (6 pt) According to the above mechanism what are the differential rate equations for the formation (or consumption) of $\ce{O3}$, $\ce{O2}$, and O at time $t$, assuming step 2 is irreversible.

7-2 (6 pt) Simplification in obtaining the rate law may be found by making appropriate assumptions. Assuming that the concentration of O atoms reaches equilibrium rapidly, its concentration may be given by the equilibrium constant of the reaction (1). The second step is rate determining. Under this equilibrium approximation, deduce the differential rate equation for the $\ce{O3}$ depletion as a function of $\ce{O2}$ and $\ce{O3}$ concentrations.

7-3 (6 pt) Another assumption frequently made is that the rates of oxygen atom production and consumption are equal (this is called steady state). Under the steady state approximation, that is $\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{O}]/\mathrm{d}t = 0$, show that the rate equation is:

$$-\frac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{O3}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{2k_1k_2[\ce{O3}]^2}{k_{-1}[\ce{O2}] + k_2[\ce{O3}]}.$$

One pathway for the destruction of ozone ($\ce{2 O3 -> 3 O2}$) in the upper atmosphere is catalyzed by Freons. For instance, when $\ce{CCl2F2}$ (Freon-12) migrates to the upper atmosphere, the ultraviolet photolysis of $\ce{CCl2F2}$ may give rise to Cl atoms according to the following reaction:

$$\ce{CCl2F2} \xrightarrow{h\nu} \ce{CF2Cl + Cl} \qquad (3)$$

7-4 (4 pt) Chlorine atom can act as a catalyst for the destruction of ozone. The first slow step of a Cl-catalyzed mechanism is proposed as follows:

$$\ce{Cl_{(g)} + O3_{(g)} -> ClO_{(g)} + O2_{(g)}} \qquad (4)$$

Assuming a two-step mechanism, propose the second step in the mechanism.

7-5 (6 pt) The activation energy for Cl-catalyzed destruction of ozone is $2.1\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$, while the activation energy for the reaction without the presence of catalyst is $14.0\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. Estimate the ratio of the rate constant for the catalyzed reaction to that for the uncatalyzed reaction at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assume the frequency factor is the same for each reaction.

problems.title: Protein Folding
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (26 points). Protein Folding

Most proteins exist usually only in two forms, the native form (N) and the unfolded form (U) when they are thermally or chemically denatured, without appreciable concentrations of other stable intermediates in equilibrium with the native and unfolded forms. For these proteins, the folding-unfolding equilibrium can be described by the following simple chemical equation:

$$\mathrm{N} \overset{K(T)}{\rightleftharpoons} \mathrm{U}$$

where N and U denote the folded state (native state) and the unfolded state (denatured state) of the protein, respectively. $K(T)$ is the equilibrium constant for the process at absolute temperature $T$.

8-1 (2 pt) What is the equilibrium constant for the process when the native and denatured states are present in equal proportions at equilibrium?

8-2 (2 pt) What is the standard free energy change of the process ($\Delta G^\circ(T)$) when the native and denatured states are present in equal proportions at equilibrium? Express your answer in SI units.

8-3 (6 pt) If $(C_\mathrm{N})_\mathrm{eq}$ and $(C_\mathrm{U})_\mathrm{eq}$ denote the equilibrium concentrations of N and U in solution, respectively, and $C$ is the total concentration of the protein, the fraction of the total protein that is unfolded under the equilibrium condition is given by $f_\mathrm{U} = (C_\mathrm{U})_\mathrm{eq}/C$. Deduce an expression for $f_\mathrm{U}$ in terms of the equilibrium constant $K$. Show all work on the answer sheet.

When a protein is denatured by increasing the temperature of the solution, the fraction of the unfolded protein increases with temperature, as shown in the following Figure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2005-8-fig1.png

The mid-point of the denaturation curve is given by $f_\mathrm{U} = 1/2$ and $T = T_{1/2}$. The latter is often referred to as the denaturation temperature. At temperatures higher than $T_{1/2}$, $f_\mathrm{U}$ increases above $1/2$, but at temperatures lower than $T_{1/2}$, $f_\mathrm{U}$ decreases below $1/2$.

8-4 (4 pt) What is the sign of $\Delta G^\circ(T)$ at temperatures below and above $T_{1/2}$? Select your answer from the following choices.

(a) Negative both below and above $T_{1/2}$

(b) Positive both below and above $T_{1/2}$

(c) Positive below $T_{1/2}$, but negative above $T_{1/2}$

(d) Negative below $T_{1/2}$, but positive above $T_{1/2}$.

8-5 (4 pt) How does the standard Gibbs free energy change for the process vary when the temperature (i) increases above $T_{1/2}$ and (ii) decreases below $T_{1/2}$? Select your answer from the following choices.

(a) Decrease in both cases.

(b) Increase in both cases.

(c) Increases above $T_{1/2}$, but decreases below $T_{1/2}$

(d) Decreases above $T_{1/2}$, but increases below $T_{1/2}$

The kinetics of unfolding and refolding of a protein has recently become an intense area of study. We could rewrite the chemical equation for the process as follows:

$$\mathrm{N} \underset{k_\mathrm{b}}{\overset{k_\mathrm{f}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \mathrm{U}$$

where $k_\mathrm{f}$ and $k_\mathrm{b}$ denote the forward and backward reaction rate constants, respectively., assuming that both the forward and reverse processes are elementary steps that follow first-order kinetics.

8-6 (2 pt) For the simple chemical equation and elementary kinetic steps used to describe the protein folding-unfolding process outlined above, what is the relationship between equilibrium constant $K$ and the rate constants $k_\mathrm{f}$ and $k_\mathrm{b}$?

8-7 (6 pt) Derive a rate law for the overall process, that is $\mathrm{d}C_\mathrm{U}/\mathrm{d}t$ in terms of only rate constants, $C_\mathrm{U}$ and $(C_\mathrm{U})_\mathrm{eq}$.

problems.title: Detection of Hydrogen
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (5 pts). Detection of Hydrogen

Hydrogen is prevalent in the universe. Life in the universe is ultimately based on hydrogen.

2-1. (30 marks) There are about $10^{23}$ stars in the universe. Assume that they are like our sun (radius, $700{,}000\,\mathrm{km}$; density, $1.4\,\mathrm{g/cm^{3}}$; 3/4 hydrogen and 1/4 helium by mass). Estimate the number of stellar protons in the universe to one significant figure.

The ground state of hydrogen is split into two hyperfine levels due to the interaction between the magnetic moment of the proton and that of the electron. In 1951, Purcell discovered a spectral line at $1420\,\mathrm{MHz}$ due to the hyperfine transition of hydrogen in interstellar space.

2-4. (20 marks) Hydrogen in interstellar space cannot be excited electronically by starlight. However, the cosmic background radiation, equivalent to $2.7\,\mathrm{K}$, can cause the hyperfine transition. Calculate the temperature of a blackbody whose peak intensity corresponds to the $1420\,\mathrm{MHz}$ transition.

2-5. (10 marks) Wien generated hydrogen ions by discharge of hydrogen gas at a very low pressure and determined the $e/m$ value, which turned out to be the highest among different gases tested. Rutherford named this particle the "proton". Fill in the blank.

$$\ce{^{14}N + ^{4}He} \longrightarrow (\qquad\quad) + \ce{^{1}H}$$

problems.title: Interstellar Chemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (5 pts). Interstellar Chemistry

Early interstellar chemistry is thought to have been a prelude to life on Earth. Molecules can be formed in space via heterogeneous reactions at the surface of dust particles, often called the interstellar ice grains (IIGs). Imagine the reaction between H and C atoms on the IIG surface that forms CH. The CH product can either desorb from the surface or further react, through surface migration, with adsorbed H atoms to form $\ce{CH2}$, $\ce{CH3}$, etc.

Depending on how energetically a molecule "jumps" from its anchored site, it either leaves the surface permanently (desorption) or returns to a new position at the surface (migration). The rates of desorption and migratory jump follow the Arrhenius formula, $k = A\exp(-E/RT)$, where $k$ is the rate constant for desorption or migratory jump, $A$ the jumping frequency, and $E$ the activation energy for the respective event.

3-1. (30 marks) Desorption of CH from the IIG surface follows first-order kinetics. Calculate the average residence time of CH on the surface at $20\,\mathrm{K}$. Assume that $A = 1\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $E_\mathrm{des} = 12\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

3-2. (30 marks) Consider the shortest time it would take for one CH unit to move from its initial position to the opposite side of an IIG by successive migratory jumps. Assume that the activation energy for migration ($E_\mathrm{mig}$) is $6\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, and the IIG is a sphere with a $0.1\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ radius. Each migratory jump laterally advances the molecule by $0.3\,\mathrm{nm}$. Show work and choose your answer from (a)–(e) below.

(a) $t \le 1$ day     (b) $10$ day $\le t \le 10^{2}$ yr     (c) $10^{3}$ yr $\le t \le 10^{6}$ yr     (d) $10^{7}$ yr $\le t \le 10^{10}$ yr     (e) $t \ge 10^{11}$ yr

3-3. (25 marks) Consider the reaction of CO with $\ce{H2}$ to form $\ce{H2CO}$. The activation energy on a metal catalyst is $20\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, which produces formaldehyde at a rate of 1 molecule/s per site at $300\,\mathrm{K}$. Esitmate the rate of formaldehyde formation per site if the reaction takes place at $20\,\mathrm{K}$.

3-4. (15 marks) Which is a set of all true statements? Circle one.

(a) Most CH species desorb from the IIG surface before encountering other reactants by surface migration.

(b) IIGs can assist transformation of simple molecules to more complex ones in interstellar space.

(c) For a reaction on the IIG to occur at an appreciable speed during the age of the Universe ($1\times10^{10}$ yr), the reaction energy barrier must be absent or negligible.

(a)     (b)     (c)     (a, b)     (a, c)     (b, c)     (a, b, c)

problems.title: The Chemistry of DNA
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (5 pts). The Chemistry of DNA

4-1. (20 marks) In 1944 Oswald Avery isolated a genetic material and showed, by elemental analysis, that it was a sodium salt of deoxyribonucleic acid. A segment of DNA with formula mass of 1323.72 is shown.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2006-4-fig1.png

Assuming that equimolar amounts of the four bases are present in DNA, write the number of H atoms per P atom. Calculate, to 3 significant figures, the theoretical weight percentage of H expected upon elemental analysis of DNA.

problems.title: Electrochemistry

Problem 6 (5 pts). Electrochemistry

Water is a very stable molecule, abundant on earth and essential for life. As such, water was long thought to be a chemical element. However, soon after the invention of a voltaic cell in 1800, Nicholson and Carlyle decomposed water into hydrogen and oxygen by electrolysis.

6-1. (5 marks) Water can be thought of as hydrogen oxidized by oxygen. Thus, hydrogen can be recovered by reduction of water, using an aqueous solution of sodium sulfate, at a platinum electrode connected to the negative terminal of a battery. The solution near the electrode becomes basic. Write a balanced half-reaction for the reduction of water.

6-2. (5 marks) Water can also be thought of as oxygen reduced by hydrogen. Thus, oxygen can be recovered by oxidation of water at the Pt electrode connected to the positive terminal. Write a balanced half-reaction for the oxidation of water.

6-3. (5 marks) When copper is used at both electrodes, gas is generated only at one electrode during the initial stage of electrolysis. Write the half-reaction at the electrode that does not generate gas.

Another species in solution that can be reduced is sodium ion. The reduction of sodium ion to metallic sodium does not occur in aqueous solution, because water is reduced first. However, as Humphrey Davy discovered in 1807, sodium can be made by electrolysis of fused sodium chloride.

6-4. (20 marks) Based on these observations, connect the half-reactions with the standard reduction potential (in volts).

Problem 8 (5 pts). Chemistry of Iron Oxides

The nucleus of iron is the most stable among all elements and, therefore, iron accumulates at the core of massive red giant stars where nucleosynthesis of many elements essential for life (such as C, N, O, P, S, etc.) takes place. $$\begin{array}{lll} \ce{C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g)} & \Delta H^\circ = -393.51\ \mathrm{kJ(/mol)} & \text{①} \\ \ce{CO2(g) + C(s) -> 2CO(g)} & \Delta H^\circ = 172.46\ \mathrm{kJ(/mol)} & \text{②} \\ \ce{Fe2O3(s) + CO(g) -> Fe(s) + CO2(g)} & \Delta H^\circ = \ ? & \text{③} \end{array}$$

$\ce{Fe3O4}$ (magnetite) itself is a mixed oxide containing $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ ions and belongs to a group of compounds with a general formula of $\ce{AB2O4}$. problems.problem:
Problem 11 (7 pts). Enzyme Reaction

Shikimic acid biosynthesis is an important pathway for amino acids, alkaloids and heterocyclic natural product production. Nature converts shikimic acid to chorismic acid through a cascade of enzymatic reactions. Then chorismate mutase catalyzes the conversion of chorismic acid to prephenic acid at the branch point for the biosynthesis of aromatic amino acids such as tyrosine and phenylalanine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2006-11-fig1.png

11-1. (10 marks) During the transformation of shikimic acid to chorismic acid, dehydration is occurring. Choose the hydroxyl group in shikimic acid that is lost through above dehydration among all possible reactions.

11-2. (30 marks) Chorismate mutase rearranges chorismic acid into prephenic acid without changing the molecular formula. Chorismic acid becomes prephenic acid through the Claisen rearrangement, a concerted pericyclic process like the Cope rearrangement as shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2006-11-fig2.png

Based on the following spectral data, propose the structure of prephenic acid.

$\ce{^1H}$-NMR ($\ce{D2O}$, 250 MHz): $\delta$ 6.01 (2H, d, $J = 10.4\,\mathrm{Hz}$), 5.92 (2H, dd $J = 10.4$, $3.1\,\mathrm{Hz}$), 4.50 (1H, t, $J = 3.1\,\mathrm{Hz}$), 3.12 (2H, s). Note that there are three protons, which have been exchanged by $\ce{D2O}$ very fast, and two protons at $\delta$ 3.12, which are exchanged slowly in prephenic acid. $\ce{^{13}C}$-NMR ($\ce{D2O}$, 75 MHz): $\delta$ 203, 178, 173, 132 (for two identical carbons), 127 (for two identical carbons), 65, 49, 48.

$\delta$, chemical shift; H, integrals; d, doublet; dd, doublet of doublet; $J$, coupling constant; t, triplet; s, singlet

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2006-11-fig3.png

Inhibitors, called transition state analog (TSA)s that resemble the transition state (TS, e.g., the species in brackets "[ ]" above) of the reaction are designed to occupy the active site. Several inhibitors were designed and synthesized, and among them eight turned out to be potent inhibitors of the enzyme. The lower the $\mathrm{IC}_{50}$ (inhibitor concentration of 50% of the enzymatic activity) value, the better the inhibitor.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2006-11-fig4.png

(b) The presence of both carboxylic groups is important in the TS and inhibitor design.

(c) Transition state of the reaction contains two six-membered rings with one chair and one twist-boat conformation.

(d) $\mathbf{7}$ and $\mathbf{8}$ can be distinguished on the basis of the $\ce{^1H}$-NMR of $\mathrm{H_a}$.

Problem 1. Proton tunneling

Proton tunneling through energy barriers is an important effect, which can be observed in many complex species containing hydrogen bonds (DNA, proteins, etc.). Propanedial (malonaldehyde) is one of the simplest molecules for which intramolecular proton transfer can occur.

1.1.1 Draw the condensed formula of propanedial and the structures of two of its isomers, which can exist in equilibrium with propanedial.

1.1.2 In a water solution propanedial is a weak acid, its strength being comparable with that of acetic acid. Specify the acidic hydrogen atom. Explain its acidity (choose one version in the Answer Sheet).

On the plot below an energy profile of the intramolecular proton transfer is given (the dependence of energy on the distance of proton motion (in nm)). Energy curve has a symmetric double-well form.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2007-1-fig1.png

1.2.1 Draw the structures corresponding to two minima on this curve.

A proton is delocalized between two atoms and oscillates between two minima L and R with an angular frequency $\omega = 6.48\cdot10^{11}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Probability density for a proton depends on time as follows:

$$\Psi^2(x,t) = \frac{1}{2}\left[\Psi_\mathrm{L}^2(x) + \Psi_\mathrm{R}^2(x) + \left(\Psi_\mathrm{L}^2(x) - \Psi_\mathrm{R}^2(x)\right)\cos(\omega t)\right],$$

wave functions $\Psi_\mathrm{L}(x)$ and $\Psi_\mathrm{R}(x)$ describe a proton localized in the left and right wells, respectively:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2007-1-fig2.png

1.3.1 Write down the expressions for the probability density at three moments: (a) $t = 0$, (b) $t = \pi/(2\omega)$, (c) $t = \pi/\omega$. Sketch the graphs of these three functions.

1.3.2 Without calculations, determine the probability of finding the proton in the left well at $t = \pi/(2\omega)$

1.3.3 How much time is required for a proton to move from one well to another? What is the proton mean speed during the transfer?

1.3.4 From the energy curve, estimate the uncertainty of the position of proton forming hydrogen bonds. Estimate the minimal uncertainty of the proton speed. Compare this value with that obtained in 1.3.3 and draw a conclusion about the proton tunneling (choose one of the versions in the Answer Sheet).
