b.iii (6 pt) Use this model to create an energy level diagram for benzene and fill the pertinent energy levels with electrons. Include energy levels up to and including the lowest unoccupied energy level. Label each energy level in your diagrams with the corresponding $n_x$, $n_y$. Do not assume that the particle-in-a-square-box model used here gives the same energy levels as other models.

b.iv (4 pt) Often the reactivity of PAHs correlates inversely with the energy gap $\Delta E$ between the highest energy level occupied by $\pi$-electrons and the lowest unoccupied energy level. Calculate the energy gap $\Delta E$ (in Joules) between the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied energy levels for benzene, anthracene and pentacene. Use your result from parts ii) and iii) for anthracene or benzene, respectively, or use (2, 2) for the highest occupied energy level and (3, 2) for the lowest unoccupied energy level for these two molecules (these may not be the true values).

Rank benzene ($\mathbf{B}$), anthracene ($\mathbf{A}$), and pentacene ($\mathbf{P}$) in order of increasing reactivity by placing the corresponding letters from left to right in the box below.

Least reactive ----------------------------------> Most reactive

b.v (2 pt) The electronic absorption spectra (molar absorptivity vs. wavelength) for benzene ($\mathbf{B}$), anthracene ($\mathbf{A}$), and pentacene ($\mathbf{P}$) are shown below. Based on a qualitative understanding of the particle in the box model, indicate which molecule corresponds to which spectrum by writing the appropriate letter in the box to its right.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-8-fig2.png

c. Graphene is a sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a two-dimensional honeycomb pattern. It can be considered as an extreme case of a polyaromatic hydrocarbon with essentially infinite length in the two dimensions. The Nobel Prize for Physics was awarded in 2010 to Andrei Geim and Konstantin Novoselov for groundbreaking experiments on graphene.

Consider a sheet of graphene with planar dimensions of $L_x = 25\ \mathrm{nm}$ by $L_y = 25\ \mathrm{nm}$. A section of this sheet is shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-8-fig3.png

c.i (5 pt) The area of one hexagonal 6-carbon unit is $\sim 52400\ \mathrm{pm^2}$. Calculate the number of $\pi$ electrons in a ($25\ \mathrm{nm}\times25\ \mathrm{nm}$) sheet of graphene. For this problem you can ignore edge electrons (i.e., those outside the full hexagons in the picture).

c.ii (8 pt) We can think about the $\pi$ electrons in graphene as being free electrons in a 2-dimensional box.

In systems containing large numbers of electrons, there is no single highest occupied energy level. Instead, there are many states of nearly the same energy above which the remaining are empty. These highest occupied states determine the so-called Fermi level. The Fermi level in graphene consists of multiple combinations of $n_x$ and $n_y$ quantum numbers. Determine the energy of the Fermi level for the $25\ \mathrm{nm}\times25\ \mathrm{nm}$ square of graphene relative to the lowest filled level. The lowest filled level has a non-zero energy; however, it is negligible, and can be assumed to be zero. To solve this problem it might be helpful to represent the ($n_x$,$n_y$) quantum states as points on a 2-D grid (as shown below) and consider how the energy levels are filled with pairs of electrons. For the number of electrons use your result from part $\textbf{i}$ or use a value of 1000 (this may not be the true value).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2012-8-fig4.png

c.iii (2 pt) The conductivity of graphene-like materials correlates inversely with the energy gap between the lowest unoccupied and highest occupied energy levels. Use your analysis and understanding of $\pi$ electrons in PAHs and graphene to predict whether the conductivity of a $25\ \mathrm{nm}\times25\ \mathrm{nm}$ square of graphene, at a given temperature, is less than, equal to or greater than the conductivity of a $1\ \mathrm{m}\times1\ \mathrm{m}$ square of graphene (which is the largest obtained to date). Circle the correct answer:

less / equal / greater

problems.title: Clathrate gun
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (8 points; 19 marks). Clathrate gun

The only gun that is able to kill all living people in one shot

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-1-fig1.png

On the floors of oceans and seas there are vast reserves of methane in the form of clathrate compounds called methane hydrates. These reserves can be mined and serve as a source of energy or raw materials for organic synthesis. However, scientists are seriously worried about the possibility of spontaneous decomposition of hydrates caused by the raising ocean temperature. It is believed that if a sufficient amount of methane is released into the atmosphere, the oceans will warm up quicker due to the greenhouse effect, further accelerating the decomposition of clathrates. Due to the explosion of the resulting methane-air mixture and/or changes in the composition of the atmosphere, all living creatures may become extinct. This apocalyptic scenario is called a clathrate gun.

Upon decomposition of $1.00\,\mathrm{g}$ of a methane hydrate with a fixed composition at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and atmospheric ($101.3\,\mathrm{kPa}$) pressure, $205\,\mathrm{mL}$ of methane is released.

1. (2 marks) Determine $n$ (not necessarily integer) in the formula of methane hydrate, $\ce{CH4}\cdot n\ce{H2O}$.

Real methane hydrate has a non-stoichiometric composition close to $\ce{CH4.6H2O}$. At atmospheric pressure, methane hydrate decomposes at $-81\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. However, under high pressures (e.g. on the ocean floor) it is stable at much higher temperatures. Decomposition of methane hydrate produces gaseous methane and solid or liquid water depending on temperature.

2. (1 mark) Write down the equation of decomposition of 1 mole of $\ce{CH4.6H2O}$ producing solid water (ice) $\ce{H2O(s)}$.

The enthalpy of this process equals $17.47\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Assume that the enthalpies do not depend on temperature and pressure, the volume change upon decomposition of hydrate is equal to the volume of released methane, and methane is an ideal gas.

3. (3 marks) At what external pressure does decomposition of methane hydrate into methane and ice take place at $-5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

4. (5 marks) What is the minimum possible depth of pure liquid water at which methane hydrates can be stable?

To answer this question, you should first deduce at which minimum temperature methane hydrate can coexist with liquid water. Choose the correct answer.

$\square\ 272.9\,\mathrm{K} \qquad \square\ 273.15\,\mathrm{K} \qquad \square\ 273.4\,\mathrm{K}$

Large methane hydrate stocks on the floor of Baikal lake, the largest freshwater lake in Russia and in the world, have been discovered in July 2009 by the crew of a deep-submergence vehicle «Mir-2». During the ascent from the depth of $1400\,\mathrm{m}$ methane hydrate samples started to decompose at the depth of $372\,\mathrm{m}$.

5. (6 marks) Determine the temperature in Baikal lake at the depth of $372\,\mathrm{m}$. The enthalpy of fusion of ice is $6.01\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

Total amount of methane in hydrates on Earth is no less than $5\cdot10^{11}$ tons.

6. (2 marks) By how many degrees would the Earth atmosphere heat up, if such amount of methane is burned by reacting with atmospheric oxygen? The enthalpy of combustion of methane is $-889\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, the total heat capacity of the Earth's atmosphere is about $4\cdot10^{21}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$.

problems.title: Break down photosynthesis – the Hill reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (7 points; 19 marks). Break down photosynthesis – the Hill reaction

In the history of photosynthesis research, there were some breakthrough experiments which added much to our knowledge of this very complex process. One of such experiments was performed in 1930s by an English biochemist Robert Hill. In this problem, we consider some of his data together with the data of more recent experiments.

1. (1 mark) In plants, under illumination, carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrates (denote as $\{\ce{CH2O}\}$) and oxygen is produced. Write the overall equation of photosynthesis in plants.

Much of the photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts – organelles found in plant cells and containing chlorophyll – the light-absorbing substance. Hill isolated chloroplasts from the cells by grinding the leaves in the sucrose solutions. The cell-free chloroplasts did not produce oxygen under illumination even in the presence of $\ce{CO2}$. However, upon adding potassium ferrioxalate $\ce{K3[Fe(C2O4)3]}$ (with the excess of potassium oxalate) to the chloroplast suspension Hill observed oxygen liberation under illumination even without $\ce{CO2}$.

2. (2 marks) Hill's experiment enabled to determine the source of oxygen during photosynthesis. Write the formulas of the oxidant and the reducing agent in the photosynthesis inside the plant cells and in the cell-free chloroplasts (the Hill reaction).

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Natural photosynthesis: oxidant} & \text{Natural photosynthesis: reducing agent} & \text{Hill reaction: oxidant} & \text{Hill reaction: reducing agent} \\ \hline \phantom{X} & & & \end{array}$$

Hill measured the amount of evolved oxygen using muscle haemoglobin (Hill denoted it Hb) which binds all molecular oxygen in a 1:1 ratio to form $\ce{HbO2}$. The initial concentration of Hb was $0.6\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M}$. Kinetic curves corresponding to different ferrioxalate concentrations are shown in the figure (the upper curve corresponds to $2.0\cdot10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-2-fig1.png

The fraction of bound haemoglobin $\ce{HbO2}$ (with respect to the initial amount of Hb) as function of time. Crosses denote the end of reaction (Figure 2a from the original Hill's paper: R. Hill. Oxygen produced by isolated chloroplasts. – Proc. R. Soc. B, 1939, v. 127, pp. 192-210)

3. a. (2 marks) From the figure, estimate the Fe / $\ce{O2}$ mole ratio at the end of reaction. Do not take into account the iron from Hb.

b. (2 marks) Write the equation of Hill reaction assuming that it proceeds with a high yield.

c. (3.5 marks) Using the table of standard electrode potentials, determine the Gibbs energy of the Hill reaction at $T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$, oxygen pressure $1\,\mathrm{mmHg}$, pH = 8 and standard concentrations of other species. Is this reaction spontaneous at such conditions?

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Half-reaction} & E^\circ,\ \mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{O2 + 4H+ + 4e- -> 2H2O} & +1.23 \\ \ce{CO2 + 4H+ + 8e- ->} \{\ce{CH2O}\} \ce{+ H2O} & -0.01 \\ \ce{Fe^{3+} + e- -> Fe^{2+}} & +0.77 \\ \ce{Fe^{3+} + 3e- -> Fe^0} & -0.04 \\ \ce{[Fe(C2O4)3]^{3-} + e- -> [Fe(C2O4)3]^{4-}} & +0.05 \\ \ce{[Fe(C2O4)3]^{4-} + 2e- -> Fe + 3C2O4^{2-}} & -0.59 \end{array}$$

The reaction is: $\square$ spontaneous $\qquad \square$ not spontaneous

Now, the name "Hill reaction" denotes photochemical oxidation of water by any oxidant other than carbon dioxide which is sensitized by plant cells or isolated chloroplasts.

In another experiment (1952), quinone in an acid solution was used as an oxidant in the Hill reaction initiated by light flashes in the Chlorella algae. Experimental data are shown in the figure. The volume of oxygen (in $\mathrm{mm^3}$, at temperature $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and pressure $740\,\mathrm{mmHg}$) per one gram of chlorophyll per one flash was determined as a function of light intensity for natural photosynthesis and for isolated chloroplasts. It was found that the maximum yield of oxygen is the same for natural photosynthesis and the Hill reaction.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-2-fig2.png

(Figure 1 from: H. Ehrmantraut, E. Rabinovitch. Kinetics of Hill reaction. – Archives of Biochemistry and Biophysics, 1952, v. 38, pp. 67-84)

4. a. (1 mark) Determine the reaction order of a photochemical Hill reaction with respect to light intensity at low and high intensity. For each case choose one of three values:

Low intensity: $\square\ 0 \quad \square\ 1 \quad \square\ 2 \qquad$ High intensity: $\square\ 0 \quad \square\ 1 \quad \square\ 2$

b. (2 marks) How many chlorophyll molecules participate in the formation of one oxygen molecule in the saturation limit of the Hill reaction? (The molecular mass of chlorophyll is about $900\,\mathrm{Da}$).

The quantum requirement of the light redox reactions is defined as the average number of light photons (not necessarily integer) needed for the transfer of one electron from a reducing agent to an oxidant. The isolated chloroplasts were irradiated during 2 hours by a monochromatic light (wavelength $672\,\mathrm{nm}$) with the energy input $0.503\,\mathrm{mJ/s}$, and the total volume of oxygen formed was $47.6\,\mathrm{mm^3}$ (under the same conditions as in question 4).

5. (3 marks) Calculate the quantum requirement for the Hill reaction.

6. (2.5 marks) Try to make conclusions from the above experiments (questions 2-5). For each of the following statements choose either "Yes" or "No".

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & \text{Yes} & \text{No} \\ \hline \text{In natural photosynthesis, water oxidation and } \ce{CO2} \text{ reduction are separated in space.} & & \\ \text{In chloroplasts, } \ce{O2} \text{ is produced from } \ce{CO2}. & & \\ \text{Oxidation of water in chloroplasts requires light illumination.} & & \\ \text{Most of chlorophylls in chloroplasts participate directly in the photochemical } \ce{O2} \text{ production.} & & \\ \text{In isolated chloroplasts, every absorbed photon causes transfer of one electron.} & & \end{array}$$

problems.title: Meerwein-Schmidt-Ponndorf-Verley reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (8 points; 32.5 marks). Meerwein-Schmidt-Ponndorf-Verley reaction

Meerwein-Schmidt-Ponndorf-Verley (MSPV) reaction is a useful tool for reduction of carbonyl compounds to alcohols. The reaction is the reduction of carbonyl compounds by low molecular weight alcohols in the presence of alkoxides of aluminium or other metals:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-3-fig1.png

(1)

The mechanism of the reaction includes coordination of carbonyl compound by aluminium alkoxide, hydride transfer in the inner sphere of the complex and subsequent transalkoxylation. It can be schematically represented as follows (transalkoxylation is shown as a one-step process for brevity):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-3-fig2.png

(2)

The reaction is reversible and shifting the equilibrium to the desired product requires some excess of the reductant. In some cases (e.g. in the case of reduction of aromatic aldehydes and ketones) the equilibrium constant is so large that the reverse reaction can be neglected.

The table below contains standard entropies and standard enthalpies of formation of liquid substances at 298 K. The boiling points of the substances at 1 bar are also given.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} \text{Substance} & \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ_{298},\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} & S^\circ_{298},\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)} & t_\mathrm{vap},\ ^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ \hline \text{Acetone} & -248.4 & 200.4 & 56 \\ \text{Isopropanol} & -318.1 & 180.6 & 82 \\ \text{Cyclohexanone} & -271.2 & 229.0 & 156 \\ \text{Cyclohexanol} & -348.2 & 203.4 & 161 \end{array}$$

1a. (7 marks) Calculate the minimum isopropanol:cyclohexanone mass ratio which is required to reach a 99% yield of reaction at 298 K. Assume that a) the reaction mixture eventually gets at equilibrium and b) no products are initially present.

[The answer box asks for the ratio $m(\ce{C3H8O}) : m(\ce{C6H10O})$.]

1b. (3 marks) Choose the appropriate way(s) to increase the cyclohexanol yield.

Warning: erroneously ticked boxes will result in penalty points

$\square$ Increase the temperature up to $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ using a reflux

$\square$ Increase the temperature up to $60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, evaporating (distilling) the acetone

$\square$ Add some ethanol to the reaction mixture

$\square$ Add some ethanal to the reaction mixture

2. (8.5 marks) Often the rate-limiting step in the MSPV reaction is the hydride transfer or the alcoholysis of the alkoxide after hydride transfer. For these two cases, using the above mechanism (2), derive an expression for the rate of reaction as a function of current concentrations of a carbonyl compound, isopropanol and a catalyst. In both cases determine the rate orders in the reactants and the catalyst. Assume that all reaction steps before the limiting step are fast and reversible. Use equilibrium approximation, if necessary. For brevity use the following notation: $\mathbf{A}$ for carbonyl compound, $\mathbf{B}$ for isopropanol, $\mathbf{C}$ for catalyst. Denote intermediates as you wish.

• Rate-limiting step is the hydride transfer
• Rate-limiting step is the transalkoxylation of the alcoholate by isopropanol

[For each case: the rate $r$, and the orders in carbonyl compound, in isopropanol and in the catalyst.]

MSPV reaction can be used to obtain chiral alcohols, if the chiral catalyst is employed. For instance, Campbell et al. used the catalyst based on the chiral 2,2'-dihydroxy-1,1'-binaphtyl (BINOL), which is synthesized in situ from binaphtol and trimethylaluminium:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-3-fig3.png

(3)

The chirality of BINOL is due to the sterically hindered rotation around the C-C bond. Though perfectly stable at room temperature, BINOL may racemize when heated.

3. (6 marks) Which of the phenols below can form stable (at room temperature) enantiomers so that they can be used in the same fashion to produce a chiral catalyst?

Warning: erroneously ticked boxes will result in penalty points

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-3-fig4.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-3-fig5.png

4. (8 marks) Enantiomeric excess, $ee$, is used to characterize the enantiomeric purity of the substance. This quantity equals ratio of the difference of concentrations of enantiomers $R$ and $S$ to their sum:

$$ee = \frac{[R]-[S]}{[R]+[S]}$$

Enantiomeric excess of the pure $R$ isomer is unity, $ee$ of the racemic mixture is zero.

When using the enantiomerically pure (BINOL)Al(OiPr) as a catalyst for reduction of $\alpha$-bromoacetophenone, the $ee$ of the product equals 81%. What is the $ee$ of the product if the catalyst $ee$ equals 50%? Provide your calculation with an illustration or derivation of the final formula.

problems.title: A simple inorganic experiment
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (6 points; 24 marks). A simple inorganic experiment

Compound $\mathbf{A}$ which contains metal $\mathbf{X}$ is a colorless crystalline solid and highly soluble in water. It is used as a reagent in analysis and gives in alkali media a binary compound $\mathbf{B}$ containing 6.9 % (mass) of oxygen. Under heating $\mathbf{A}$ decomposes with a mass loss of 36.5%.

1. (5 marks) Determine the metal $\mathbf{X}$ and compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$.

2. (12 marks) Upon adding some amount of sodium thiosulphate to the solution of $\mathbf{A}$ the color immediately becomes red, then changes to reddish-brown, and after some minutes a dark-brown precipitate $\mathbf{C}$ forms (reaction 1). The solution over it is colorless. Being heated on air at $600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\mathbf{C}$ gives a grey powder $\mathbf{X}$ (reaction 2), so as $0.90\,\mathrm{g}$ of residue can be obtained from $1.10\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathbf{C}$. A gas evolved by heating $\mathbf{C}$ in vacuum (reaction 3) can be absorbed by calcium hydroxide suspension (reaction 4). Being stored for a long time under saturated solution of barium perchlorate in $0.1\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HClO4}$, the color of the precipitate becomes lighter, while the use of magnesium perchlorate doesn't give such effect. What is $\mathbf{C}$? Write the equations of the reactions (1 – 4).

3. (7 marks) The compound $\mathbf{C}$ being stored under the mother liquor (containing an excess of $\mathbf{A}$) its color changes to yellow due to the transformation into $\mathbf{D}$. If barium ions are added to the suspension of $\mathbf{C}$ in the mother liquor, a mixture of $\mathbf{D}$ and of a white precipitate forms. Propose the formula of $\mathbf{D}$, taking into account that it contains 77.5% (mass) of $\mathbf{X}$. Give the equation of $\mathbf{D}$ formation.

problems.title: Simple estimates of graphene properties
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (7 points; 14 marks). Simple estimates of graphene properties

Graphene is a two-dimensional, one atom thick carbon material (Fig. 1 a). Many layers of graphene stack together to form graphite (Fig. 1b).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-5-fig1.png

Fig. 1. (a) The structure of graphene. Spheres are carbon atoms. They are arranged in hexagons. The area of one carbon hexagon is $5.16\cdot10^{-20}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ (b) Crystal lattice of graphite. Three graphene layers are shown

Such atomic structure was long considered to be unstable. However, in 2004 Andrey Geim and Konstantin Novoselov have reported production of the first samples of this unusual material. This groundbreaking invention was awarded by Nobel prize in 2010.

Experimental studies of graphene are still restricted. Production of massive portions of the new substance still is a challenging synthetic problem. Many properties of graphene were estimated. Usually, there is not enough information for rigorous calculations, so we have to make assumptions and neglect unimportant factors. In this problem, you will estimate the adsorption properties of graphene.

1a. (2 marks) Estimate the specific surface of graphene open for adsorption in units $\mathrm{m^2/g}$. Consider that graphene plane is separated from any other solid or liquid substance.

The single layer of nitrogen molecules adsorbed on the outer surface of graphite is shown in Fig. 2. Assume that the same arrangement of nitrogen molecules is formed on a graphene surface.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-5-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Nitrogen molecules $\ce{N2}$ (grey circles) on the outer surface of graphite

1b. (2.5 marks) How many grams of nitrogen can be adsorbed on 1 gram of graphene assuming that the graphene layer is placed onto the surface of a solid support? Estimate the volume occupied by these nitrogen molecules after the complete desorption from 1 g of graphene (pressure 1 bar, temperature 298 K).

Let us consider adsorption as a common chemical equilibrium

$$\mathrm{A_{gas}} \rightleftarrows \mathrm{A_{ads}}, \qquad (1)$$

($\mathrm{A_{gas}}$ are molecules A in the gaseous state, $\mathrm{A_{ads}}$ are the same molecules on the surface) with the equilibrium constant $K$:

$$K = \frac{n_{\mathrm{A_{ads}}}\,(\mathrm{mol/m^2})}{p_{\mathrm{A_{gas}}}\,(\mathrm{bar})}$$

(such assumption holds if a small number of molecules is adsorbed on the surface)

Adsorption properties of graphene can be estimated from the data for adsorption on a regular three-dimensional graphite. The enthalpy of adsorption ($\Delta H^\circ$ of reaction (1)) of any molecule A on graphene is on average by 10% less negative compared to that on graphite. On graphite, the adsorbed molecule is bound more strongly due to the interaction with the lower graphene layers in the lattice (Fig. 1b) and hence the enthalpy of adsorption is more negative. The standard entropies of adsorption on graphene and graphite are assumed to be the same.

2. (4 marks) How many moles, $n$, of $\ce{CCl4}$ are adsorbed on 1 g of graphene at $p(\ce{CCl4}) = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{bar}$ if $2.0\cdot10^{-7}\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\ce{CCl4}$ are adsorbed on $1\,\mathrm{m^2}$ of graphite at $p(\ce{CCl4}) = 6.6\cdot10^{-5}\,\mathrm{bar}$? Assume that graphene is placed onto the surface of a solid support and the interaction of $\ce{CCl4}$ with the support does not change the enthalpy of adsorption of $\ce{CCl4}$ on graphene. The temperature in both cases is 293 K. $\Delta H^\circ$ of adsorption of $\ce{CCl4}$ on graphite is $-35.1\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

The graphene films are expected to be sensitive gas detectors. If $10^9$ particles of a gas are adsorbed on $1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ of a graphene surface this is enough to measure an electrical resistivity change of the graphene layer and to detect the presence of a gas in the environment.

3. (5.5 marks) Determine the minimal content of ethane, $\ce{C2H6}$, in the air (in mol.%) at atmospheric pressure ($T = 293\,\mathrm{K}$) at which a graphene sensor will detect this gas. The known data for the adsorption of alkanes on graphite are shown in Fig 3. Assume that air doesn't affect the adsorption properties of ethane.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-5-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Thermodynamic properties for adsorption of alkanes on a graphite surface. (a) $\ln K$ $\{\mathrm{mol/m^2/bar}\}$ as a function of $\ln M$ ($M$ – molecular mass of alkane in g/mol); (b) $\Delta H^\circ$ of adsorption as a function of $\ln M$. Linear dependences are assumed in both cases

problems.title: Cyclopropanes. So simple. So fancy…
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (8 points; 100 marks). Cyclopropanes. So simple. So fancy…

Cyclopropanes bearing donor and acceptor substituents at the neighboring C-atoms, for example, $\mathbf{A}$, demonstrate high reactivity behaving similar to 1,3-zwitterion $\mathbf{B}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-6-fig1.png

Thus, $\mathbf{A1}$ (X = 4-OMe) undergoes the three-membered ring opening in the Lewis acid-catalyzed reaction with 1,3-dimethoxybenzene as a nucleophile giving the product $\mathbf{C}$.

1. (8 marks) Write down structural formula of $\mathbf{C}$.

$\mathbf{A1}$ participates in cycloadditions, annulations, oligomerizations, and other processes. Thus, formal [3+2]-cycloaddition between $\mathbf{A1}$ and 4-methoxybenzaldehyde leads to a five-membered ring in $\mathbf{D}$. Decarboxylation of all carboxylic groups in $\mathbf{D}$ produces $\mathbf{E}$ ($\ce{C18H20O3}$), the molecule of the latter having a plane of symmetry.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-6-fig2.png

2. (22 marks) Write down structural formulae of $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ indicating their stereochemistry.

Also, $\mathbf{A}$ can undergo various transformations in the absence of any reaction partners except catalysts. Some transformations typical of $\mathbf{A1}$ are shown in the Scheme below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-6-fig3.png

To determine the structures of $\mathbf{F}$-$\mathbf{J}$, a set of physico-chemical data was obtained (see Table 1 for some results). It was found that:

a) $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ have the same molecular formula as $\mathbf{A1}$;

b) $\mathbf{G}$ is formed as the most stable stereoisomer;

c) $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{I}$ are structural isomers;

d) $\mathbf{H}$ is formed as a single diastereomer with $C_2$ axis of symmetry (the molecule looks the same after rotation through the angle of 180°);

e) $\mathbf{I}$ is formed as a mixture of two diastereomers;

f) $\mathbf{J}$ is naphthalene derivative.

In the process leading to $\mathbf{I}$, one molecule of $\mathbf{A1}$ demonstrates the described above common reactivity (analogous to that of $\mathbf{B}$). The other molecule of $\mathbf{A1}$ behaves differently. Also, the latter behavior is demonstrated by cyclopropane $\mathbf{A2}$ (dimethyl 2-(3,4,5-trimethoxyphenyl)cylopropane-1,1-dicarboxylate; X in $\mathbf{A}$ = 3,4,5-(MeO)$_3$) when treated with $\ce{SnCl4}$ affording $\mathbf{K}$ as a mixture of two diastereomers. The major isomer has the center of symmetry. Similar reactivity is shown by $\mathbf{A2}$ in $\ce{Sn(OTf)2}$-catalyzed reaction with $\mathbf{G}$ furnishing $\mathbf{L}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-6-fig4.png

Table 1. Information about the compounds.

problems.title: Diverse permanganatometry
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (8 points; 34 marks). Diverse permanganatometry

The amount of many reducing agents can be determined by permanganatometric titration in alkaline medium allowing permanganate ion reduction to manganate.

1. (2 marks) Write down the ionic equation of the reaction for formate titration with permanganate in an aqueous solution containing ~0.5 M $\ce{NaOH}$.

Titration with permanganate in alkaline medium is often supplemented by addition of a barium salt, which leads to precipitation of manganate as $\ce{BaMnO4}$.

2. (2 marks) Which side redox processes involving manganate is suppressed by the barium salt? Write down an example of equation of the corresponding reaction.

$10.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ ($V_\mathrm{Mn}$) of $0.0400\,\mathrm{M}$ ($c_\mathrm{Mn}$) $\ce{KMnO4}$ solution was placed in each of flasks $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ and different reactions were conducted in each flask.

3. To flask $\mathbf{A}$, a sample solution containing unknown amount of crotonic acid (CA) $\ce{CH3-CH=CH-COOH}$ ($m_\mathrm{CA}$), an alkali and barium nitrate (both in an excess) were added, and the reaction mixture was incubated for 45 min. It is known that each molecule of crotonic acid loses 10 electrons under the experiment conditions. The molar mass of CA is $86.09\,\mathrm{g/mol}$.

a) (4 marks) Write down the total ionic equation of the reaction.

$8.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ ($V_\mathrm{CN}$) of $0.0100\,\mathrm{M}$ ($c_\mathrm{CN}$) potassium cyanide solution was further added to the incubated mixture. This resulted in completion of the following reaction:

$$\ce{2Ba^{2+} + 2MnO4^- + CN^- + 2OH^- = 2BaMnO4 + CNO^- + H2O}$$

$\ce{BaMnO4}$ precipitate was then filtered off, and the excess of cyanide in the filtrate was titrated with $0.0050\,\mathrm{M}$ ($c_\mathrm{Ag}$) $\ce{AgNO3}$ solution till detectable precipitation was observed. Note that both $\ce{CN^-}$ and $\ce{CNO^-}$ are analogs of halide ions, but $\ce{CNO^-}$ affords soluble silver salt.

b) (2 marks) Give the formula for the complex formed when $\ce{Ag^+}$ ions were initially added to the cyanide solution (until the precipitate was formed).

c) (2 marks) Give the formula of the precipitate formed.

d) (6 marks) Calculate the mass of crotonic acid (in mg) if $5.40\,\mathrm{mL}$ ($V_\mathrm{Ag}$) of the silver salt solution was consumed for the titration to the endpoint.

4. (7 marks) Another sample with different concentration of crotonic acid and alkali (in an excess) were added to flask $\mathbf{B}$, this mixture lacking barium salt. An excess of $\ce{KI}$ (instead of cyanide) was added as a reducing agent. The mixture was further acidified, and the iodine evolved was titrated with $0.1000\,\mathrm{M}$ ($c_\mathrm{S}$) thiosulfate solution. $4.90\,\mathrm{mL}$ ($V_\mathrm{S1}$) of the titrant was used to reach the endpoint.

Calculate the mass of crotonic acid (in mg).

5. A sample containing tin(II) was added to flask $\mathbf{C}$, and the medium was adjusted to weak alkaline. Tin(II) was quantitatively oxidized to $\ce{Sn(OH)6^{2-}}$, whereas a precipitate formed as a result of permanganate reduction. The precipitate was isolated, washed off, dried at $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, weighed (the mass of the water-free precipitate ($m_\mathrm{prec}$), representing a binary compound $\ce{Mn_{x}O_{y}}$, was of $28.6\,\mathrm{mg}$), and dissolved in $\ce{H2SO4}$ in the presence of an excess of potassium iodide. The evolved iodine was titrated with $0.1000\,\mathrm{M}$ thiosulfate solution. $2.50\,\mathrm{mL}$ ($V_\mathrm{S2}$) of the latter was consumed to attain the endpoint.

a) (7 marks) Determine x and y. Write down the reaction of precipitation.

b) (2 marks) Calculate the mass of tin in the sample (in mg).

problems.title: Unique life of archaea
problems.problem:
Problem 8 (8 points; 45 marks). Unique life of archaea

Archaea (or archaebacteria) are single-celled microorganisms significantly differing from bacteria and eukaryotes at the molecular level.

Enzymatic reaction of methylamine with water is the major energy source for some archaea. In a particular experiment, an archaea strain was cultivated at pH 7 under anaerobic (oxygen free) conditions with the nutrient medium containing $\ce{^{13}CH3NH2}$ as the only energy source. After a certain incubation period, the gas over the archaea culture was sampled and analyzed. It was found that the gas contains two substances $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ in the molar ratio of 1.00:3.00 correspondingly. The sample density rel. $\ce{H2}$ is of 12.0.

1. (2 marks) Calculate the volume fractions (in %) of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ in the mixture.

2. (7 marks) Determine $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ if there is no N atoms in gas collected.

3. (3 marks) Write down the equation of enzymatic reaction of methylamine with water described in the above experiment using predominant form of each species.

Enzymes containing the residue of $\alpha$-amino acid $\mathbf{X}$ are found in many archaea. It is known that $\mathbf{X}$:

• is composed of atoms of 4 elements;
• is 18.8 % oxygen by mass;
• possesses the single individual tRNA and is incorporated into proteins during translation.

Amino acid L-lysine (see the structure in scheme below) was identified as the $\mathbf{X}$ precursor in archaea. All C and N atoms found in $\mathbf{X}$ originate from two starting lysine molecules. Different isotope-labeled L-lysines were introduced into a model system to clarify the biosynthetic pathways of $\mathbf{X}$. The results are summarized in the table.

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Isotope composition of } L\text{-lysine} & \text{Molecular mass (rounded to integer) of the } \mathbf{X} \text{ residue } [\ce{RCH(NH2)CO}] \text{, bound to tRNA, g/mol} \\ \hline \text{Normal} & 238 \\ \text{All carbons } \ce{^{13}C}\text{, all nitrogens } \ce{^{15}N} & 253 \\ \varepsilon\text{-Amino group with } \ce{^{15}N} & 239 \end{array}$$

4. (8 marks) Determine the molecular formula of $\mathbf{X}$.

$\mathbf{X}$ is biosynthesized in archaea according to the following scheme ($\mathrm{E_1}$–$\mathrm{E_3}$ – enzymes):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-8-fig1.png

At the first step, lysine is transformed into its structural isomer ($\alpha$–amino acid, $\mathbf{C}$), whereas $\mathbf{D}$ contains a peptide bond, and $\mathbf{E}$ a formyl group [$\ce{-CHO}$]. All reaction coefficients in the above scheme equal 1.

5. (4 marks) Give the chemical formula of $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$. From the reaction types given hereunder, choose (tick) only one corresponding to the $\mathrm{E_3}$ catalyzed reaction.

$\square$ Oxidative deamination;

$\square$ Decarboxylation;

$\square$ Intermolecular deamination;

$\square$ Hydroxylation;

$\square$ Peptide bond hydrolysis.

$\mathbf{X}$ contains the fragment:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-8-fig2.png

R is a massive substituent (M>100 g/mol). The 3rd C atom is non-asymmetric, 4th and 5th C atoms are stereogenic centers. All C atoms in the cycle are bound with at least one H atom. Each substituent (H, Me and R) is found only once.

6. (4 marks) Determine the positions of substituents H, Me, and R.

7. (5 marks) Draw structural formulae of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{X}$ with stereochemical details. There are no stereo centers affected on the way from $\mathbf{C}$ to $\mathbf{X}$. Mark every stereocenter of $\mathbf{X}$ with either $R$ or $S$.

Only one codon is responsible for incorporation of $\mathbf{X}$ residues into proteins in archaea. The nitrogen bases forming this codon contain two exocyclic amino groups and three exocyclic oxygen atoms in total.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2013-8-fig3.png

8. (4 marks) Fill in the hereunder table to determine the nucleotide composition of the codon encoding $\mathbf{X}$. Tick only one box in each line.

The number of bases in the codon:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Nitrogen base} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 0 \text{ or } 1 & 1 \text{ or } 2 \\ \hline \text{A} & & & & & \\ \text{C} & & & & & \\ \text{G} & & & & & \\ \text{U} & & & & & \end{array}$$

The fragment of mRNA coding sequence given below contains the codons encoding $\mathbf{X}$ residue incorporation into an archaea enzyme:

5'…AAUAGAAUUAGCGGAACAGAGGGUGAC…3'

9a. (3 marks) Using the table of the genetic code, decide how many amino acid residues are incorporated into the enzyme chain due to this fragment translation.

9b. (5 marks) Write down the amino acid sequence translated from this fragment. Note that more than one $\mathbf{X}$ residue is found in the fragment.

Fill in the boxes with the amino acid abbreviations (from N- to C-terminus).

Note that the number of boxes is excessive. If there is more than one possibility, write all separated by "/". If the translation is stopped in a particular position, write "STOP" and leave all the boxes to the right empty.

[Ten boxes are printed in the answer sheet.]

problems.title: Particles in a box: polyenes
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (27 points, 5.0% of the total). Particles in a box: polyenes

In quantum mechanics, the movement of $\pi$ electrons along a neutral chain of conjugated carbon atoms may be modeled using the 'particle in a box' method. The energy of the $\pi$ electrons is given by the following equation:

$$E_n = \frac{n^2 h^2}{8 m L^2}$$

where $n$ is the quantum number ($n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$), $h$ is Planck's constant, $m$ is the mass of electron, and $L$ is the length of the box which may be approximated by $L = (k + 2)\times 1.40\ \text{Å}$ ($k$ being the number of conjugated double bonds along the carbon chain in the molecule). A photon with the appropriate wavelength $\lambda$ may promote a $\pi$ electron from the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) to the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO). An approximate semi-empirical formula based on this model which relates the wavelength $\lambda$, to the number of double bonds $k$ and constant $B$ is as follows:

$$\lambda\ (\mathrm{nm}) = B \times \frac{(k+2)^2}{(2k+1)} \qquad \text{Equation 1}$$

1 (3 pt) Using this semi-empirical formula with $B = 65.01\ \mathrm{nm}$ calculate the value of the wavelength $\lambda$ (nm) for octatetraene ($\ce{CH2=CH-CH=CH-CH=CH-CH=CH2}$).

2 (7 pt) Derive Equation 1 (an expression for the wavelength $\lambda$ (nm) corresponding to the transfer of an electron from the HOMO to the LUMO) in terms of $k$ and the fundamental constants, and hence calculate theoretical value of the constant $B_\text{calc.}$.

3 (6 pt) We wish to synthesize a linear polyene for which the excitation of a $\pi$ electron from the HOMO to the LUMO requires an absorption wavelength of close to $600\ \mathrm{nm}$. Using your expression from part 2, determine the number of conjugated double bonds ($k$) in this polyene and give its structure. [If you did not solve Part 2, use the semi-empirical Equation 1 with $B = 65.01\ \mathrm{nm}$ to complete Part 3.]

4 (4 pt) For the polyene molecule found in Part 3, calculate the difference in energy between the HOMO and the LUMO, $\Delta E$, ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$).

In case Part 3 was not solved, take $k = 5$ to solve this problem.

5 (7 pt) The model for a particle in a one-dimensional box can be extended to a three dimensional rectangular box of dimensions $L_x$, $L_y$ and $L_z$, yielding the following expression for the allowed energy levels:

$$E_{n_x, n_y, n_z} = \frac{h^2}{8m}\left(\frac{n_x^2}{L_x^2} + \frac{n_y^2}{L_y^2} + \frac{n_z^2}{L_z^2}\right)$$

The three quantum numbers $n_x$, $n_y$, and $n_z$ must be integer values and are independent of each other.

5.1 Give the expressions for the three different lowest energies, assuming that the box is cubic with a length of $L$.

5.2 Levels with the same energy are said to be degenerate. Draw a sketch showing all the energy levels, including any degenerate levels, that correspond to quantum numbers having values of 1 or 2 for a cubic box.

problems.title: Dissociating Gas Cycle
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (33 points, 5.0% of the total). Dissociating Gas Cycle

Dininitrogen tetroxide forms an equilibrium mixture with nitrogen dioxide:

$$\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$$

$1.00$ mole of $\ce{N2O4}$ was put into an empty vessel with a fixed volume of $24.44\ \mathrm{dm^3}$. The equilibrium gas pressure at $298\ \mathrm{K}$ was found to be $1.190\ \mathrm{bar}$. When heated to $348\ \mathrm{K}$, the gas pressure increased to its equilibrium value of $1.886\ \mathrm{bar}$.

1a (12 pt) Calculate $\Delta G^0$ of the reaction at $298\ \mathrm{K}$, assuming the gases are ideal.

1b (8 pt) Calculate $\Delta H^0$ and $\Delta S^0$ of the reaction, assuming that they do not change significantly with temperature.

If you cannot calculate $\Delta H^0$, use $\Delta H^0 = 30.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ for further calculations.

The tendency of $\ce{N2O4}$ to dissociate reversibly into $\ce{NO2}$ enables its potential use in advanced power generation systems. A simplified scheme for one such system is shown below in Figure (a). Initially, "cool" $\ce{N2O4}$ is compressed ($1\to2$) in a compressor ($\mathbf{X}$), and heated ($2\to3$). Some $\ce{N2O4}$ dissociates into $\ce{NO2}$. The hot mixture is expanded ($3\to4$) through a turbine ($\mathbf{Y}$), resulting in a decrease in both temperature and pressure. The mixture is then cooled further ($4\to1$) in a heat sink ($\mathbf{Z}$), to promote the reformation of $\ce{N2O4}$. This recombination reduces the pressure, thus facilitates the compression of $\ce{N2O4}$ to start a new cycle. All these processes are assumed to take place reversibly.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-2-fig1.png

To understand the benefits of using reversible dissociating gases such as $\ce{N2O4}$, we will focus on step $3\to4$ and consider an ideal gas turbine working with 1 mol of air (which we assume to be an inert, non-dissociating gas). During the reversible adiabatic expansion in the turbine, no heat is exchanged.

2 (3 pt) Give the equation to calculate the work done by the system $w(\text{air})$ during the reversible adiabatic expansion for 1 mol of air during stage $3\to4$. Assume that $C_{v,m}(\text{air})$ (the isochoric molar heat capacity of air) is constant, and the temperature changes from $T_3$ to $T_4$.

3 (10 pt) Estimate the ratio $w_{(\ce{N2O4})}/w_{(\text{air})}$, in which $w_{(\ce{N2O4})}$ is the work done by the gas during the reversible adiabatic expansion process $3\to4$ with the cycle working with 1 mol of $\ce{N2O4}$. $T_3$ and $T_4$ are the same as in Part 2. Take the conditions at stage 3 to be $T_3 = 440\ \mathrm{K}$ and $P_3 = 12.156\ \mathrm{bar}$ and assume that:

(i) the gas is at its equilibrium composition at stage 3;

(ii) $C_{v,m}$ for the gas is the same as for air;

(iii) the adiabatic expansion in the turbine takes place in a way that the composition of the gas mixture ($\ce{N2O4 + NO2}$) is unchanged until the expansion is completed.

problems.title: High-valent Silver Compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (36 points, 9.0% of the total). High-valent Silver Compounds

Silver chemistry is dominated by $\ce{Ag}$(I) compounds. Compounds of silver in higher oxidation state (from $+2$ to $+5$) are not very abundant due to their instability with respect to reduction. High-valent silver compounds are very reactive and can be synthesized from $\ce{Ag}$(I) compounds in electro-chemical oxidations or in chemical oxidations using powerful oxidizing agents.

1 (8 pt) In some peroxydisulfate ($\ce{S2O8^{2-}}$) oxidations catalyzed by $\ce{Ag+}$, black solid ($\mathbf{A}$) with the composition $\ce{AgO}$ can be isolated.

1a Choose the appropriate magnetic behaviour of $\mathbf{A}$ if it exists as $\mathrm{Ag^{II}O}$.

• Diamagnetic
• Paramagnetic

Single crystal X-ray studies reveal that the lattice of $\mathbf{A}$ contains two nonequivalent $\ce{Ag}$ atom sites (in equal proportions) of which one denoted as Ag1 and the other denoted as Ag2. Ag1 shows a linear O atom coordination ($\ce{O-Ag-O}$) and Ag2 shows a square-planar O atom coordination. All O atoms are in equivalent environments in the structure. Thus, $\mathbf{A}$ should be assigned as $\mathrm{Ag^{I}Ag^{III}O_2}$ rather than $\mathrm{Ag^{II}O}$.

1b Assign the oxidation number of Ag1 and Ag2.

1c What is the coordination number of O atoms in the lattice of $\mathbf{A}$?

1d How many $\mathrm{Ag^{I}}$ and $\mathrm{Ag^{III}}$ bond to one O atom in the lattice of $\mathbf{A}$?

1e Predict the magnetic behaviour of $\mathbf{A}$. Check the appropriate box below.

• Diamagnetic
• Paramagnetic

1f The compound $\mathbf{A}$ can also be formed on warming a solution of $\ce{Ag+}$ with peroxydisulfate. Write down the equation for the formation of $\mathbf{A}$.

2 (14 pt) Among the silver oxides which have been crystallographically characterized, the most surprising is probably that compound $\mathbf{A}$ is not a $\mathrm{Ag^{II}O}$. Thermochemical cycles are useful to understand this fact. Some standard enthalpy changes (at $298\ \mathrm{K}$) are listed:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Atom} & \begin{array}{c}\text{Standard enthalpy}\\ \text{of formation}\\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{1st ionization}\\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{2nd ionization}\\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{3rd ionization}\\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{1st electron}\\ \text{affinity}\\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}})\end{array} & \begin{array}{c}\text{2nd electron}\\ \text{affinity}\\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}})\end{array} \\ \hline \ce{Cu(g)} & 337.4 & 751.7 & 1964.1 & 3560.2 & & \\ \ce{Ag(g)} & 284.9 & 737.2 & 2080.2 & 3367.2 & & \\ \ce{O(g)} & 249.0 & & & & -141.0 & 844.0 \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Compounds} & \Delta H^\mathrm{o}_\mathrm{f}\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) \\ \hline \mathrm{Ag^{I}Ag^{III}O_2\,(s)} & -24.3 \\ \mathrm{Cu^{II}O\,(s)} & -157.3 \end{array}$$

The relationship between the lattice dissociation energy ($U_\mathrm{lat}$) and the lattice dissociation enthalpy ($\Delta H_\mathrm{lat}$) for monoatomic ion lattices is: $\Delta H_\mathrm{lat} = U_\mathrm{lat} + nRT$, where $n$ is the number of ions in the formula unit.

2a Calculate $U_\mathrm{lat}$ at $298\ \mathrm{K}$ of $\mathrm{Ag^{I}Ag^{III}O_2}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{II}O}$. Assume that they are ionic compounds.

If you can not calculate the $U_\mathrm{lat}$ of $\mathrm{Ag^{I}Ag^{III}O_2}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{II}O}$, use following values for further calculations: $U_\mathrm{lat}$ of $\mathrm{Ag^{I}Ag^{III}O_2} = 8310.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; $U_\mathrm{lat}$ of $\mathrm{Cu^{II}O} = 3600.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

The lattice dissociation energies for a range of compounds may be estimated using this simple formula:

$$U_\mathrm{lat} = C \times \left(\frac{1}{V_\mathrm{m}}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}$$

Where: $V_\mathrm{m}$ ($\mathrm{nm^3}$) is the volume of the formula unit and $C$ ($\mathrm{kJ\,nm\,mol^{-1}}$) is an empirical constant which has a particular value for each type of lattice with ions of specified charges.

The formula unit volumes of some oxides are calculated from crystallographic data as the ratio between the unit cell volume and the number of formula units in the unit cell and listed as below:

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{Oxides} & V_\mathrm{m}\ (\mathrm{nm^3}) \\ \hline \mathrm{Cu^{II}O} & 0.02030 \\ \mathrm{Ag^{III}_2O_3} & 0.06182 \\ \mathrm{Ag^{II}Ag^{III}_2O_4} & 0.08985 \end{array}$$

2b Calculate $U_\mathrm{lat}$ for the hypothetical compound $\mathrm{Ag^{II}O}$. Assume that $\mathrm{Ag^{II}O}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{II}O}$ have the same type of lattice, and that $V_\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{Ag^{II}O}) = V_\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{Ag^{II}Ag^{III}_2O_4}) - V_\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{Ag^{III}_2O_3})$.

2c By constructing an appropriate thermodynamic cycle or otherwise, estimate the enthalpy change for the solid-state transformation from $\mathrm{Ag^{II}O}$ to 1 mole of $\mathrm{Ag^{I}Ag^{III}O_2}$.

(Use $U_\mathrm{lat}$ $\mathrm{Ag^{II}O} = 3180.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $U_\mathrm{lat}$ $\mathrm{Ag^{I}Ag^{III}O_2} = 8310.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ if you cannot calculate $U_\mathrm{lat}$ $\mathrm{Ag^{II}O}$ in Part 2b).

2d Indicate which compound is thermodynamically more stable by checking the appropriate box below.

• $\mathrm{Ag^{II}O}$
• $\mathrm{Ag^{I}Ag^{III}O_2}$

3 (2 pt) When $\mathrm{Ag^{I}Ag^{III}O_2}$ is dissolved in aqueous $\ce{HClO4}$ solution, a paramagnetic compound ($\mathbf{B}$) is first formed then slowly decomposes to form a diamagnetic compound ($\mathbf{C}$). Given that $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are the only compounds containing silver formed in these reactions, write down the equations for the formation of $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

4 (12 pt) Oxidation of $\ce{Ag+}$ with powerful oxidizing agents in the presence of appropriate ligands can result in the formation of high-valent silver complexes. A complex $\mathbf{Z}$ is synthesized and analyzed by the following procedures:

An aqueous solution containing $0.500\ \mathrm{g}$ of $\ce{AgNO3}$ and $2\ \mathrm{mL}$ of pyridine ($d = 0.982\ \mathrm{g/mL}$) is added to a stirred, ice-cold aqueous solution of $5.000\ \mathrm{g}$ of $\ce{K2S2O8}$. The reaction mixture becomes yellow, then an orange solid ($\mathbf{Z}$) is formed which has a mass of $1.719\ \mathrm{g}$ when dried.

Elemental analysis of $\mathbf{Z}$ shows the mass percentages of C, H, N elements are $38.96\%$, $3.28\%$, $9.09\%$, respectively.

A $0.6164\ \mathrm{g}$ $\mathbf{Z}$ is added to aqueous $\ce{NH3}$. The suspension is boiled to form a clear solution during which stage the complex is destroyed completely. The solution is acidified with excess aqueous $\ce{HCl}$ and the resulting suspension is filtered, washed and dried (in darkness) to obtain $0.1433\ \mathrm{g}$ of white solid ($\mathbf{D}$). The filtrate is collected and treated with excess $\ce{BaCl2}$ solution to obtain $0.4668\ \mathrm{g}$ (when dry) of white precipitate ($\mathbf{E}$).

4a Determine the empirical formula of $\mathbf{Z}$ and calculate the percentage yield in the preparation.

4b $\ce{Ag}$(IV) and $\ce{Ag}$(V) compounds are extremely unstable and found only in few fluorides. Thus, the formation of their complexes with organic ligands in water can be discounted. To confirm the oxidation number of silver in $\mathbf{Z}$, the effective magnetic moment ($\mu_\mathrm{eff}$) of $\mathbf{Z}$ was determined and found to be $1.78\ \mathrm{BM}$. Use the spin only formula to determine the number of unpaired electrons in $\mathbf{Z}$ and the molecular formula of $\mathbf{Z}$. ($\mathbf{Z}$ contains a mononuclear complex with only one species of Ag and only one type of ligand in the ligand sphere.)

4c Write down all chemical equations for the preparation of $\mathbf{Z}$, and its analysis.

problems.title: Zeise's Salt
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (27 points, 4.0% of the total). Zeise's Salt

1 Zeise's salt, $\ce{K[PtCl3C2H4]}$, was one of the first organometallic compounds to be reported. W. C. Zeise, a professor at the University of Copenhagen, prepared this compound in 1827 by reacting $\ce{PtCl4}$ with boiling ethanol and then adding potassium chloride (Method 1). This compound may also be prepared by refluxing a mixture of $\ce{K2[PtCl6]}$ and ethanol (Method 2). The commercially available Zeise's salt is commonly prepared from $\ce{K2[PtCl4]}$ and ethylene (Method 3).

1a (4 pt) Write balanced equations for each of the above mentioned preparations of Zeise's salt, given that in methods 1 and 2 the formation of 1 mole of Zeise's salt consumes 2 moles of ethanol.

1b (1 pt) Mass spectrometry of the anion $\ce{[PtCl3C2H4]-}$ shows one set of peaks with mass numbers 325–337 $\textit{au}$ and various intensities.

Calculate the mass number of the anion which consists of the largest natural abundance isotopes (using given below data).

$$\begin{array}{c|cccccccccc} \text{Isotope} & \ce{^{192}_{78}Pt} & \ce{^{194}_{78}Pt} & \ce{^{195}_{78}Pt} & \ce{^{196}_{78}Pt} & \ce{^{198}_{78}Pt} & \ce{^{35}_{17}Cl} & \ce{^{37}_{17}Cl} & \ce{^{12}_{6}C} & \ce{^{13}_{6}C} & \ce{^{1}_{1}H} \\ \hline \text{Natural abundance, }\% & 0.8 & 32.9 & 33.8 & 25.3 & 7.2 & 75.8 & 24.2 & 98.9 & 1.1 & 99.99 \end{array}$$

2 Some early structures proposed for Zeise's salt anion were:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-4-fig1.png

In structure $\mathbf{Z1}$, $\mathbf{Z2}$, and $\mathbf{Z5}$ both carbons are in the same plane as dashed square. [You should assume that these structures do not undergo any fluxional process by interchanging two or more sites.]

2a (10 pt) NMR spectroscopy allowed the structure for Zeise's salt to be determined as structure $\mathbf{Z4}$. For each structure $\mathbf{Z1}$–$\mathbf{Z5}$, indicate in the table below how many hydrogen atoms are in different environments, and how many different environments of hydrogen atoms there are, and how many different environments of carbon atoms there are?

Calculate the solubility (in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$) of a subtancce $\ce{M(OH)2}$ in $\mathbf{Z}$, given that the anions $\ce{A-}$ and $\ce{B-}$ can form complexes with $\ce{M^{2+}}$:

problems.title: Chemical Kinetics
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (32 points, 7.0% of the total). Chemical Kinetics

The transition-metal-catalyzed amination of aryl halides has become one of the most powerful methods to synthesize arylamines. The overall reaction for the nickel-catalyzed amination of aryl chloride in basic conditions is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-6-fig1.png

in which NiLL' is the nickel complex catalyst. The reaction goes through several steps in which the catalyst, reactants, and solvent may be involved in elementary steps.

6a (6 pt) To determine the reaction order with respect to each reactant, the dependence of the initial rate of the reaction on the concentrations of each reagent was carried out with all other reagents present in large excess. Some kinetic data at $298\ \mathrm{K}$ are shown in the tables below. (Use the grids if you like)

$$\begin{array}{c|c} [\mathbf{ArCl}]\ (\mathrm{M}) & \text{Initial rate}\ (\mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}) \\ \hline 0.1 & 1.88\times10^{-5} \\ 0.2 & 4.13\times10^{-5} \\ 0.4 & 9.42\times10^{-5} \\ 0.6 & 1.50\times10^{-4} \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{c|c} [\mathbf{NiLL'}]\ (\mathrm{M}) & \text{Initial rate}\ (\mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}) \\ \hline 6\times10^{-3} & 4.12\times10^{-5} \\ 9\times10^{-3} & 6.01\times10^{-5} \\ 1.2\times10^{-2} & 7.80\times10^{-5} \\ 1.5\times10^{-2} & 1.10\times10^{-4} \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{c|c} [\mathbf{L'}]\ (\mathrm{M}) & \text{Initial rate}\ (\mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}) \\ \hline 0.06 & 5.8\times10^{-5} \\ 0.09 & 4.3\times10^{-5} \\ 0.12 & 3.4\times10^{-5} \\ 0.15 & 2.8\times10^{-5} \end{array}$$

Determine the order with respect to the reagents assuming they are integers.

6b (8 pt) To study the mechanism for this reaction, $\ce{^1H}$, $\ce{^{31}P}$, $\ce{^{19}F}$, and $\ce{^{13}C}$ NMR spectroscopy have been used to identify the major transition metal complexes in solution, and the initial rates were measured using reaction calorimetry. An intermediate, NiL(Ar)Cl, may be isolated at room temperature. The first two steps of the overall reaction involve the dissociation of a ligand from NiLL' (step 1) at $50\ ^\mathrm{o}\mathrm{C}$, followed by the oxidation addition (step 2) of aryl chloride to the NiL at room temperature (rt):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-6-fig2.png

Using the steady state approximation, derive an expression for the rate equation for the formation of [NiL(Ar)Cl].

The next steps in the overall reaction involve the amine ($\ce{RNH2}$) and $^t$BuONa. To determine the order with respect to $\ce{RNH2}$ and $^t$BuONa, the dependence of the initial rates of the reaction on the concentrations of these two reagents was carried with the other reagents present in large excess. Some results are shown in the tables below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} [\mathbf{NaO^{\mathit{t}}Bu}]\ (\mathrm{M}) & \text{Initial rate}\ (\mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}) \\ \hline 0.2 & 4.16\times10^{-5} \\ 0.6 & 4.12\times10^{-5} \\ 0.9 & 4.24\times10^{-5} \\ 1.2 & 4.20\times10^{-5} \end{array} \qquad \begin{array}{c|c} [\mathbf{RNH_2}]\ (\mathrm{M}) & \text{Initial rate}\ (\mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}) \\ \hline 0.3 & 4.12\times10^{-5} \\ 0.6 & 4.26\times10^{-5} \\ 0.9 & 4.21\times10^{-5} \\ 1.2 & 4.23\times10^{-5} \end{array}$$

6c (4 pt) Determine the order with each of these reagents, assuming each is an integer. (Use the grids if you like)

During a catalytic cycle, a number of different structures may be involved which include the catalyst. One step in the cycle will be rate-determining.

A proposed cycle for the nickel-catalyzed coupling of aryl halides with amines is as follows:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-6-fig3.png

6d (12 pt) Use the steady-state approximation and material balance equation to derive the rate law for d[ArNHR]/dt for the above mechanism in terms of the initial concentration of the catalyst $[\mathrm{NiLL'}]_0$ and concentrations of [ArCl], $[\mathrm{NH_2R}]$, $[\mathrm{NaO^{\mathit{t}}Bu}]$, and [L'].

6e (2 pt) Give the simplified form of the rate equation in 6d assuming that $k_1$ is very small.

problems.title: Synthesis of Artemisinin
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (64 points, 8.0% of the total). Synthesis of Artemisinin

(+)-Artemisinin, isolated from $\textit{Artemisia annua}$ L. (Qinghao, $\textit{Compositae}$) is a potent antimalarial effective against resistant strains of $\textit{Plasmodium}$. A simple route for the synthesis of Artemisinin is outlined below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-7-fig1.png

First, pyrolysis of (+)-2-Carene broke the cyclopropane ring forming, among other products, (1$R$)-(+)-$\textit{trans}$-isolimonene $\mathbf{A}$ ($\ce{C10H16}$), which then was subjected to regioselective hydroboration using dicyclohexylborane to give the required alcohol $\mathbf{B}$ in 82% yield as a mixture of diastereoisomers. In the next step, $\mathbf{B}$ was converted to the corresponding $\gamma,\delta$-unsaturated acid $\mathbf{C}$ in 80% yield by Jones' oxidation.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-7-fig2.png

7a (12 pt) Draw the structures (with stereochemistry) of the compounds $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{C}$.

The acid $\mathbf{C}$ was subjected to iodolactonization using KI, $\ce{I2}$ in aqueous. $\ce{NaHCO3}$ solution to afford diastereomeric iodolactones $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ (which differ in stereochemistry only at $\mathrm{C_3}$) in 70% yield.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-7-fig3.png

7b (8 pt) Draw the structures (with stereochemistry) of the compounds $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$.

The iodolactone $\mathbf{D}$ was subjected to an intermolecular radical reaction with ketone $\mathbf{X}$ using tris(trimethylsilyl)silane (TTMSS) and AIBN (azobisisobutyronitrile) in a catalytic amount, refluxing in toluene to yield the corresponding alkylated lactone $\mathbf{F}$ in 72% yield as a mixture of diastereoisomers which differ only in stereochemistry at $\mathrm{C_7}$ along with compound $\mathbf{G}$ (~10%) and the reduced product $\mathbf{H}$, $\ce{C10H16O2}$ (<5%).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-7-fig4.png

7c (8 pt) Draw the structures (with stereochemistry) of compound $\mathbf{H}$ and the reagent $\mathbf{X}$.

The keto group of $\mathbf{F}$ reacted with ethanedithiol and $\ce{BF3.Et2O}$ in dichloromethane (DCM) at $0\ ^\mathrm{o}\mathrm{C}$ to afford two diastereomers: thioketal lactones $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ in nearly quantitative yield (98%). The thioketalization facilitated the separation of the major isomer $\mathbf{J}$ in which the thioketal group is on the opposite face of the ring to the adjacent methyl group.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-7-fig5.png

7d (12 pt) Draw the structures (with stereochemistry) of the compounds $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$.

The isomer $\mathbf{J}$ was further subjected to alkaline hydrolysis followed by esterification with diazomethane providing hydroxy methyl ester $\mathbf{K}$ in 50% yield. The hydroxy methyl ester $\mathbf{K}$ was transformed into the keto ester $\mathbf{L}$ using $\mathbf{PCC}$ ($\mathbf{P}$yridium $\mathbf{C}$hloro$\mathbf{C}$hromate) as the oxidizing agent in dichloromethane (DCM).

A two-dimensional NMR study of the compound $\mathbf{L}$ revealed that the two protons adjacent to the newly-formed carbonyl group are $\textit{cis}$ to each other and confirmed the structure of $\mathbf{L}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-7-fig6.png

7e (12 pt) Draw the structures (with stereochemistry) of the compounds $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{L}$.

The ketone $\mathbf{L}$ was subjected to a Wittig reaction with methoxymethyl triphenylphosphonium chloride and KHMDS ($\mathbf{P}$otassium $\mathbf{H}$exa$\mathbf{M}$ethyl$\mathbf{D}$i$\mathbf{S}$ilazid - a strong, non-nucleophilic base) to furnish the required methyl vinyl ether $\mathbf{M}$ in 45% yield. Deprotection of thioketal using $\ce{HgCl2}$, $\ce{CaCO3}$ resulted in the key intermediate $\mathbf{N}$ (80%). Finally, the compound $\mathbf{N}$ was transformed into the target molecule Artemisinin by photo-oxidation followed by acid hydrolysis with 70% $\ce{HClO4}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2014-7-fig7.png

7f (12 pt) Draw the structures (with stereochemistry) of the compounds $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{N}$.

problems.title: New and well-forgotten old refrigerants
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (8 points; 33 marks). New and well-forgotten old refrigerants

The problem of choosing a refrigerant for refrigeration and air conditioning systems attracted the attention of scientists and technologists throughout the last century. It has been suggested that during this time refrigerants progressed through four generations. Ammonia, which was ascribed to the first generation, had been used in most of the oldest refrigeration units. It was later replaced by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) – derivatives of methane and ethane with the hydrogen atoms replaced by fluorine and chlorine.

In Baku, at "Bakkonditsioner" factory, production of the first Soviet serial household air conditioners BK-1500 had been launched. A second-generation refrigerant chlorodifluoromethane $\ce{CHF2Cl}$ was used in them. In this problem, we compare various refrigerants in terms of thermodynamics.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-1-fig1.png

First air conditioner of Baku factory in a souvenir shop in the Old City ("Icheri Sheher")

Thermodynamic properties of various refrigerants

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Refrigerant} & \text{"Generation"} & \Delta H_\mathrm{vap}\ /\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\ (\text{at } 280\,\mathrm{K}) & C_{V(\mathrm{gas})}\ /\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}} \\ \hline \ce{NH3} & 1 & 21.3 & 26.7 \\ \ce{CHF2Cl} & 2 & 20.0 & 48.8 \\ \ce{CF3CH2F} & 3 & 22.1 & 79 \\ \ce{CF3CF=CH2} & 4 & 19.1 & 120 \end{array}$$

Consider a model refrigeration cycle consisting of 4 steps schematically shown below in the pressure ($p$) – internal energy ($U$) coordinates.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-1-fig2.png

Diagram 1 (dashed line indicates the phase boundaries)

During the first step of the cycle (line 0-1 in diagram 1), a liquid refrigerant is boiling at constant pressure $p_1$ and temperature $T_1$ (boiling temperature) until it completely evaporates. At this step, the refrigeration unit absorbs heat from surrounding objects. At the second step, the refrigerant undergoes reversible adiabatic compression and heats up to temperature $T_2$ (line 1-2). After that the compressed refrigerant is cooled in a condenser at constant pressure $p_2$ (line 2-3) and then returns to the initial state (line 3-0).

Let the cycle involve 1 mole of refrigerant, which is initially (point 0) completely liquid, $T_1 = 280\,\mathrm{K}$, $T_2 = 380\,\mathrm{K}$, assume that the vapor of any refrigerant behaves like an ideal gas. The thermodynamic characteristics of refrigerants are listed in the table above.

1.1 (4 marks) For each of refrigerants, ammonia and chlorodifluoromethane, calculate the amount of heat $Q$ absorbed by refrigeration unit during heat exchange (line 0-1) and the work $W$ required to compress its vapor adiabatically (line 1-2).

1.2 (2 marks) Which quantity(ies) remain(s) constant during the adiabatic compression step? Indicate by the circle(s).

$U \qquad H \qquad S \qquad G \qquad V$

To compare the energy efficiency of refrigeration cycles with different parameters and refrigerants, the coefficient of performance ($COP$) is used, which is defined as a ratio of heat removed from a cooled system to the work of compressor: $COP = Q/W$.

1.3 (2 marks) Calculate the values of $COP$ in a considered cycle for ammonia and chlorodifluoromethane.

2.1 (1 mark) Why was ammonia replaced by CFCs in household refrigeration units? (Choose only one option)

a) to increase the energy efficiency of refrigeration cycles
b) because the density of ammonia is less than that of air under the same conditions
c) for user safety reasons

A search for replacement of CFCs as refrigerants started when it was shown that their use can cause irreparable damage to the protective ozone layer of the atmosphere. The third, ozone-friendly generation of refrigerants came on the scene. Its typical representatives are fluoroalkanes.

2.2 (1 mark) What is the cause of the damage made by CFCs to the ozone layer? (Choose only one option)

a) ozone molecule easily adds to C–F bond
b) C–F bond is easily broken by radiation, which leads to the formation of free radicals
c) ozone molecule easily adds to C–Cl bond
d) C–Cl bond is easily broken by radiation, which leads to the formation of free radicals

However, under the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, fluoroalkanes also had to be replaced because they accumulate in the atmosphere and rapidly absorb infrared radiation, causing a rise in temperature of the atmosphere (the greenhouse effect). The refrigerants of the fourth generation such as 2,3,3,3-tetrafluoropropene $\ce{CF3CF=CH2}$ have been suggested and are coming into use.

2.3 (1 mark) Why does this compound enhance the greenhouse effect less than fluoroalkanes? (Choose only one option)

a) it is more reactive and easier to decompose
b) it easily reacts with ozone
c) it is better soluble in water

3 (3 marks) Calculate the values of the $COP$ in the refrigeration cycle considered above for two refrigerants of the third and fourth generations – $\ce{CF3CH2F}$ and $\ce{CF3CF=CH2}$. Did the energy efficiency improve in comparison with $\ce{CHF2Cl}$? Choose "Yes" or "No".

Unlike household appliances, industrial refrigeration systems are often still using ammonia. It does not contribute to the greenhouse effect nor does it destroy the ozone layer. Industrial units can have a huge size and a large cost. Prior to their construction, they should be carefully modeled taking into account many different factors. In real systems, some part of the refrigerant at the start of the heat exchange with the environment is in the vapor phase (point 0 in the diagram below), and at the end (point 1) it is always overheated above the boiling point.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2015-1-fig3.png

Diagram 2 (dashed line indicates the phase boundaries)

Consider a cycle with 1 mole of ammonia. Its thermodynamic properties are the following: enthalpy of vaporization $\Delta H_\mathrm{vap} = 23.35\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ at $T_\mathrm{vap} = 239.8\,\mathrm{K}$ (boiling temperature at 1 bar pressure). Heat capacity of the liquid phase $C_{V(\mathrm{liq})} = 77\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$, of the gas phase $C_{V(\mathrm{gas})} = 26.7\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. Assume that the heat capacities are temperature-independent and the vapor behaves like an ideal gas. The temperature dependence of the saturated vapor pressure of ammonia can be described by the empirical equation:

$$\log\,(p/\mathrm{bar}) = 4.87 - 1114\,/\,(T/\mathrm{K} - 10.4).$$

During the first step of the cycle (line 0-1 in diagram 2), the equilibrium mixture of liquid refrigerant and its vapor receives heat from the environment at constant pressure $p_1 = 3.0\,\mathrm{bar}$. The refrigerant completely evaporates and overheats up to the temperature $T_1 = 275\,\mathrm{K}$. In the beginning of the process (point 0), the molar fraction of gaseous ammonia is $x = 0.13$.

4.1 (10 marks) Calculate the initial temperature of refrigerant $T_0$, its volume change $\Delta V$ and the amount of heat $Q$ absorbed by refrigeration unit during this step. Take into account that the dependence of $\Delta H_\mathrm{vap}$ from the temperature cannot be neglected.

Then the refrigerant is reversibly and adiabatically compressed. It heats up to the temperature $T_2 = 393\,\mathrm{K}$ (line 1-2).

At the next step corresponding to the line 2-3 in diagram, the compressed refrigerant is cooled in a condenser at constant pressure. Then it returns to the initial state through adiabatic expansion with zero work (line 3-0).

In the production of refrigeration units it is necessary to consider climatic factors. If a condenser is cooled by atmospheric air, the temperature $T_3$ increases as the air temperature increases.
