problems.title: Chromium in Ancient and Modern Times
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (21 points, 11% of the total). Chromium in Ancient and Modern Times

Black glazed porcelain is a special Chinese porcelain and was popular in the Tang and Song dynasties (ca. 1000 years ago). The ceramic ware contained iron oxides as the main color rendering agent, which was mixed with other transition metal oxides to exhibit different color appearance such as auburn, dark brown or black. Currently, the black glazed porcelain is still popular in China.

The typical black glaze is composed of Fe-containing oxides with a spinel structure. Spinel oxides have the general formula $\ce{AB2O4}$ and the structure consists of a cubic close packing array of $\ce{O^{2-}}$ ions in which the $\mathbf{A}$ cations occupy one-eighth of the tetrahedral vacancies and the $\mathbf{B}$ cations occupy half of the octahedral vacancies, as shown in Figure 2.1(a) for a unit cell.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-2-fig1.png

Figure 2.1 Illustration of spinel structure

The cubic unit cell of a spinel structure can be divided into 8 cubic subunits, and the dashed lines represent the internal edges of the subunits. 4 of the subunits belong to type I, and the other 4 subunits are type II (Figure 2.1(b)). The details of adjacent subunits of type I and type II are shown in Figure 2.1(c).

2.1 (2.0 pt) How many cations of type $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are there in a unit cell?

The black ceramic glaze with spinel structure can be produced by roasting $\ce{Fe2O3}$ and $\ce{Cr2O3}$ in a certain proportion in a reducing atmosphere (reaction (I)). When $\ce{Fe2O3}$ and $\ce{Cr2O3}$ are reacted with the mass ratio of $63.6 : 36.4$, they completely transform into a pure stoichiometric compound. The product has a spinel structure, in which the tetrahedral $\mathbf{A}$ sites are occupied by iron cations only.

2.2 (1.0 pt) In reaction (I), which element is reduced?

2.3 (6.0 pt) Calculate the numbers of $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ and $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ in the $\mathbf{B}$ sites of one unit cell.

Besides doping in black ceramic glaze, chromium-containing pigments are used in painting and printing due to the abundant color originating from chromium with different oxidation states, such as $+2$, $+3$ and $+6$. The pigment, chrome green ($\ce{Cr2O3}$) can be converted into a series of other compounds ($\mathbf{D}$–$\mathbf{G}$) in the following process, where $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{G}$ are yellow, orange and red respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-2-fig2.png

2.4 (1.0 pt) Write the chemical formula of $\mathbf{E}$.

2.5 (2.0 pt) Write the reaction equation of $\mathbf{F} \longrightarrow \mathbf{G}$.

2.6 (1.0 pt) Choose the agent which could be $\mathbf{H}$.

(A) $\ce{FeSO4}$
(B) $\ce{FeCl3}$
(C) $\ce{ZnSO4}$
(D) $\ce{CuSO4}$

The variable valence of chromium is not only important for the production of pigments, but also useful for catalysis. For example, a typical Phillips catalyst for the polymerization of ethylene consists of chromium oxide species grafted onto a porous support material such as amorphous silica. The tetra-coordinated $\mathrm{Cr(VI)}$ specie is the core in the pre-catalyst ($\mathbf{1}$), which is proposed to be reduced quickly into a six-coordinated $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ specie ($\mathbf{2}$) by the ethylene molecules at the beginning. $\mathbf{2}$ is proposed to further catalyze polymerization of ethylene molecules.

2.7 (1.0 pt) The reaction of $\mathbf{1}$ with ethylene can be traced by UV–vis spectra, which show the light absorption of $\mathbf{1}$ at $21500\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and the light absorption of $\mathbf{2}$ at $16700\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in the visible region, respectively. Choose the appropriate combination of colors of $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{2}$.

(A) orange and white, respectively
(B) orange and blue, respectively
(C) blue and orange, respectively
(D) blue and white, respectively

2.8 (5.0 pt) Assuming that the $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ ion in $\mathbf{2}$ is located in a regular octahedral crystal field with a splitting energy $\Delta_\mathrm{o}$ of $16000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, draw the configurations of d electrons of the $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ ion in $\mathbf{2}$, and calculate the crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) for the $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ ion in $\mathbf{2}$. (Note: The pairing energy $P$ for $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ in $\mathbf{2}$ is $23500\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$)

2.9 (2.0 pt) Coordination compounds/ions exhibit paramagnetism when containing unpaired electrons, and the corresponding magnetic moment ($\mu$) of transition metal cations is calculated by the function $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mu_\mathrm{B}$ where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. Calculate the magnetic moment in term of $\mu_\mathrm{B}$ for the $\mathrm{Cr(II)}$ ion in $\mathbf{2}$.

problems.title: Capture and Transformation of Carbon Dioxide
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (42 points, 14% of the total). Capture and Transformation of Carbon Dioxide

Climate change is one of the most critical global challenges nowadays. The increase of $\ce{CO2}$ concentration in the atmosphere has been recognized as the primary driver of global warming. The study of the capture and transformation of $\ce{CO2}$ has attracted considerable attention.

Direct air capture (DAC) technology which aims to extract $\ce{CO2}$ directly from ambient air is promising. The conventional method of DAC is wet scrubbing with alkaline hydroxide solutions (typically NaOH), where $\ce{CO2}$ in air is absorbed till pH ≈ 10 (step 1). The spent sorbent is regenerated by dosing calcium hydroxide into the system (step 2). The white precipitate $\mathbf{A}$ received in step 2 decomposes at $700\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, giving rise to $\ce{CO2}$ and another white compound $\mathbf{B}$ (step 3). Finally, calcium hydroxide can be generated by the hydration of $\mathbf{B}$. This process is highly energy-demanding. ($\ce{H2CO3}$: $K_\mathrm{a1} = 4.5\times10^{-7}$, $K_\mathrm{a2} = 4.7\times10^{-11}$)

3.1 (2.0 pt) Write the formulas for $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ respectively.

3.2 (5.0 pt) Write the balanced equations of all possible reactions in steps 1-3. NaOH solution is used as sorbent.

Recently, an electrochemical process was developed for regenerating the alkaline solution in the wet scrubbing process for DAC application, and pure $\ce{CO2}$ gas could be recovered that is suitable for storage or utilization. The process is based on a $\ce{H2}$-recycling electrochemical system (HRES), as shown in Figure 3.1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig1.png

Figure 3.1 Schematic drawing of the experimental setup

The electrochemical cell contains three compartments: an anode region (A), an acidifying region (B), and a cathode region (C). They are separated by ion-selective permeable membranes M1 and M2. During the operation, protons produced from $\ce{H2}$ oxidation at the anode are transported to the acidifying compartment where the spent solution ($\ce{Na2CO3}$-$\ce{NaHCO3}$) coming from the air contactor is fed. The decreasing pH of the solution leads to the conversions of carbonate to hydrocarbonate (reaction 1) and hydrocarbonate to carbonic acid (reaction 2). When the solution is saturated by dissolved $\ce{CO2}$ (solubility: $0.033\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$), a further pH decrease leads to the release of $\ce{CO2}$ gas (reaction 3). $\ce{H2}$ generated in the cathode is introduced to the anode and the solution from the cathode can be reused as a DAC absorbent.

3.3 (2.0 pt) Write the electrode reactions in the anode (A) and the cathode (C) respectively.

3.4 (3.0 pt) Write the balanced equations for the reactions 1–3 in the acidifying region (B).

3.5 (2.0 pt) Check all that correctly describe the movement of cations during the system operation.

(a) $\ce{H+}$ ions permeate through M1 from A to B.
(b) $\ce{H+}$ ions permeate through M2 from B to C.
(c) $\ce{Na+}$ ions permeate through M1 from B to A.
(d) $\ce{Na+}$ ions permeate through M2 from B to C.
(e) Both $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{Na+}$ ions can permeate through M1and M2.

The cell works at a steady state when the current passing through the cell is $2.00\,\mathrm{A}$ and the flow rate of the solution ($0.050\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ $\ce{Na2CO3}$ - $0.10\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ $\ce{NaHCO3}$) into the region B is $10.0\,\mathrm{mL\,min^{-1}}$. The pH in the anode compartment is maintained at 1 in the steady state.

3.6 (8.0 pt) Calculate the generation rate of $\ce{CO2}$ gas (in $\mathrm{mmol\,min^{-1}}$).

Zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs), a sub-class of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising materials for the capture and utilization of $\ce{CO2}$. The structures of ZIFs resemble zeolites. They form 3D frameworks with tetrahedrally coordinated metal ions (e.g. $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$, $\ce{Co^{2+}}$) bridged by imidazolate ($\mathrm{Im^{-}}$) and its derivatives. As the conjugated base of imidazole (HIm), imidazolate anion binds to metal cations (M) by its two N atoms. The fact that the M-Im-M angle is similar to the Si-O-Si angle ($145^\circ$) preferred in zeolites (as shown below) has led to the synthesis of a large number of ZIFs with zeolite-type tetrahedral topologies.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig2.png

ZIF-8 is one of the representative ZIFs, which adopts a sodalite framework (SOD), as shown in Figure 3.2. ZIF-8 was firstly synthesized by Chinese scientists Xiao-Ming Chen et al. (they named it as MAF-4) by the reaction of $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ with 2-methylimidazole ($\ce{CH3(C3N2H3)}$, HmIm). It crystalizes in the cubic system with the cell parameter $a = 1.632\,\mathrm{nm}$ for a solvent-free phase with the effective pore diameter (shown by the inside virtual sphere in Figure 3.2d) of $1.16\,\mathrm{nm}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig3.png

Figure 3.2 Topology of SOD and structure of ZIF-8. (a) Topology of SOD cage; (b) SOD cage in ZIF-8 formed by $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ (at the centers of the tetrahedra) and imidazolate (H atoms are omitted for clarity); (c) Framework of SOD with the unit cell shown by the square box; (d) Some of the pores are highlighted by virtual spheres in ZIF-8.

Note: If you wish, you may use the symbol "HmIm" and "mIm" representing 2-methylimidazole and 2-methylimidazolate respectively in solving the following questions.

3.7 (2.0 pt) Write the formula of the single sodalite cage.

3.8 (2.0 pt) Write the composition of the unit cell of ZIF-8.

3.9 (5.0 pt) Calculate the inner surface area ($S$) of the pores (modeled by the virtual spheres) of 1 g ZIF-8 (in $\mathrm{m^2}$). If you failed to get the composition of the unit cell, use 3500 as the formula weight of the unit cell.

3.10 (7.0 pt) Calculate the porosity $R$ of ZIF-8 ($R$ is the ratio of pore volume to the actual volume of the material) and the pore volume of 1 g ZIF-8 ($V_p$, in $\mathrm{cm^3}$).

ZIF-8 can also act as a catalyst to promote the conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ to high value-added chemicals. One of the most promising routes for $\ce{CO2}$ fixation is the preparation of cyclic carbonates via $\ce{CO2}$ cycloaddition. An example is shown as below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig4.png

A mechanism of catalytic conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ to cyclic carbonate over ZIF-8 catalyst is proposed:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig5.png

3.11 (2.0 pt) If ZIF-8 provides acid sites in the above catalytic process, complete the mechanism by choosing the reasonable intermediates from the following species:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-3-fig6.png

Choose the intermediates corresponding to I and II respectively.

ZIF-8 shows a relatively high thermal stability. However, a recent study revealed that its structure would be destroyed if applied in a wet acidic environment. The co-existence of $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ with ZIF-8 resulted in the formation of $\ce{ZnCO3}$.

3.12 (2.0 pt) Write the balanced equation of ZIF-8 with $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$.

problems.title: A New Journey for Ancient Sulfur
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (45 points, 16% of the total). A New Journey for Ancient Sulfur

Sulfur has been known and used since the ancient times. Nowadays, sulfur is widely used in chemical production and pharmaceutical industry as an inexpensive chemical raw material.

Pyrite ($\ce{FeS2}$) is commonly used as a raw material in the industrial production of elemental sulfur. By heating pyrite in the presence of limited air supply, the theoretical yield of elemental sulfur is 100% and a black magnetic oxide ($\ce{Fe3O4}$) is the other product.

4.1 (2.0 pt) Write the balanced reaction equation that describes the above conversion.

In addition to sulfur, a small amount of $\ce{SO2}$ is generated as a by-product during the actual process. This reaction can be monitored by measuring the amount of $\ce{SO2}$. The following recipe is used for the monitoring:

Raw ore powder is heated in a temperature-controlled tube furnace. The generated $\ce{SO2}$ is absorbed by $2\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ NaOH solution. When the reaction is completed, the solution is transferred to a $500\,\mathrm{mL}$ volumetric flask and diluted by distilled water to the mark. $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of this diluted solution is then added into an iodine flask containing $50.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ $0.05122\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ $\ce{I2}$ standard solution and $5\,\mathrm{mL}$ 20% $\ce{H2SO4}$ solution. After maintaining the iodine flask in dark for 5 min, the solution is titrated with $0.1012\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ standard solution. When the color of the solution turns light brown, $3\,\mathrm{mL}$ 0.5% starch indicator is added. Continue the titration until the blue color disappears.

4.2 (4.0 pt) Write the balanced reaction equations involving $\ce{I2}$ in the above measurement.

4.3 (4.0 pt) In such a test experiment starting from pyrite, $17.6\,\mathrm{g}$ of elemental sulfur was collected. The analysis of the by-product gases according to the above procedure resulted in the consumption of $18.47\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ standard solution. Assuming that no other sulfur containing species were produced, calculate what percentage of the sulfur in pyrite was lost as the by-product?

The lithium-sulfur battery is a compelling energy storage system because its high theoretical energy density exceeds conventional Li-ion batteries. The net reaction of a lithium-sulfur battery can be simplified as: $\ce{16 Li + S8 -> 8 Li2S}$. Sulfur is the cathode and metallic lithium is the anode active material during discharge.

4.4 (3.0 pt) Write the balanced equations for reactions that take place at cathode (a) and anode (b) during discharge.

4.5 (1.0 pt) Calculate the mass ratio of the cathode active material to the anode active material, according to the net battery reaction.

A lithium-ion battery (LIB) that possesses an average operating voltage of $3.8\,\mathrm{V}$ and a deliverable capacity of $3110\,\mathrm{mAh}$ can provide energy for a mobile phone to play videos continuously for 22 hours upon a full charge.

4.6 (5.0 pt) If the LIB is replaced by an ideal lithium-sulfur battery pack, which has an average operating voltage of $4.2\,\mathrm{V}$ and contains $23\,\mathrm{g}$ sulfur as the active electrode material that can react stoichiometrically during discharge, calculate how many hours the new battery pack will provide energy for the phone to play videos continuously after a full charge.

Elemental sulfur generally exist as $\ce{S8}$ molecules. In real lithium-sulfur batteries, $\ce{S8}$ is not directly reduced to $\ce{Li2S}$ during discharge, but it undergoes stepwise reactions generating different soluble lithium polysulfides ($\ce{Li2S_{n}}$, $n = 3-8$). These lithium polysulfides could diffuse to the anode and corrode it, which results in the loss of active electrode materials. This phenomenon is called "shuttle effect".

4.7 (2.0 pt) Write the balanced reaction equation for the corrosion of anode by soluble lithium polysulfides ($\ce{Li2S_{n}}$) that produces $\ce{Li2S}$.

In order to suppress the "shuttle effect", the forms of polysulfides in an electrolyte have been extensively studied. $\ce{Li2S6}$ is one of the most representative intermediate products:

$$\ce{2Li+ + S8 + 2e- -> Li2S6 + 2S}$$

A theoretical study shows that two conformers with comparable energies, $\ce{Li2S6}\mathrm{(I)}$ and $\ce{Li2S6}\mathrm{(II)}$ coexist in 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME), a common electrolyte solvent in lithium-sulfur batteries. The dissociation of $\ce{Li2S6}$ in DME is shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-4-fig1.png

Chemical equilibria of $\ce{Li2S6}$, $\ce{LiS6^-}$, $\ce{S6^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{LiS_3^{\bullet}}$ in DME

Table 4.1 Dissociation Gibbs energies ($\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) of different reactions in DME (298.15 K, 1 bar)

$$\begin{array}{ccccc} \Delta G^\ominus_\mathrm{d1}(\mathrm{I}) & \Delta G^\ominus_\mathrm{d1}(\mathrm{II}) & \Delta G^\ominus_\mathrm{d2} & \Delta G^\ominus_\mathrm{dr}(\mathrm{I}) & \Delta G^\ominus_\mathrm{dr}(\mathrm{II}) \\ \hline 20.68 & 18.92 & 100.55 & 45.13 & 43.37 \end{array}$$

4.8 (4.0 pt) Using the data from Table 4.1, calculate the equilibrium concentration ratio of two conformers in DME (298.15 K, 1 bar), $\dfrac{[\ce{Li2S6}\mathrm{(II)}]}{[\ce{Li2S6}\mathrm{(I)}]}$.

4.9 (5.0 pt) Using the data from Table 4.1, calculate the apparent dissociation constant of $\ce{Li2S6 -> Li+ + LiS6^-}$ in DME (298.15 K, 1 bar).

4.10 (4.0 pt) Sort the following equilibrium concentrations in decreasing order: $[\ce{Li2S6}]$, $[\ce{LiS6^-}]$, $[\ce{S6^{2-}}]$, $[\mathrm{LiS_3^{\bullet}}]$ in DME.

4.11 (6.0 pt) The standard reduction potential of metallic lithium in water at 298.15 K and 1 bar is:

$$E^\ominus\left(\ce{Li+}/\ce{Li}\right) = -3.040\,\mathrm{V}$$

The standard solvation Gibbs energies of gaseous $\ce{Li+(g)}$ to $\ce{Li+(sol)}$ in different solvents.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & \ce{Li+(H2O)} & \ce{Li+}\mathrm{(DME)} \\ \hline \Delta G^\ominus/\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} & -116.9 & -114.6 \end{array}$$

Calculate the standard reduction potential of metallic lithium electrode in DME.

Studies have shown that electromotive force of a lithium-sulfur battery would be increased by replacing DME with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). Therefore, the forms of polysulfides in DMSO also attract researchers' attention.

In a test, a certain amount of $\ce{Li2S}$ and $4.81\,\mathrm{mg}$ sulfur powder were added into $10.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ DMSO, then heated and stirred until completely dissolved (ignoring the change in volume). Suppose that only the following polysulfides were present in the DMSO: $\mathrm{S_3^{\bullet-}}$, $\ce{S4^{2-}}$, $\ce{S5^{2-}}$, $\ce{S6^{2-}}$, $\ce{S7^{2-}}$, $\ce{S8^{2-}}$. The equilibrium concentration ratio of the sulfur containing species was:

$$[\mathrm{S_3^{\bullet-}}] : [\ce{S4^{2-}}] : [\ce{S5^{2-}}] : [\ce{S6^{2-}}] : [\ce{S7^{2-}}] : [\ce{S8^{2-}}] = 17.50 : 1.00 : 4.50 : 55.00 : 5.00 : 0.75$$

4.12 (5.0 pt) Calculate the original mass $m$ (in mg) of $\ce{Li2S}$ added to DMSO.

problems.title: Interconversion among Nitrogen Oxides
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (45 points, 15% of the total). Interconversion among Nitrogen Oxides

Nitrogen oxides (including $\ce{N2O}$, $\ce{NO}$, $\ce{NO2}$, $\ce{N2O4}$ and etc., usually written as $\ce{NO_{x}}$) are one of the main air pollutants that can cause a series of problems such as ozone depletion, acid rain, photochemical smog, and greenhouse effect. Therefore, the emission and conversion of $\ce{NO_{x}}$ must be controlled to improve air quality. Here let us investigate the oxidation of NO to $\ce{NO2}$ via the reaction of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$.

Part A

It is generally accepted that this reaction proceeds through the following mechanism in the atmosphere:

$$\ce{2NO <=> N2O2} \qquad (1)$$

$$\ce{N2O2 + O2 -> 2NO2} \qquad (2)$$

Reaction (1) and (2) and the reverse of reaction (1) are elementary reactions. Reaction (1) is a pre-equilibrium reaction, and its equilibrium constant in terms of concentrations is denoted as $K_{c1}$. Reaction (2) is the rate-determining step of the overall reaction, and its rate constant is $k_2$.

5.1 (4.0 pt) Deduce the rate expression for the overall reaction of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$ as a function of $[\ce{NO}]$, $[\ce{O2}]$, $K_{c1}$ and $k_2$.

The temperature dependence of $K_{c1}$ could be approximately described as $\ln K_{c1} = M - (N/T)$ ($M$ and $N$ are constants). The change of $k_2$ with temperature follows the Arrhenius equation with the pre-exponential factor of $A_2$ and apparent activation energy of $E_{a,2}$. Assume that $E_{a,2}$ and $A_2$ are independent of the temperature.

5.2 (4.0 pt) Deduce the expressions for the pre-exponential factor ($A_+$) and apparent activation energy ($E_{a^+}$) of the reaction of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$ as functions of $M$, $N$, $A_2$ and $E_{a,2}$.

The apparent rate constant ($k_+$) of the overall reaction is $6.63\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{L^2\,mol^{-2}\,min^{-1}}$ at $600\,\mathrm{K}$, and its apparent activation energy is $1.20\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

5.3 (2.0 pt) Calculate the rate constant (in $\mathrm{L^2\,mol^{-2}\,min^{-1}}$) of this reaction at $700\,\mathrm{K}$.

The standard enthalpies of formation ($\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\ominus_\mathrm{m}$) and standard entropies ($S^\ominus_\mathrm{m}$) at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ are as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l|ccc} & \ce{NO(g)} & \ce{O2(g)} & \ce{NO2(g)} \\ \hline \Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\ominus_\mathrm{m}\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & 91.3 & & 33.1 \\ S^\ominus_\mathrm{m}\ (\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}) & 210.8 & 205.2 & 240.1 \end{array}$$

The standard reaction enthalpy and entropy changes of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$ can be regarded as temperature independent. All the gases are taken to be ideal for the following questions.

5.4 (4.0 pt) Calculate the thermodynamic equilibrium constant ($K_p^\ominus$) of this reaction at $600\,\mathrm{K}$.

5.5 (3.0 pt) Calculate the standard internal energy change $\Delta_\mathrm{r}U^\ominus_\mathrm{m}$ (in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) of this reaction at $600\,\mathrm{K}$.

Experimental observation shows that the rate of the reaction of $\ce{2NO2 -> 2NO + O2}$ is independent on the concentration of NO and $\ce{O2}$.

5.6 (8.0 pt) Deduce the expression of the rate for this reaction (the apparent rate constant could be directly used as $k_-$) and calculate the value of $k_-$ apparent at $600\,\mathrm{K}$. (If you failed to find the $K_p^\ominus(600\,\mathrm{K})$ in question 5.4, use $K_p^\ominus(600\,\mathrm{K}) = 350.0$)

$\ce{NO2}$ gas is introduced to a container with a fixed volume which is held at $600\,\mathrm{K}$ and allowed to reach equilibrium. 20 percent of the reactant is converted to NO and $\ce{O2}$. All the gases are taken to be ideal.

5.7 (4.0 pt) Calculate the total pressure of this reaction system at equilibrium. (If you failed to find the $K_p^\ominus(600\,\mathrm{K})$ in question 5.4, use $K_p^\ominus(600\,\mathrm{K}) = 350.0$)

Part B

Industrial exhaust is a main source of $\ce{NO_{x}}$. One of the approaches to reduce the emission of $\ce{NO_{x}}$ is through the oxidation of NO to $\ce{NO2}$ and the subsequent absorption of the formed $\ce{NO2}$ by absorbents. However, because of the low concentration of NO in exhaust, its spontaneous oxidation in the atmosphere is too slow to meet the demand of industry. Generally, solid catalysts are used to accelerate this reaction. The NO oxidation proceeds on the surface of a specific catalyst (CatX) through the following mechanism (adsorption site is denoted as Site):

$$\ce{O2(g)} + 2\,\text{Site} \underset{k_{\mathrm{S}-1}}{\overset{k_{\mathrm{S}+1}}{\rightleftharpoons}} 2\,\text{O-Site} \qquad \text{(S1)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+1} = k_{\mathrm{S}+1}\,[\ce{O2}]\,\theta_v^2 \qquad r_{\mathrm{S}-1} = k_{\mathrm{S}-1}\,\theta_\mathrm{O}^2$$

$$\ce{NO(g)} + \text{Site} \underset{k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}{\overset{k_{\mathrm{S}+2}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \text{NO-Site} \qquad \text{(S2)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+2} = k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]\,\theta_v \qquad r_{\mathrm{S}-2} = k_{\mathrm{S}-2}\,\theta_\mathrm{NO}$$

$$\ce{NO(g)} + \text{O-Site} \xrightarrow{k_{\mathrm{S}+3}} \ce{NO2}\text{-Site} \qquad \text{(S3)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+3} = k_{\mathrm{S}+3}[\ce{NO}]\,\theta_\mathrm{O}$$

$$\ce{NO2}\text{-Site} \underset{k_{\mathrm{S}-4}}{\overset{k_{\mathrm{S}+4}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \ce{NO2(g)} + \text{Site} \qquad \text{(S4)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+4} = k_{\mathrm{S}+4}\,\theta_{\mathrm{NO_2}} \qquad r_{\mathrm{S}-4} = k_{\mathrm{S}-4}\,[\ce{NO2}]\,\theta_v$$

Assume that the adsorptions of NO, $\ce{NO2}$ and O (from the dissociation of $\ce{O2}$) cannot proceed beyond a monolayer coverage, and these species are adsorbed by the same kind of surface sites. Their fractional coverages ($\theta$, defined as the ratio of the number of adsorption sites occupied to the number of total adsorption sites) are denoted as $\theta_\mathrm{NO}$, $\theta_{\mathrm{NO_2}}$ and $\theta_\mathrm{O}$, respectively. Thus, the fraction of unoccupied adsorption sites ($\theta_\mathrm{v}$) is $\theta_\mathrm{v} = 1 - \theta_\mathrm{NO} - \theta_{\mathrm{NO_2}} - \theta_\mathrm{O}$. Assume that all the adsorption and desorption processes are much faster than reaction (S3).

5.8 (6.0 pt) Deduce the expression for $\theta_\mathrm{v}$ as a function of $[\ce{NO}]$, $[\ce{O2}]$, $[\ce{NO2}]$ and the rate constants involved in reactions (S1)–(S4).

5.9 (4.0 pt) Choose the correct expression for the rate of $\ce{2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ at the beginning of the reaction. Assume that the concentration and adsorption of $\ce{NO2}$ are both negligible.

(A) $r_{\mathrm{S}+} = \dfrac{k_{\mathrm{S}+3}(k_{\mathrm{S}+1}/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5}[\ce{NO}][\ce{O2}]^{0.5}}{1 + (k_{\mathrm{S}+1}[\ce{O2}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5} + k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}$
(B) $r_{\mathrm{S}+} = \dfrac{0.5k_{\mathrm{S}+3}(k_{\mathrm{S}+1}/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5}[\ce{NO}][\ce{O2}]^{0.5}}{1 + (k_{\mathrm{S}+1}[\ce{O2}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5} + k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}$
(C) $r_{\mathrm{S}+} = \dfrac{k_{\mathrm{S}+3}(k_{\mathrm{S}+1}/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})[\ce{NO}][\ce{O2}]^{0.5}}{1 + k_{\mathrm{S}+1}[\ce{O2}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-1} + k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}$
(D) $r_{\mathrm{S}+} = \dfrac{k_{\mathrm{S}+4}k_{\mathrm{S}+3}(k_{\mathrm{S}+1}/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5}[\ce{NO}][\ce{O2}]^{0.5}/k_{\mathrm{S}-4}}{1 + k_{\mathrm{S}+1}([\ce{O2}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-1})^{0.5} + k_{\mathrm{S}+2}[\ce{NO}]/k_{\mathrm{S}-2}}$

For some catalysts, the surface reaction proceeds via an alternative way instead of reaction (S3):

$$\text{NO-Site} + \text{O-Site} \xrightarrow{k_{\mathrm{S}+5}} \text{Site} + \ce{NO2}\text{-Site} \qquad \text{(S5)}$$

$$r_{\mathrm{S}+5} = k_{\mathrm{S}+5}\,\theta_\mathrm{NO}\,\theta_\mathrm{O}$$

This step is also rate-determining for the overall reaction.

A catalyst (CatY) is used to promote the reaction of $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$. When the temperature and NO concentration are constant, the initial reaction rate changes with the concentration of $\ce{O2}$ as follows:

problems.title: Enabling Phosphines
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (36 points, 7% of the total). Enabling Phosphines

Phosphines are phosphorus analogues of amines. They also carry a lone pair of electrons at the phosphorus atom and thus exhibit Lewis basicity or nucleophilicity. But in contrast with tertiary amines, chiral phosphines like $\mathbf{P1}$ with three different substituents can be isolated as single enantiomers. Chiral phosphines are often used as chiral ligands in transition metal catalysis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig1.png

6.1 (3.0 pt) Using $R/S$ symbol, assign the absolute configuration of $\mathbf{P1}$.

In the past two decades, as organocatalysis grew rapidly, a large number of nucleophilic phosphine-catalyzed synthetic reactions have emerged. Among them, one of the most famous phosphine-catalyzed reactions is the Lu (3+2) cycloaddition reaction, which was first developed by Chinese scientist Xiyan Lu. For instance, under the catalysis of triphenylphosphine, ethyl allenoate $\mathbf{1}$ and methyl acrylate $\mathbf{2}$ smoothly produce two cyclopentene derivatives $\mathbf{3}$ (major) and $\mathbf{4}$ (minor).

Lu (3+2) cycloaddition:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig2.png

In a generally accepted mechanism, the Lu (3+2) reaction is a formal cycloaddition reaction. Initially, the catalyst triphenylphosphine engages in a nucleophilic addition to ethyl allenoate $\mathbf{1}$ to generate a zwitterionic intermediate $\mathbf{A}$, which subsequently cyclizes with methyl acrylate $\mathbf{2}$ by two paths. In the path leading to compound $\mathbf{3}$, an in situ generated phosphorus ylide intermediate $\mathbf{B}$ reversibly converts into intermediate $\mathbf{C}$ via proton transfer; $\mathbf{C}$ undergoes an elimination to deliver the major product $\mathbf{3}$ and release the phosphine catalyst. In the path leading to compound $\mathbf{4}$, a phosphorus ylide intermediate $\mathbf{B'}$ is formed, which also reversibly converts into intermediate $\mathbf{C'}$ via proton transfer; $\mathbf{C'}$ undergoes an elimination to give the minor product $\mathbf{4}$ and regenerate the phosphine catalyst.

Mechanism:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig3.png

6.2 (6.0 pt) Draw the two major resonance structures that make up the shown resonance hybrid $\mathbf{A}$ (the involvement of ester group is not considered, and stereochemistry is not required).

6.3 (8.0 pt) Draw the structures of intermediates $\mathbf{B'}$ and $\mathbf{C'}$ (stereochemistry is not required).

Under similar conditions, ethyl allenoate $\mathbf{1}$ and diethyl fumarate $\mathbf{5}$ readily deliver the corresponding cycloaddition product $\mathbf{6}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig4.png

6.4 (5.0 pt) Draw the structure of compound $\mathbf{6}$ (stereochemistry is not required).

Asymmetric Lu (3+2) cycloaddition reaction can be readily realized by utilizing chiral phosphine catalysts. For example, under the catalysis of a chiral bicyclic phosphine $\mathbf{P2}$, ethyl allenoate $\mathbf{1}$ and methyl acrylate $\mathbf{2}$ smoothly delivered an enantio-enriched cycloaddition product $\mathbf{3}$ in 80% ee (enantiomeric excess).

Asymmetric Lu (3+2) cycloaddition:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig5.png

Calculation equation of ee:

$$\mathrm{ee} = \frac{n_\mathrm{major} - n_\mathrm{minor}}{n_\mathrm{major} + n_\mathrm{minor}} \times 100\%$$

$n_\mathrm{major}$ = the amount of major enantiomer

$n_\mathrm{minor}$ = the amount of minor enantiomer

6.5 (6.0 pt) Mark the chirality centers in the chiral phosphine $\mathbf{P2}$ by using asterisks. (Note: points will be deducted for every wrong asterisk until 0 points)

6.6 (3.0 pt) Give the ratio of $n_\mathrm{major}/n_\mathrm{minor}$ of product $\mathbf{3}$.

Lu (3+2) cycloaddition reaction is a versatile tool in organic synthesis. For example, it was successfully used to synthesize (–)-hinesol, an important component of the Chinese medicinal herb Chang Zhu (Atractylodes lancea var Chinensis). Under the catalysis of $\ce{PPh3}$, a chiral cyclohexanone $\mathbf{7}$ cyclized with tert-butyl allenoate $\mathbf{8}$, affording a major product $\mathbf{9}$ and three minor products $\mathbf{10}$, $\mathbf{11}$ and $\mathbf{12}$. Minor products $\mathbf{10}$–$\mathbf{12}$ are all the isomers of $\mathbf{9}$. Compound $\mathbf{9}$ could be readily transformed into (–)-hinesol by a multistep process.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig6.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-6-fig8.png

problems.title: Organic Molecules in Life
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (32 points, 9% of the total). Organic Molecules in Life

The synthesis of complex peptides and proteins is a challenging task. On September 17, 1965, Chinese scientists synthesized crystalline bovine insulin artificially for the first time, marking a crucial step in the journey of exploring the secret of life and opening the era of protein synthesis.

Coupling of carboxylic acid groups with amine groups to forge an amide bond is the most elementary reaction in the synthesis of peptides and proteins. Allenone $\mathbf{2}$ was reported to be able to activate the carboxylic acid $\mathbf{1}$ under mild reaction conditions forming the intermediate $\mathbf{3}$. Intermediate $\mathbf{3}$ then reacts with amine $\mathbf{4}$ to give amide $\mathbf{5}$ with high yield, along with the byproduct $\mathbf{6}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig1.png

Similarly, N-ethynyl-N-methyl-p-toluenesulfonamide (MYTsA) with its major resonance structure $\mathbf{7}$ (involvement of Ts group is not considered) can activate carboxylic acid in the same way as allenone $\mathbf{2}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig2.png

7.1 (12.0 pt) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{7}$, intermediate $\mathbf{9}$ and compound $\mathbf{12}$. Show the stereochemistry of any stereocenters.

As the length of peptide chain grows, formation of amide bonds becomes more difficult, and conventional condensation methods are not applicable in the synthesis of proteins. In the first synthesis of crystalline bovine insulin, a method based on the chemistry of acylhydrazine $\mathbf{13}$ was developed to achieve the challenging amide coupling between two peptides. As the following equations, compound $\mathbf{15}$ reacts with $\mathbf{16}$ smoothly in the presence of triethylamine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig3.png

Note: P1, P2 = peptides

7.2 (8.0 pt) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{15}$ and $\mathbf{16}$.

In addition to de novo synthesis, scientists can modify existing proteins. Although there are multiple reactive sites on the surface of protein, such as amino groups, thiol groups, and carboxyl groups, the most nucleophilic thiol groups are the preferred site when the protein is treated with electrophilic reagents such as N-phenyl maleimide $\mathbf{18}$ via Michael addition.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig4.png

Under mild basic conditions (pH = 7.5), reagent $\mathbf{19}$ was proposed to react with the thiol group of protein $\mathbf{20}$ to give a neutral intermediate $\mathbf{21}$ which is attacked by hydroxide to give compound $\mathbf{22}$. Compound $\mathbf{22}$ can equilibrate with an acyclic form $\mathbf{23}$, and subsequently react with another protein $\mathbf{20}$. The resulting major product can exist either in the acyclic form $\mathbf{24}$ or in the cyclic form $\mathbf{25}$ in a similar way as the equilibration between $\mathbf{22}$ and $\mathbf{23}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2022-7-fig5.png

7.3 (12.0 pt) Draw the structures of intermediate $\mathbf{21}$, compounds $\mathbf{24}$ and $\mathbf{25}$. Stereochemistry is not required.

problems.title: Electrochemical CO2 Reduction
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (33 points, 5% of the total). Electrochemical $\ce{CO2}$ Reduction

In recent years, the electrochemical conversion of $\ce{CO2}$ into higher value products has been considered a promising and technologically feasible approach to mitigate the negative climatic effects caused by its increasing levels in the atmosphere. Several technologies have been developed to achieve this goal. Among these, $\ce{CO2}$ reduction through electrochemical means ($\ce{CO2}$RR) warrants particular attention due to its ability to be powered by renewable energy to transform environmentally harmful $\ce{CO2}$ into platform chemicals.

Electrocatalysts are essential not only to accelerate the intrinsically slow $\ce{CO2}$RR but also to direct the electrolysis reaction towards the desired reaction products (product selectivity). In this context, it is not only the chemical nature of the catalyst itself which governs the resulting $\ce{CO2}$RR product distribution but also its morphological characteristics on various length scales. A new concept of $\ce{CO2}$RR catalyst design relies on the electrodeposition of foam-type materials, which offer a large surface area that is accessible to reactants (e.g. $\ce{H2O}$, $\ce{H2}$, and $\ce{CO2}$). Copper-based materials are the only known metallic $\ce{CO2}$RR catalysts that can produce hydrocarbons and alcohols in significant amounts from $\ce{CO2}$ electrolysis.

Given below are thermodynamic data of selected substances:

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & \Delta_f H^\ominus\ (\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & S^\ominus\ (\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) \\ \hline \ce{H2O (l)} & -285.83 & 69.95 \\ \hline \ce{O2 (g)} & 0 & 205.15 \\ \hline \ce{H2 (g)} & 0 & 130.68 \\ \hline \ce{CO2 (g)} & -393.52 & 213.79 \\ \hline \text{ethanol (l)} & -276.00 & 159.86 \\ \hline n\text{-propanol (l)} & -302.54 & 192.80 \end{array}$$

Table 1. Standard formation enthalpy $\Delta_f H^\ominus$ and standard entropy $S^\ominus$ for some substances under standard conditions ($T = 298.15\,\mathrm{K}$, $p = 1\,\mathrm{bar}$).

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Cell reaction} & E,\ \mathrm{V}\ \text{vs. SHE} \\ \hline \ce{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- <-> Cu} & +0.34 \\ \hline \ce{2H^+ + 2e^- <-> H2} & 0.00 \end{array}$$

Table 2. Selected half-cell reactions and corresponding standard potentials under the standard conditions.

2.1 (2 pt) Write and balance the chemical equation of the half-cell reactions for the following electrochemical reduction processes in acidic environment (i) $\ce{CO2}$ to ethanol; (ii) $\ce{CO2}$ to $n$-propanol.

2.2 (8 pt) Combine the half-cell of the reduction process with an $\ce{H2}/\ce{2H^+}$ half-cell where the latter acts as anode. Calculate the value of the standard cell potential of the $\ce{CO2}$ to ethanol reduction.

Cu foam electrodeposition processes (see Figure 1) were carried out in an aqueous $1.5\,\mathrm{M}$ sulfuric acid solution containing $0.2\,\mathrm{M}$ copper sulfate ($\ce{CuSO4*5H2O}$) as the copper source. A Cu disk ($1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$) and a Pt foil served as the cathode and the anode, respectively.

2.3 (3 pt) Write all the reduction and oxidation half-cell reactions taking place at the cathode and the anode, respectively.

Figure 1 shows the principle of dynamic hydrogen bubble-templated metal deposition.

Figure 2 displays top-down scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of three different Cu foams obtained upon interruption of the metal deposition at different times: $5\,\mathrm{s}$, $20\,\mathrm{s}$, and $80\,\mathrm{s}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-2-fig1.png

Figure 1. Depiction of the electrodeposition of foam-type materials. In the course of electrochemical metal deposition (black arrows) at high current densities in aqueous media, the Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER) takes place on the metallic (Cu) support (1). The surface becomes thus partially covered by $\ce{H2}$ bubbles (2). The $\ce{H2}$ bubbles act as a template for metal deposition (3). As a result a highly porous metal foam emerges (4).

2.4 (3 pt) Considering this mechanism, assign the correct deposition time to the Cu foams shown in Figure 2 (white boxes upper left corner).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-2-fig2.png

Figure 2. Cu foams obtained by galvanostatic Cu electrodeposition at a current density of $j = -3\,\mathrm{A\,cm^{-2}}$. The deposition was, in each case, interrupted at distinct elapsed duration: $5\,\mathrm{s}$, $20\,\mathrm{s}$, and $80\,\mathrm{s}$. The scale bar is the same in all panels.

Bimetallic CuAg systems are excellent catalysts for the electrosynthesis of alcohols from $\ce{CO2}$. $5.4\,\mathrm{mg}$ of a bimetallic Cu-Ag foam catalyst ($90\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ Cu, $M_{Cu} = 63.546\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$; $10\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ Ag, $M_{Ag} = 107.868\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) was galvanostatically deposited onto a Cu foil ($1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$) at a current density of $j = -3\,\mathrm{A\,cm^{-2}}$ applied for $20\,\mathrm{s}$ (the minus sign accounts for a reductive/cathodic process).

2.5 (5 pt) Calculate the Faradaic efficiency (FE in %) of this metal deposition process. FE is defined as $Q_\text{product}/Q_\text{total}\cdot 100\%$. $Q$ denotes the charge.

We consider a $\ce{CO2}$ electrolysis experiment carried out in $35\,\mathrm{mL}$ $\ce{CO2}$-saturated $0.5\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{KHCO3}$ electrolyte solution over the bimetallic Cu-Ag foam catalyst ($90\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ Cu; $10\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ Ag). The $\ce{CO2}$ electrolysis was carried out at a constant (total) current density of $j(tot) = -30\,\mathrm{mA\,cm^{-2}}$ for $3600\,\mathrm{s}$ (note the current density is normalized to the geometric surface area of $1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$; the minus sign accounts for a reductive/cathodic process). A product analysis, carried out after the electrolysis, revealed mass concentrations of $41.3\,\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$ and $7.4\,\mathrm{mg\,L^{-1}}$ for ethanol and $n$-propanol, respectively. Both alcohols are liquid reaction products and accumulate in the electrolyte in the course of the electrolysis reaction. We assume that gaseous hydrogen ($\ce{H2}$) is formed as the only by-product of the process.

2.6 (8 pt) Calculate the current densities required for the formation of (a) ethanol ($MW_\text{ethanol} = 46.08\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) and (b) $n$-propanol ($MW_{n\text{-propanol}} = 60.10\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) assuming that the current densities do not change with electrolysis time.

2.7 (4 pt) Calculate the volume of the formed hydrogen on the $1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ catalyst area at $298.15\,\mathrm{K}$ and $1\,\mathrm{bar}$, assuming ideal behavior of the formed hydrogen, and its complete release into the gas phase. If you did not get a result in Task 2.5, continue with $FE_{(EtOH)} = 45.1\%$ and $FE_{(PrOH)} = 4.8\%$.

problems.title: Artificial Photosynthesis
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (29 points, 6% of the total). Artificial Photosynthesis

The field of artificial photosynthesis research aims at storing solar energy in chemical bonds. Photons are absorbed by exciting sensitizers, thereby producing a charge-separated state. The excited electron is transferred to a catalyst (hydrogen evolving catalyst, HER), which is reduced twice and then produces $\ce{H2}$. The photosensitizer or light absorber is often $\ce{[Ru(bpy)3]^{2+}}$ (bpy=2,2'-bipyridine), and the HERs are often cobalt complexes.

Energetics of Water Splitting

3.1 (3 pt) Calculate the enthalpy of the reaction $\ce{H2(g) -> 2H^+(aq) + 2e^-}$.

Solvation enthalpy of proton: $\Delta H_{aq}(\ce{H^+}) = -1190\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

Ionization energy of hydrogen: $\mathrm{IE}_1 = 13.6\,\mathrm{eV}$

Dissociation enthalpy of $\ce{H2}$: $\Delta H_\mathrm{diss}(\ce{H2}) = 432\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

Ideally, electrochemical water splitting into $\ce{O2}$ and $\ce{H2}$ runs at $1.23\,\mathrm{V}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Since $T\Delta S$ for this process is $> 0$, heat from the environment is needed. If additional voltage produces the heat required to compensate the decrease in temperature the process is called thermoneutral.

The enthalpy of $\ce{H2O(l)}$ formation at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\Delta H^\circ_{\ce{H2O}}$, is $-285\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

3.2 (4 pt) Calculate (a) the water splitting reaction entropy $\Delta S^\circ_\mathrm{R}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ of 1 mol of $\ce{H2O}$ and (b) the voltage at which water splitting is thermoneutral.

Catalysts

Cobalt-salen (salcomin) type complexes are potential catalysts for $\ce{H2}$ formation from protons and electrons. The structure of salcomin is given below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-3-fig1.png

Figure 1. The structure of salcomin.

3.3 (3 pt)

• Determine the oxidation state of the cobalt atom in salcomin.
• Determine the geometric structure around the cobalt center of salcomin, choosing from these three possibilities: tetrahedral, square planar or octahedral.

In solution, salcomin can bind $\ce{O2}$; that links two salcomin moieties by coordinating to the two Co centres. The oxidation state of both Co centres is then +III.

3.4 (2 pt) Draw the resulting structure.

The $\ce{H2}$ formation takes place exclusively at the cobalt center. The reaction is described by a 4-step catalytic cycle starting with $\ce{Co^{2+}}$ using 2 $\ce{H^+}$ and 2 electrons. During one step a hydride is formed by an intramolecular electron transfer.

3.5 (6 pt) Write down two possible variations of the catalytic cycle with charges of the complex and oxidations states of the Co center. The oxidation state on the Co center should not be larger than +III. Mark the hydride formation step with an asterisk and label $\ce{H^+}$ uptake with C (chemical reaction), and electron uptake with E (electrochemical reaction), see example cycle in Figure 2 below. $[\mathrm{Co^{II}}]$ stands for the Cobalt-salen complex.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-3-fig2.png

Figure 2. An example cycle for task 3.5.

Redox Potentials

3.6 (6 pt)

• Using the redox potential values of different cobalt complexes given in Table 1, write down which complex is suitable for a) water oxidation at neutral pH b) water reduction at neutral pH.
• Write down the corresponding overall reaction for both processes (only for the complexes, capable of performing it) and calculate the cell potentials at neutral pH.
• The half-cell potential for the proton reduction at pH = 7, $T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$ is $-0.41\,\mathrm{V}$.

$$\begin{array}{l|l} \text{Co(III/II) redox couple} & E^\circ\ \text{vs normal hydrogen electrode} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(H2O)6]}^{3+/2+} & +1.92\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(C2O4)3]}^{3-/4-} & +0.55\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(EDTA)]}^{1-/2-} & +0.38\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(NH3)6]}^{3+/2+} & +0.06\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(en)3]}^{3+/2+} & -0.18\,\mathrm{V} \\ \hline \ce{[Co(CN)5]}^{2-/3-} & -0.6\,\mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

Table 1. Possible redox couples for task 3.6. $\ce{[C2O4]^{2-}}$ = oxalate, en = 1,2-ethylendiamine.

A Glimpse at the Natural Process

The natural storage of biological $\ce{H2}$ equivalents is NADPH, which is produced from $\ce{NADP^+}$ through the addition of a hydride ion. The structure of NADPH is shown in Figure 3.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-3-fig3.png

Figure 3. The structure of NADPH.

3.7 (1 pt) Draw the structure of $\ce{NADP^+}$.

Chlorophyll has an extinction coefficient of about $\varepsilon = 8\cdot 10^4\,\mathrm{M^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at $680\,\mathrm{nm}$.

3.8 (4 pt) Assuming an efficiency (photon to hydrogen H atom) of $\phi = 20\%$ at $680\,\mathrm{nm}$ and at a photon flux of $100\,\mathrm{nE\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$ ($1\,\mathrm{E} = 1\,\mathrm{mol}$ of photons), calculate a) the number of photons per second and b) the concentration of chlorophyll in a 1x1x1 cm cell needed to get a turnover frequency of $1\,\mathrm{nmol}\ \ce{H2}$ per second.

problems.title: Fluorinated and Hypervalent Compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (34 points, 6% of the total). Fluorinated and Hypervalent Compounds

Introduction - Fluorine forms stable and isolable compounds with essentially all elements, including the noble gases Kr and Xe. Fluorine-containing molecules often feature uncommon structures. Thus, fluorine is frequently involved in the formation of compounds with elements of groups 14-18, which are defined as hypervalent. The synthesis of fluorinated organic compounds is nowadays heavily based on the availability of specifically designed reagents, compound $\mathbf{4}$ below being an example.

Hint: Any element E in the series $\mathbf{E^1}$-$\mathbf{E^8}$ may be represented more than once.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-4-fig1.png

I Molecular Geometry

4.1 (4.0 pt) Identify elements $\mathbf{E^1}$, $\mathbf{E^2}$, $\mathbf{E^3}$, and $\mathbf{E^4}$ in the three species $\mathbf{1}$, $[\mathbf{2}]^-$, and $[\mathbf{3}]^-$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-4-fig2.png

$\mathbf{1}$: neutral, non-zwitterionic molecule, $\mathbf{E^1}$, square pyramidal; $\mathbf{E^2}$, octahedral, av. $d(\mathrm{E^1{-}F}) = 1.91\,\text{Å}$; av. $d(\mathrm{E^2{-}F}) = 1.58\,\text{Å}$

$[\mathbf{2}]^-$: anion, square pyramidal, av. $d(\mathrm{E^3{-}F}) = 1.96\,\text{Å}$

$[\mathbf{3}]^-$: anion, pentagonal planar, av. $d(\mathrm{E^4{-}F}) = 1.98\,\text{Å}$

$$\begin{array}{l|l|l|l} 15 & 16 & 17 & 18 \\ \hline d(\text{P–F}),\ 1.50\text{-}1.68\,\text{Å} & d(\text{S–F})\ 1.52\text{-}1.60\,\text{Å} & d(\text{Cl–F}),\ 1.63\text{-}1.85\,\text{Å} & \\ \hline d(\text{As–F}),\ 1.68\text{-}1.72\,\text{Å} & d(\text{Se–F}),\ 1.75\text{-}1.80\,\text{Å} & d(\text{Br–F}),\ 1.77\text{-}1.97\,\text{Å} & d(\text{Kr–F}),\ 1.77\text{-}1.89\,\text{Å} \\ \hline d(\text{Sb–F}),\ 1.85\text{-}2.05\,\text{Å} & d(\text{Te–F}),\ 1.80\text{-}2.00\,\text{Å} & d(\text{I–F}),\ 1.90\text{-}2.00\,\text{Å} & d(\text{Xe–F}),\ 1.77\text{-}2.00\,\text{Å} \end{array}$$

Table 1. Typical E–F bond distance ranges for a selection of elements in Groups 15 - 18

Hints:

• The specified molecular geometries refer to the arrangement of atoms bonding to $\mathbf{E^1}$-$\mathbf{E^4}$
• The elemental analysis of $\mathbf{1}$ gives a carbon content of $17.75\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$

Assume that molecule $\mathbf{1}$ is a zwitterion, with single formal charges at both $\mathbf{E^1}$ and $\mathbf{E^2}$, thereby giving rise to the hypothetic molecules $\mathbf{1'}$ and $\mathbf{1''}$, shown below.

4.2 (4.0 pt) Choose which elements $\mathbf{E^5}$ / $\mathbf{E^6}$ and $\mathbf{E^7}$ / $\mathbf{E^8}$, respectively, would display the given molecular geometry, including E-F bond distances close to those in $\mathbf{1}$ (see table 1).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-4-fig3.png

II Reactivity and structure

Consider the reaction shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-4-fig4.png

4.3 (4.0 pt)

• Specify the ideal geometry of compound $\mathbf{6}$ in terms of the arrangement of the valence-shell electron-pair domains around the Te atom. Tick one of the following: square planar; trigonal bipyramidal; tetrahedral; square pyramidal; octahedral.
• Provide the expected ideal bond angles $\mathrm{C^1}$-Te-I, $\mathrm{C^2}$-Te-I, I-Te-O, and $\mathrm{C^1}$-Te-$\mathrm{C^2}$.

4.4 (2.0 pt) Write the number of $\ce{^1H}$-NMR signals you expect for the two methyl groups in compounds $\mathbf{4}$ and $\mathbf{6}$ respectively.

4.5 (6.0 pt) Compound $\mathbf{6}$ reacts consecutively with AgF and $\ce{(H3C)3SiCF3}$ (TMSCF$_3$). Formulate the Te-containing intermediate $\mathbf{A}$ and final product $\mathbf{B}$, including their correct geometry, as well as the byproducts $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$. Draw $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ and write the by-products $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$. Hint: MW of $\mathbf{D}$ is $92.08\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

Assume that compound $\mathbf{6}$ reacts with a sterically bulky, chiral, enantiomerically pure Lewis acid, such as the known boron derivative $\mathbf{8}$, as shown below. This reaction should lead to the formation of a new product $\mathbf{9}$ the composition of which corresponds to the sum of $\mathbf{6}$ and $\mathbf{8}$. Further assume that $\mathbf{9}$ is a salt, in which the cation derives from $\mathbf{6}$ and the anion from $\mathbf{8}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-4-fig5.png

III Synthesis of a $\lambda^3$-difluoroiodane and rotation around a single bond

problems.title: Hydrodesulfurization
problems.problem:
Problem 5 (34.5 points, 7% of the total). Hydrodesulfurization

The production of sulfur-free fuels is the general trend towards lowering the emission of sulfur-containing compounds that are toxic to the environment. To remove sulfur, the hydrogen-assisted hydrodesulfurization process is used at the refineries.

5.1 (2.5 pt) Draw the structure of products $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{E}$ of thiophene hydrodesulfurization, knowing that $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are cyclic regioisomers and $\mathbf{C}$ is cyclic.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-5-fig1.png

Figure 1. Thiophene hydrodesulfurization process.

Sulfur has two most common natural stable isotopes, $\ce{^{32}S}$ and $\ce{^{34}S}$, with a relative molar abundance of $\chi(\ce{^{32}S}) = 94.8\%$ and $\chi(\ce{^{34}S}) = 4.37\%$, respectively. For hydrogen, the stable natural isotopes are $\ce{^1H}$ and $\ce{^2H}$(D), with a relative molar abundance of $\chi(\ce{^1H}) = 99.986\%$ and $\chi(\ce{^2H}) = 0.014\%$, respectively.

5.2 (3 pt) Considering only the isotopes listed above, list all isotopologues of $\ce{H2S}$.

5.3 (3.5 pt) Considering only the isotopes listed above, list all isotopologue of $\ce{H2S}$ containing simultaneously D and $\ce{^{34}S}$ nuclei and for each calculate the respective relative molar abundance in %.

The desulfurization is a catalytic process typically carried out over $\ce{MoS2}$ supported on $\ce{SiO2}$ ($\ce{MoS2}/\ce{SiO2}$) catalyst. To study the surface of the catalyst, isotope exchange methods can be employed. The isotope exchange reaction takes place at the gas-solid interface, resulting in the exchange of the surface atoms exclusively. In a first approximation, the bulk atoms do not participate in the exchange (Figure 2).

In the experiment, the isotope exchange between the $\ce{MoS2}/\ce{SiO2}$ catalyst (Mo mass fraction $w_\mathrm{Mo} = 4.280\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$, initially containing only $\ce{^{32}S}$) and gaseous isotopically-labeled $\ce{H2^{34}S}$ was studied in a flow reactor (Figure 2). The $\ce{MoS2}/\ce{SiO2}$ catalyst ($m_\mathrm{cat} = 1.2350\,\mathrm{g}$) was kept in a flow ($\mathrm{p} = 1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$, $v = 20.0\,\mathrm{mL\,min^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{T} = 23.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) of gas mixture containing $\ce{H2^{34}S}$ balanced with Ar (volume fraction $\phi_{\ce{H2^{34}S}} = 1.00\,\mathrm{vol.\%}$ $\ce{H2^{34}S}$, $\ce{^{34}S}$ isotopic purity $\alpha = 99.95\,mol.\%$).

The experiment duration was $t = 10.0\,\mathrm{min}$ and gas from the outlet was collected during the entire experiment. The measured fraction of $\ce{^{34}S}$ isotope among the sulfur atoms ($\gamma$) in the collected gas phase was $\gamma = 87.3\,\mathrm{mol.\%}$. Assume ideal gas behavior, and that the elemental (not isotopic!) composition of $\ce{MoS2}$ on the surface and in the bulk are identical, and by the end of the experiment all sulfur atoms from the surface are exchanged with the gas phase.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-5-fig2.png

Figure 2. Schematic representation of the experiment in the course ($\mathbf{A}$) and at the final stage ($\mathbf{B}$). Sulfur atoms on the surface are shown in red, sulfur atoms in the bulk are shown in blue. Molybdenum atoms are not shown.

5.4 (5 pt) Calculate the number of exchanged sulfur atoms $n(S)_\mathrm{surface}$, give your answer in mol.

If you have been unable to calculate the number of total exchanged sulfur atoms, use the value $1.53\cdot 10^{-5}\,mol$ in all the following calculations.

Assume that the $\ce{MoS2}$ phase consists of uniform spherical particles, and at the end of the experiment all sulfur atoms located on the surface are exchanged, while the bulk atoms did not participate in the exchange reaction. The density $\rho$ of $\ce{MoS2}$ is $\rho = 5.06\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, the average area occupied by S and Mo atoms on the surface is equal to $A_\mathrm{S} = 3.00\cdot 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and $A_\mathrm{Mo} = 5.00\cdot 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m^2}$, respectively. The area of a sphere with radius $R$ can be calculated as $S = 4\pi R^2$, and its volume as $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$. Assume that isotopic composition does not affect the density of $\ce{MoS2}$.

5.5 (8 pt) Calculate the particle radius $R$ of the $\ce{MoS2}$ particles, give your answer in nm.

In reality, the isotopically-labeled atoms from the surface diffuse into the bulk and the non-labeled atoms from the bulk travel to the surface, undergoing a gradual exchange (Figure 3A). Therefore, for a given moment, the fraction of the labeled atoms inside the particle decreases from the surface of the particle to its center. Simultaneously, with an increase in time of exchange, the involvement of bulk atoms to the exchange reaction increases, as sketched in Figure 3B.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-5-fig3.png

Figure 3. $\mathbf{A}$) Schematic representation of the diffusion of sulfur isotopes from the surface to the bulk in $\ce{MoS2}$ particle. Sulfur atoms on the surface are shown in red, sulfur atoms in the bulk are shown in blue. Molybdenum atoms are not shown. $\mathbf{B}$) The fraction of $\ce{^{34}S}$ atoms in the bulk as function of time and distance from center of the particle. $r_\mathrm{edge}$ corresponds to the radius of $\ce{MoS2}$ particle.

At the end of the experiment, the surface atoms are completely exchanged, and additionally a fraction of the bulk is exchanged due to the diffusion. The fraction $F$ of the exchanged bulk atoms ($n(S)^{ex}_{bulk}$) and the total bulk atoms of sulfur ($n(S)^{total}_{bulk}$) can be calculated as follows: $F = n(S)^{ex}_{bulk}/n(S)^{total}_{bulk} = 1 - e^{-\frac{D\cdot t}{R^2}}$, where $t$ is the time of exchange experiment (described above), $R$ is the particle size (radius for a spherical shape particle) and $D$ is the diffusion coefficient. The catalyst described above was independently studied by means of electron microscopy, which showed that the $\ce{MoS2}$ particles are uniformly distributed spheres with a radius of $35.0\,\mathrm{nm}$.

5.6 (12.5 pt) Using $R = 35.0\,\mathrm{nm}$ as the radius and the data of the exchange experiment described above, calculate the diffusion coefficient $D$ for the diffusion of sulfur atoms in $\ce{MoS2}$, give your answer in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$. In your calculations, use the following approximation: $e^x \approx 1 + x$ for $x \ll 1$.

problems.title: Direct conversion of methane to methanol
problems.problem:
Problem 6 (32 points, 7% of the total). Direct conversion of methane to methanol

Methane is widely available as natural gas making it an attractive feedstock for the chemical industry, such as for the production of methanol. However, control of this process is challenging as methanol is more easily oxidized than methane.

Overoxidation is avoided in a chemical looping process, where active sites of copper-exchanged zeolite catalysts provide only the single oxygen atom required for oxidation to methanol and are consumed. In a second step, the catalyst is regenerated with oxygen in the absence of methane. The scheme below shows two potential catalytic copper sites.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-6-fig1.png

During the reaction, $\mathrm{Cu^{II}}$ is reduced to $\mathrm{Cu^{I}}$.

6.1 (2 pt) Give the number of $\mathbf{S1}$ sites and the number of $\mathbf{S2}$ sites required to oxidize one methane molecule to methanol.

In the absence of oxygen, the formed methanol does not desorb from zeolite. If the reaction is performed in a container with constant volume and temperature (an autoclave), a pressure drop results only from the consumption of methane, which can be considered as an ideal gas. In a $1\,\mathrm{L}$ autoclave containing $200\,\mathrm{mg}$ of zeolite loaded with $4.3\,\mathrm{wt.\%}$ copper, the initial methane pressure $p_0 = 933\,\mathrm{Pa}$ dropped to $p_\infty = 925\,\mathrm{Pa}$ after completion of the reaction at $528\,\mathrm{K}$.

6.2 (4 pt) Compute the percentage of copper that reacted.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-6-fig2.png

Figure 1: Semi-logarithmic graph of normalized methane pressure $p$ versus time for the reaction with copper-loaded zeolite containing sites $\mathbf{S1}$ and $\mathbf{S2}$ in an autoclave at various temperatures. The symbols denote experimental data points. The solid lines are linear fits to appropriate time ranges. The dotted lines are guides to the eyes.

6.3 (1 pt) Experimental data is plotted in Figure 1. Based on this, decide on the (pseudo) order of the oxidation of $\ce{CH4}$. Tick the box with the correct statement:

• The reaction is of (pseudo) zeroth order.
• The reaction is of (pseudo) first order.
• The reaction is of (pseudo) second order.

6.4 (2 pt) Write down the (pseudo) rate law for the oxidation of $\ce{CH4}$ that is consistent with the experimental data under the given conditions. Note that it may depend on the concentrations of $\ce{CH4}$ as well as of sites $\mathbf{S1}$ and $\mathbf{S2}$ and on the rate constants.

6.5 (4 pt) Tick the boxes with correct statements:

• At least two types of copper sites react, each with a different rate constant.
• The overall methane oxidation by copper-loaded zeolite is faster at higher temperature.
• At higher temperature, a larger fraction of the copper sites will have reacted with methane after completion of the reaction.
• One of the reactions becomes slower at higher temperature.

Paramagnetic sites $\mathbf{S1}$ can be observed by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, whereas diamagnetic sites $\mathbf{S2}$ do not give an EPR signal. EPR spectroscopy measures the number of electron spins. Thus, the number of $\mathbf{S1}$ sites is proportional to the double integral $I_2$ of the EPR spectrum, i.e. $[\mathbf{S1}] \propto I_2$. Spectra were measured at different temperatures $T$ and at each temperature at different times $t$ after initiating the reaction.

6.6 (3 pt) Derive the equation linear in time that relates $I_2(t)$ to the rate constant for the loss of $\mathbf{S1}$ sites.

6.7 (3 pt) Tick the boxes for each measurement that needs to be calibrated with a known Cu(II) standard:

• Total number of paramagnetic Cu(II) sites in the sample
• Concentration of paramagnetic Cu(II) sites in the sample
• Rate constant
• Types of different paramagnetic Cu(II) species in the sample

From EPR measurements, it is known that the rate constant for the reaction with $\mathbf{S1}$ sites at $528\,\mathrm{K}$ is $2.604\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

6.8 (3 pt) Considering Figure 1 and based on a calculation, decide if methane reacts faster or slower with $\mathbf{S2}$ sites than with $\mathbf{S1}$ sites:

problems.title: Enzyme Kinetics
problems.problem:
Problem 7 (34 points, 7% of the total). Enzyme Kinetics

The Michaelis–Menten (MM) mechanism was introduced in 1913 to describe the kinetics of enzyme catalysis. In this mechanism, enzyme $\mathbf{E}$ catalyzes the conversion of substrate $\mathbf{S}$ to the product $\mathbf{P}$:

$$\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{S} \underset{k_2}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftarrows}} \mathbf{ES} \overset{k_3}{\rightarrow} \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{P}$$

The initial rate for an enzymatic reaction following the MM mechanism is usually given as:

$$v_0 = \frac{v_\mathrm{max}[\mathbf{S}]_0}{[\mathbf{S}]_0 + K_M} \qquad (1)$$

when the initial concentration of $\mathbf{E}$ is much lower than the initial concentration of $\mathbf{S}$ ($[\mathbf{E}]_0 \ll [\mathbf{S}]_0$). The Michaelis constant is defined as $K_M = \frac{k_2 + k_3}{k_1}$. The initial rate can also be expressed as the product of the relative flow $j$ and $[\mathbf{E}]_0$:

$$v_0 = j[\mathbf{E}]_0 \qquad (2)$$

Note: Questions 7.1 and 7.2 can have one, multiple, or no correct answer(s).

7.1 (3 pt) Choose the correct alternative form(s) of the initial rate ($v_0$) expressions (1) and (2). $[\mathbf{ES}]_\mathrm{max}$ is the maximum concentration of the $\mathbf{ES}$ complex.

• $v_0 = \dfrac{k_3[\mathbf{E}]_0[\mathbf{S}]_0}{[\mathbf{S}]_0 + K_M}$
• $v_0 = \dfrac{k_3[\mathbf{E}]}{1 + K_M/[\mathbf{S}]_0}$
• $v_0 = j[\mathbf{ES}]_\mathrm{max}$
• $v_0 = \dfrac{k_3[\mathbf{E}]_0[\mathbf{ES}]_\mathrm{max}}{[\mathbf{S}]_0 + K_M}$
• $v_0 = \dfrac{k_3[\mathbf{E}]_0}{1 + K_M/[\mathbf{S}]_0}$
• $v_0 = \dfrac{j[\mathbf{E}]_0}{K_M + [\mathbf{S}]_0}$

7.2 (4 pt) Choose the pair(s) of axes ($y$ vs. $x$) that are expected to give a linear plot:

• $v_0$ vs. $1/[\mathbf{S}]_0$
• $v_0$ vs. $v_0/K_M$
• $v_0$ vs. $K_M/v_0$
• $1/v_0$ vs. $v_0/[\mathbf{S}]_0$
• $1/v_0$ vs. $v_0/K_M$
• $[\mathbf{S}]_0/v_0$ vs. $[\mathbf{S}]_0$

Many enzymes catalyze multi- rather than single-substrate transformations. However, if the concentration of one of the substrates is much higher than that of the other substrate or it is kept constant, the MM kinetics is also valid. Here we will look at two independent enzymatic systems that follow the MM kinetics.

Enzymatic System I

Enzyme $\mathbf{E}$ converts substrates $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ to products $\mathbf{P_A}$ and $\mathbf{P_B}$. At rapid pre-equilibrium between the free enzyme and all enzyme-substrate complexes, the following $v_0$ equation applies:

$$v_0 = \frac{k[\mathbf{E}]_0[\mathbf{A}]_0[\mathbf{B}]_0}{(K + [\mathbf{A}]_0)(K + [\mathbf{B}]_0)} \qquad (3)$$

$k$ is the rate constant of one of the reactions. The same equilibrium constant $K$ characterizes the dissociation of either substrate from the corresponding active site of $\mathbf{E}$.

7.3 (2 pt) Show that equation (3) takes the MM form (1) if the concentration of substrate $\mathbf{B}$ is maintained at a constant value $c_0$. Give the expression for $v_\mathrm{max}$ in this case.

7.4 (8 pt) Propose a kinetic scheme for the Enzymatic System I consistent with equation (3), showing all the intermediates and products. Indicate the reaction with a rate constant $k$.

Enzymatic System II

Enzyme $\mathbf{E}$ has five active sites, each of which is specific to one of the substrates $\mathbf{S_A}$, $\mathbf{S_B}$, or $\mathbf{S_C}$ that are selectively transformed to products $\mathbf{P_A}$, $\mathbf{P_B}$, or $\mathbf{P_C}$, respectively. There is at least one active site for each substrate. Each active site is independent of the others.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-7-fig1.png

For $\mathbf{E}$, it is known that:

1. The affinity for $\mathbf{S_C}$ is higher than for $\mathbf{S_B}$.

2. The plot of $v_{0i}$ vs $v_{0i}/[\mathbf{S}_i]_0$, known as Eadie–Hofstee plot, for $\mathbf{S_A}$, $\mathbf{S_B}$, $\mathbf{S_C}$, with rate given per active site ($v_{0i}$), is shown below, but the scale and the legend are omitted.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icho-2023-7-fig2.png

3. When $\mathbf{E}$ is saturated with $\mathbf{S_A}$, $\mathbf{S_B}$, $\mathbf{S_C}$, the catalytic turnover number (TON) for $\mathbf{S_C}$ per site is $10200\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$, and $2023$ $\mathbf{P_A}$, $\mathbf{P_B}$, $\mathbf{P_C}$, product molecules in total are synthesized per second. At the same time, no more than $5.94\cdot 10^6$ molecules of $\mathbf{P_A}$ and $\mathbf{P_B}$ are detected to form per hour.

4. At equimolar concentrations of $\mathbf{S_A}$, $\mathbf{S_B}$, $\mathbf{S_C}$, which are at least $1000$ times lower than corresponding $K_M$ values, the $\mathbf{P_A}$, $\mathbf{P_B}$, $\mathbf{P_C}$, concentrations become proportional to the catalytic efficiency ($\varepsilon_i = \frac{k_{i3}}{K_{M,i}}$), and their ratio is $3:2:5$, respectively.

5. Two $\mathbf{ES}_i$ complexes have equal rate constants for dissociation to $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{S}_i$. The activation barrier for the reaction of $\mathbf{ES_C}$ into the initial compounds is $1266\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ higher than for the reaction into the final products. Assume that the pre-exponential factors are equal for both reactions and $T = 25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

6. For $\mathbf{E}$ + $\mathbf{S}_i$ reaction: $k_{c1} = 1.57\cdot 10^7\,\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}}$ and $k_{a1} = k_{b1}$.

7.5 (17 pt) Fill in the following table and provide your calculations.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \text{Number of active sites} & k_1 & k_2 & k_3 & K_M \\ \hline \mathbf{S_A} & & & & & \\ \hline \mathbf{S_B} & & & & & \\ \hline \mathbf{S_C} & & 1.57\cdot 10^7\,\mathrm{M^{-1}s^{-1}} & & & \end{array}$$

Hints:

• Use information from 1. and 2. to find the relation between $K_{M,A}$, $K_{M,B}$ and $K_{M,C}$ ($<, >, =$).
• Information from 3. and 5. allows you to complete the first column (number of active sites for each substrate) and the last row (all the constants for substrate $\mathbf{S_C}$) of the table. Check that the sum of active sites is equal to 5.

Problem 1 (24 points, 7.5% of the total). Ammonia

The Haber–Bosch process to produce ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is one of the most impactful industrial processes in history and estimated to sustain around half of today’s population. The process typically occurs at constant temperature and pressure, $400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $100\,\mathrm{bar}$, respectively. Equilibrium between the reactants and the product is established over Fe-based catalysts in the reactor.

The standard gas phase thermochemistry data of $\ce{N2}$, $\ce{H2}$, and $\ce{NH3}$ are shown below. Assume the enthalpy and entropy of the reaction are temperature independent.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} & \ce{N2(g)} & \ce{H2(g)} & \ce{NH3(g)} \\ \hline \Delta_f H^\circ/(\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) & 0 & 0 & -45.9 \\ \hline S^\circ/(\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}) & 191.6 & 130.7 & 192.8 \end{array}$$

1.1 (7 pt) Find the molar nitrogen conversion (in percent) to ammonia under the production conditions from a stoichiometric mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen. Show your calculations for partial credit. If you cannot find a result, use 66% in subsequent calculations.

One of the reactants in the Haber–Bosch process is hydrogen, mainly produced by steam reforming of methane. The two-step process starts with $\ce{CH4}$ reacting with water to produce $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{CO}$. In a subsequent step, $\ce{CO}$ reacts with water to form $\ce{CO2}$ and additional hydrogen.

1.2 (2 pt) Write the overall reaction equation for the combined process. Give the mass of $\ce{CO2}$ produced in the reaction per $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of $\ce{H2}$ ($m_{\ce{CO2}}$).

In reality, $7.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of carbon dioxide is produced for each $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ of hydrogen in steam reforming. The generated ammonia is classified based on $\ce{CO2}$ management. For "gray" ammonia, the $\ce{CO2}$ is released in the atmosphere; for "blue" ammonia, it is captured and stored. "Green" ammonia is made from hydrogen produced without carbon emissions.

1.3 (3 pt) Calculate the mass of the carbon dioxide ($m_{\ce{CO2},\,\text{blue}}$) that needs to be captured to produce 40,000 kg of “blue” ammonia. Assume that carbon dioxide only comes from a real steam reforming process. Assume further that the ammonia is produced at equilibrium from a stoichiometric mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen.

Using cheap renewable hydrogen, the prospect of converting it with captured $\ce{CO2}$ into methanol appears promising. However, in this procedure, there is a competing reaction that produces $\ce{CO}$:

$$\ce{CO2(g) + 3 H2(g) <=> CH3OH(g) + H2O(g)}$$

$$\ce{CO2(g) + H2(g) <=> CO(g) + H2O(g)}$$

Into a reactor maintained at $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $50\,\mathrm{bar}$, a mixture containing $\ce{CO2}:\ce{H2}$ in a molar ratio of $1:4$ is fed. It has been found that the $\ce{CO2}$ conversion is 30% and the $\ce{H2}$ conversion is 18.5% when these two reactions are at equilibrium. No other processes need to be considered.

1.4 (5 pt) Calculate the thermodynamic equilibrium constants (at $250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) of the two reactions.

Heterogeneous copper-containing catalysts are commonly used for $\ce{CO2}$ hydrogenation. Two specific, Cu-containing catalysts ($A$ and $B$) showed promise for converting $\ce{CO2}$ to methanol. These catalysts differ not only in their catalytic rates, but also in surface area, Cu content, and Cu dispersion (the ratio of surface Cu to the total Cu in the catalyst).

Cu dispersion is important, because only Cu species at the surface are active in $\ce{CO2}$ hydrogenation. Under this assumption, 1 mole of active sites corresponds to 1 mole of surface Cu. The efficiency of these active sites is shown by their turnover frequencies ($TOF$, moles of product formed per moles of active site in a given time).

The table below reports the performance (reported as mass of produced methanol per total catalyst mass in a given time) and the specific surface areas of the two catalysts. The Cu content and dispersion of the catalysts was also measured and reported as follows:

1. At the start, all the copper in the catalysts (oxidized beforehand) is present as Cu(II); that was fully reduced to Cu(0) with hydrogen. No other species in the catalysts reacted with hydrogen besides copper oxides.
2. $\ce{N2O}$ was introduced to the reduced samples at room temperature. At this temperature, $\ce{N2O}$ only oxidizes active surface sites to Cu(I).
3. The Cu(I) active surface sites were reduced again to Cu(0) with hydrogen.
